#294. Timing of Climate Science Reports Ignites a Hot Fight at U.N. Talks

Several countries that rely heavily on fossil fuels want to delay the next round of scientific assessments that governments use to inform their climate policies.

A squabble over the publication timetable for several climate reports has turned into one of the burning issues of this year’s United Nations climate conference, as some warn that fossil fuel interests might be interfering with the world’s pre-eminent climate science organization.

The U.N.-backed Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change produces landmark reports that generally come out every five to seven years. The next round of reports would take on topics like physical changes to the earth and greenhouse gas emissions.

Timing is critical because in 2028 nations are supposed to assess their progress and then ramp up their efforts to do more, based on the best science. That process, known as a stocktake and occurring every five years, is the engine of the Paris Agreement.

Saudi Arabia, India and Russia are among those pushing to delay the reports so that at least two of them come out after 2028.

The fact that those nations rank among the largest fossil fuel exporters or importers has led to accusations that coal, oil and gas interests might be interfering with science.

“Saudi Arabia is trying to destroy the I.P.C.C. in order to prevent the next global stocktake from using the accurate scientific data on fossil fuels,” said former Vice President Al Gore, who is in Turkey for the talks.

#292. Mercedes' clever new driving assist handles complex traffic like a champ

The point-to-point driver assist is coming to the US and Germany in 2027.

SAN FRANCISCO—When Ars first drove the new Mercedes-Benz CLA last year, the automaker also gave us a sneak preview of its next driver assist. Called Drive Assist Pro, it’s for collaborative partially assisted driving, and from the passenger seat at the time, the demo was impressive. Now the automaker is getting ready to start rolling out Drive Assist Pro to customers with cars running the new MB.OS operating system here in the US and in Germany, and it let us have some time behind the wheel.

While most automakers want a reputation for safety, Mercedes has long used passive and active technology to do so in its products. It was one of the first OEMs to introduce airbags, and a decade later started adding active safety systems like anti-lock brakes, electronic stability control, and adaptive cruise control. And so, by giving the car’s electronics the ability to control the brakes and throttle, we arrive at the first level of assisted driving—called “level 1” in automotive engineer-speak.

“Level 2” assisted driving, where the car also controls the steering as well as the acceleration and braking, got famous with Tesla Autopilot. But the first lane-keeping assists predate it by almost a decade in passenger cars, when Toyota introduced a system in 2004. The human driver behind the wheel is still in charge, responsible for situational awareness (and anything that arises from a lack thereof), with the idea that long drives become less tiring and a little more effortless when the car does the boring job of keeping a constant speed or a constant distance to the car ahead and between the white lines.

The next step, numerically at least, should be level 3, where we move from assisted driving to partially automated driving; here the car takes over the task of driving fully under some circumstances, like heavy traffic. But that’s getting ahead of ourselves—the main developments over the past few years have been the inelegantly named “L2+” systems that combine more advanced driver monitoring with a higher degree of assistance, usually on geofenced highways.

General Motors’ Super Cruise was the first of these, allowing hands-free operation as long as the car can tell the driver has their eyes on the road. Now many automakers offer something similar: Ford has BlueCruise, BMW has Highway Assistant, and Mercedes is about to add a hands-free highway assist next spring to its MB. Drive Assist system, which will be standard on the 2027 S-Class and AMG GT 4-Door Coupe and an option on the 2027 CLA, GLB, C-Class, GLC, and GLE.

I tested that system while in San Francisco in a 2027 S-Class, and it’s competent within its operational design domain. The user interface is a little more subtle than Super Cruise’s big green LED in the steering wheel; instead, the icon on the dash changes, with the hands on the steering wheel going from green to gray when it’s safe to remove them. Like other systems, MB. Drive Assist has been programmed to make automatic lane changes if the car decides that’s quicker—these can be canceled with the turn signal or simply by resisting the car steering into the next lane.

MB. Drive Assist Pro takes that idea and brings it to lower speeds and much more complex traffic situations—“level 2++” (we really need to stop letting engineers name things). Instead of hands on the green steering wheel icon, there’s a large green arrowhead, showing you’re in point-to-point mode—compared to the various configurations of the highway assist, I found this much less likely to engender mode confusion. (Did the green hands mean I could take my hands on or off the wheel? On, but see what I mean?)

The driving behavior was about exactly as cautious as I would want on surface streets. The electric GLC was as smooth accelerating and braking as the entirely autonomous Waymo robotaxi I rode in the day before, and the car’s electronic brain was able to safely pass double-parked cars—waiting patiently for an oncoming bus first—and stopped for stop signs, red lights, and pedestrians on crosswalks (while making a left turn at the time). The system is collaborative—steering or accelerating won’t end the automation, but unlike BMW’s new iX5, any use of the brake will turn it off.

Some customers in Germany and California will be part of an early access program for Drive Assist Pro from next month, with a wider rollout in the first half of 2027 for model year 2026 CLAs, as well as the model year 2027 CLA, GLC Electric, GLE, GLS, and S-Class, and more coming in model year 2028. (The system is already live in China.)

The unifying factor is the MB.OS, the automaker’s latest operating system. Like other automakers, Mercedes has embraced the software-defined vehicle paradigm, replacing dozens or even hundreds of discrete ECUs with a handful of powerful domain controller computers that oversee vehicle dynamics, occupant comfort, infotainment, and automation.

Drive Assist Pro combines 10 cameras, five radars, and 12 ultrasonic sensors, all stitched together by a domain controller that uses Nvidia’s Orin processors. I’m told that in China, cars are now advertised with processor and RAM specs rather than boring information like range or performance: In that spirit, Mercedes says it can deliver 254 tera operations per second, uses a 2.5 Gbit Ethernet network, and has more than 70GB of RAM.

The driving decisions are made by Nvidia’s Alpamayo end-to-end tokenized stack that picks your driving trajectory, with a rules-based system running alongside as a safety check. That’s reassuring, as is the knowledge that Nvidia’s stack has been certified by Germany’s TÜV, which takes a less lackadaisical approach to safety than the current incarnation of the US Department of Transportation.

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#289. The charging mistakes that could ruin your Nintendo Switch's battery

Don't let bad charging habits turn your battery from Super to Super Smashed.

As great as handheld consoles can be, from the familiar-feeling Switch 2 to the Steam Deck OLED that still holds up against other PC handhelds, their batteries really are their Achilles' heel. There's only so much playtime you can squeeze out of any portable device, and the more powerful the console, the shorter that tends to be. Moreover, most recent handhelds aren't designed for quick battery replacement. It's doable — Nintendo even provides instructions — but it's not like slapping a few AAs into a flashlight.

On a long enough timeline, all Switch batteries are bound to degrade until your console is only usable when docked. It's just a fact of lithium-ion technology. But if you're careful about how you charge, you can prolong this fate. If you're lucky, you might push things off until Nintendo's next-gen console arrives, whether that's the Switch 3 or another innovation.

Mostly, this is a matter of how often you charge your Switch, and to what percentage. There are some additional factors to consider, though, and we'll touch on those so you can put the free Mario Kart 8 Deluxe Switch 2 update through its paces.

Never let your Switch drain to zero. Lithium-ion batteries have a finite number of charge cycles, and letting the battery die burns through them faster. Granted, the number of cycles is going to be well into the hundreds for any device, even beyond the 800 mark in the case of the Switch 1. But as you progress towards the end of that limit, your battery is going to offer diminished capacity. Nintendo also warns that you should charge once every six months, if you're not actively using it, to avoid permanently losing the ability to charge.

You should also avoid charging to 100% unless you need as many hours as you can get. That's because the optimal charge for lithium-ion batteries is both more than zero and less than full. On most devices, the rule of thumb is between 20% and 80%. On the Switch 2, though, Nintendo has added a Stop Charging Around 90% option, which you can find under System Settings. Just remember to toggle this off and wait a few minutes longer when you're heading out on a trip to maximize your time.

Another important factor is ambient temperature. Realistically, you may be unlikely to store or use a Switch beyond its official operating range, which is 41 to 95 Fahrenheit (5 to 35 Celsius). Charging in extreme heat can, however, accelerate capacity loss, so you might want to avoid leaving your console in sunlight for prolonged stretches, or charging outside in climates with intense summer heat. Notably, while extreme cold can have an impact, it shouldn't be permanent.

A Switch is a complex device with delicate electronics, and the battery is embedded inside, rather than in an easily accessible compartment. Making a mistake could break something critical. In fact, Nintendo strongly urges contacting its Customer Service department instead of doing things yourself, and there's no official DIY guide for any Switch 1 model.

While there is an official guide for the Switch 2, Nintendo notes that only consoles with the BEE-001(-01) marking contain user-replaceable batteries, as far as the company is concerned. On top of that, you need Nintendo's BEE-003(-01) Battery Replacement Kit, a careful touch, and an electrically grounded surface. A large enough static shock could fry circuitry.

The good news here is that if you charge your Switch properly, the odds of it surviving until your next upgrade without a battery swap are pretty good. It's more a question of whether anyone you pass it along to will enjoy the same luxury.

#286. Musk's Twitter promised a purge of blue check marks. Instead he singled out the New York Times

Some VIP Twitter users woke up on Saturday expecting to have lost their coveted blue verification check marks in a previously announced purge by Elon Musk. Instead, Twitter appeared to target a single account from a major publication Musk dislikes and changed the language on its site in a way that obscures why users are verified.

Twitter had said it would “begin winding down” blue checks granted under its old verification system — which emphasized protecting high-profile users at risk of impersonation — on April 1. In order to stay verified, Musk said, users would have to pay $8 per month to join the platform’s Twitter Blue subscription service, which has allowed accounts to pay for verification since December.

But one high-profile account did lose its blue check over the weekend: the main account for the New York Times, which had previously told CNN it would not pay for verification.

William Shatner is mad he may have to pay to keep his blue Twitter checkmark. Elon Musk says too bad

After an account that often engages with Musk posted a meme this weekend about the Times declining to pay for verification, Musk responded in a tweet saying, “Oh ok, we’ll take it off then.” Musk then lashed out at the Times — just the latest instance of the billionaire slamming journalists or media outlets — in a series of tweets that claimed the outlet’s coverage is boring and “propaganda.”

The weekend moves are just the latest example of Twitter creating confusion and whiplash for users over feature changes — and in this case, not just any users, but many of the most high-profile accounts that have long been a key selling point for the platform. It also highlights how Musk often appears to guide decisions about the platform more by whims than by policy.

Although the New York Times’ main account lost its blue check, its other accounts, such as those for its arts, travel and books content, remained verified. (It’s not clear why the New York Times doesn’t have a gold “organizations” check mark, like accounts for other news outlets, including the Associated Press and the Washington Post.) After its blue check was removed, a spokesperson for the New York Times reiterated to CNN that it does not plan to pay for verification.

Twitter, which laid off most of its public relations staff last fall, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a separate puzzling move, Twitter’s blue bird logo at the top of the site was replaced on Monday with doge, the meme representing the cryptocurrency dogecoin, which Musk has promoted. The price of dogecoin shot up 20% on Monday.

Musk has been threatening to take away “legacy” blue check marks from users verified under Twitter’s old system since shortly after he bought Twitter last fall.

In early November, Twitter launched the option for people paying for its Twitter Blue subscription service to receive blue checks. The program was quickly put on pause after being plagued by a wave of celebrity and corporate impersonators, and was relaunched in December.

Twitter also rolled out a color-coded verification system with differently colored marks for companies and government entities, but Musk continued to say that individual users would eventually have to pay for blue checks.

In the days leading up to the blue check purge that wasn’t, prominent users such as actor William Shatner and anti-bullying activist Monica Lewinksy pushed back against the idea that, as power users that draw attention to the site, they should have to pay for a feature that keeps them safe from impersonation.

By muddying the reason accounts are verified, the new label could risk making it easier for people to scam or impersonate high-profile users. Experts in inauthentic behavior have also said it’s not clear that reserving verification for paid users will reduce the number of bots on the site, an issue Musk has raised on and off over the past year.

Musk, for his part, has previously presented changes to Twitter’s verification system as a way of “treating everyone equally.”

“There shouldn’t be a different standard for celebrities,” he said in a tweet last week. The paid feature could also drive revenue, which could help Musk, who is on the hook for significant debt after buying Twitter for $44 billion.

Musk last week also said that starting on April 15, only verified accounts would be recommended in users’ “For You” feeds alongside the accounts they follow.

–CNN’s Oliver Darcy contributed to this report.

#285. How to put your iPad in recovery mode (with and without a home button)

A failed update or a forgotten passcode doesn't have to mean the end of your iPad.

Many iPad problems can be fixed with a simple restart, but sometimes that's not enough. Severe issues with the tablet's software can make it completely inoperable, and in these cases, putting the iPad in recovery mode might be your only option.

Recovery mode also lets you connect your iPad to your computer to update it, or in the worst-case scenario, restore it to its factory default settings. It's best to save recovery mode for when nothing else works, but when it's needed, it can mean the difference between a bricked iPad and one that works just like new.

There are a few situations when you might want to use recovery mode. Major software updates can sometimes fail, leaving you with a partially installed update that keeps your iPad from turning on. Your iPad might reboot itself continuously, or you might enter the wrong passcode too many times and get locked out. Your computer might also stop recognizing your iPad, or your iPad might show a screen prompting you to connect it to a computer.

To put your iPad in recovery mode, first connect it to your computer with a USB cable, and open Finder on Mac or the Apple Devices app on PC. From here, the process differs based on whether your iPad has a home button or not. If it does, hold the home and the power button down at the same time. Eventually, your iPad screen will go black and then show the Apple logo. Finally, it will show the recovery mode icon: an image of a USB cable connecting to a computer. Now release the buttons.

Newer iPads, like the iPad Pro, don't have a home button, so you need to use the power and volume buttons instead. First press and release the volume up button and then the volume down button. Next, press and hold the power button, and keep holding it through the Apple logo until the recovery mode icon appears. Then let go.

At this point, you can use the Finder or Apple Devices on your computer to find your iPad. If the process worked, you should see a pop-up explaining that the iPad needs to be restored or updated. It's best to start with the update option, which will allow your computer to reinstall iPadOS without affecting anything else stored on your device.

If this option is successful, you'll be able to use your iPad again without losing any data. If it doesn't work, though, you'll have to put it back in recovery mode and choose the restore option. This will restore the iPad to its factory settings, completely erasing your data in the process.

You can restore everything from your most recent backup (if you have enough iCloud storage), but it's a far more disruptive process that should only be used as a last resort. If your iPad still isn't working after trying both options or you can't get it to enter recovery mode, it may be time to get it professionally repaired or shop for a new iPad.

#283. ‘Get Focused on London’: How Iran’s Agents Attacked European Targets

A wave of assaults in Britain and elsewhere in the spring sowed fear across Europe. Prosecutors shed new light on how Iran took aim at U.S. allies.

As the U.S.-Israel war in Iran raged earlier this year, a man linked to Iranian criminal networks perched in front of a computer, on a video call with a teenager in London. The man wanted to make sure the teen, who was moments away from setting fire to a synagogue, carried out his plans.

“Light it up like a Christmas tree,” the man, an Iraqi named Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, urged the 17-year-old, according to U.S. prosecutors. The teen climbed over a wall and tossed a bomb through a broken window. “J’s mic is muted,” read the text on Mr. al-Hassani’s computer screen.

The synagogue arson in April was a small, violent part of Iran’s efforts to force an end to the bombing campaign that was pummeling the country, according to American investigators.

The attack was described in a federal indictment filed in New York this week. It revealed extensive new details about a wave of violence against Jewish institutions in Europe and U.S. targets, including a British air base used by American bombers. Prosecutors hold Iran’s agents responsible for the assaults.

Within days of the war starting, Mr. al-Hassani and at least two associates, including an operative for Iran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, began plotting the attacks in Europe, prosecutors said. The men talked about procuring drones and missiles from contacts in Iran. They pored over a map of London, with one saying they should “get focused” on targeting the British capital. Soon after, attacks hit temples and other Jewish sites in London.

In the fight against much stronger conventional forces, Iran has found ways to impose costs on its adversaries without inviting a full military response. One major aspect of Iran’s strategy is its embrace of small-time criminals to conduct low-cost assaults against vulnerable targets that are part of everyday life.

#282. Whether it's Black Friday or a CEO scandal, NVIDIA GPUs just don't get deep discounts

If you're hoping for a cheap RTX card this November, the memory market has other plans.

Jensen Huang threw in the towel on November 12, resigning as NVIDIA's CEO after founding the company more than three decades ago. NVIDIA's market value subsequently fell below $4 trillion for the first time since July 2025 before the week was out, leaving the market in a state of flux.

With Black Friday less than two weeks away, people want to know whether they can get their mitts on some cheap NVIDIA. While some mean the stock, which closed at around $162 on Friday, others mean the RTX 5080 they've had their eyes on all year. Spoiler alert: only one price has fallen, and it'll take more than a CEO scandal to move the needle on the other.

NVIDIA's graphics cards were already selling way beyond their list prices before Huang's scandal began, because AI data centers have spent the year swallowing the memory those cards need. The RTX 5080, for example, debuted at $999 and now starts at $1,999. The RTX 5090 was $1,999 at launch and sells at close to $7,000 at the lower end. Black Friday has a long record of barely denting GPU prices, and this year retailers have even less room than usual.

NVIDIA's stock had already dropped by around 20 percent over five straight weeks of losses before its board opened an investigation into Huang on November 8. That included a 9 percent drop following the midterm results and ballot measures that could slow data center construction.

Reports in late October then linked Jensen Huang to Alice Huang, a Singapore-based exec whom U.S. officials reportedly suspect of spying for China. He then admitted to an affair with Alice Huang on November 8. Four days later, Jensen Huang was out as NVIDIA CEO, and by Friday's close the company had posted six consecutive weekly losses. That's its longest streak since 2012, with roughly $1.7 trillion in market value shed since early October.

HSBC downgraded NVIDIA from buy to hold on November 13, cutting its price target from $365 to $170, arguing that the stock would languish until the company names a permanent CEO. Colette Kress is acting as interim CEO in the meantime while continuing as CFO, a role she has held since 2013. Shares fell another 3.7 percent in premarket trading on Monday, a day before what will be NVIDIA's first-ever earnings report without Jensen Huang.

Data centers brought in the lion's share of NVIDIA's $96.2 billion in last-quarter revenue, accounting for $89 billion. That leaves $7.2 billion for everything else, gamers included. The cause is that memory makers have been focusing on AI chips, pushing up the price of GDDR7 memory that RTX 50-series cards need.

During the crypto-era shortage of 2021, Ethereum miners were snapping up cards that'd otherwise have gone to gamers, causing prices to balloon. That Black Friday, the best GPU deals were 5 to 10 percent off prices that were themselves already way too high. A year later, the miners were gone. Crypto prices crashed in May 2022, and Ethereum's switch to proof-of-stake that September instantly wiped out GPU mining profitability on the network, yet retailers still sold the RTX 3080 at its $699 list price while calling it a Black Friday deal.

Even without miners competing for stock, Tom's Hardware saw no real GPU deals over the 2023 Black Friday weekend, and in 2024 RTX 4090s were selling above $2,000 against their $1,599 MSRP. By the run-up to last year's Black Friday event, some RTX 50-series cards had settled within $30 of their list prices, but the sales barely had an impact. A PNY RTX 5060 down $20 to $279 made Windows Central's list of NVIDIA deals, while the cheapest RTX 5090 PC Gamer could find was $2,700, $700 over the list price. Those were the best conditions for any potential GPU deals in five years, and they led to discounts measured in tens of dollars.

Retailers heading into Black Friday on November 27 are holding RTX 50-series stock bought at wholesale prices that NVIDIA's Chinese board partners raised again in November. Yes, a Black Friday sale could shave some margin off the top, but any deals will still only be a very modest cut at best from record GPU prices. NVIDIA's stock price, meanwhile, will keep reacting to the likes of earnings and the board's choice of successor. Its GPUs, however, answer to the memory market and the data centers buying up all the company's output.

#281. This boiled bag of offal is banned in the US. In Scotland it's a fine-dining treat

Anthony Bourdain loved haggis. But even the late, great American chef, writer and television host recognized that Scotland’s national dish, with its “sinister sheep parts” wrapped in a shroud of mystery and half-invented history, could be a hard sell.

“Don’t let them tell you otherwise, that’s really one of life’s great pleasures,” Bourdain said on one of his gastro-curious pilgrimages to Glasgow. “There is no more unfairly reviled food on Earth than the haggis.”

A mash-up of diced lung, liver and heart mixed with oatmeal, beef suet, onion and assorted spices, haggis was traditionally made by stuffing these raw ingredients into the stomach of a recently slain sheep and boiling the lot to a state of palatability.

Instagrammable is not the word that immediately comes to mind. In our 21st-century world, where “clean” eating and processed pap overlap, haggis can seem like an “Outlander”-style outlier from another age.

Yet, by some alchemy, once cooked to its required “warm-reekin’ (steaming)” state, it adds up to much more than the sum of its modest parts. It’s offaly charm has kept nose-to-tail eating alive among a younger generation of Scots that has largely turned its back on the tripe, liver and kidneys their predecessors enjoyed (or endured).

Carefully prepared, haggis tastes both oaty and meaty; it is dark and crumbly, a little crispy at the edges but still moist; earthy but also savory and spicy; deep-tasting and profoundly warming, the perfect foil for its traditional garnish of floury mashed potatoes and orange bashed turnip.

“It’s like a cuddle for the stomach,” says Nicola Turner, a 35-year-old office administrator from Helensburgh, a town on western Scotland’s Firth of Clyde.

For children of the 1960s and ’70s, like crime novelist Ian Rankin, haggis meals were a choice between the classic meat-and-two-veg plate and the battered and deep-fried, chip-shop iteration loved by both his friend Bourdain and his quintessentially Scottish detective character, Inspector John Rebus.

Now myriad other treatments have blossomed.

“I’m pretty sure the first time I dined with AB in Edinburgh we had haggis in filo pastry with a jam-style – maybe blackcurrant – sauce,” Rankin recalled. “He was a big fan of haggis and of chip shops. Rebus will have enjoyed the occasional haggis supper from his local chip shop. He was definitely a fan, as am I.”

“It is all about the spicing and the texture,” says the Scottish food writer, novelist and cook Sue Lawrence, a champion of haggis’ adaptability for use in other dishes. “If you didn’t know what was in it, you wouldn’t think ‘oh that tastes of liver or whatever.’ It is all nicely chopped up and the oatmeal gives it a lovely texture. It could easily be a nice, big mince dish.”

These US restaurants and chefs are James Beard Award finalists

Lawrence uses haggis as an alternative to beef and pork ragù in lasagna and in her pastilla, a version of the North African dish in which a hand-made haggis from the Isle of Mull substitutes for the traditional poultry or seafood filling. The filo pastry savory is flavored with the spice blend ras el hanout, apricots, chile, orange zest and almonds before being sprinkled with cinnamon and icing sugar.

Such cultural crossovers serve as a reminder that haggis could easily be a dish with nothing specifically Scottish about it at all. Records of similar quick and portable preparations of the fast-perishing innards of sheep and other animals date back to ancient Rome and Greece.

Haggis-like combinations of offal and grains are part of the culinary history of several countries. Spain has chireta, Romania drob and Sweden polsa, while chaudin, or ponce, is a rice and meat-stuffed pig stomach that is a staple of Cajun cooking.

In neighboring England, recipes for “hagese,” “hagws of a schepe,” “haggas” or “haggus” pop up in recipe books published between the 15th and 17th centuries, probably preceding written records north of the border.

Etymological evidence points to the term “haggis” having its roots in Old Norse, suggesting an early version of an oat-and-offal sausage might have arrived in Britain and Ireland on a Viking longboat.

But ever since it was first optioned by the poet Robert Burns in the late 1700s, the haggis backstory has been monopolized by Scotland and the Scots, sometimes mischievously.

It is, according to the kind of lore that Burns engendered, the dish a doughty Highlander would carry with him as he drove cattle through the glens to the markets of the central belt or the perfect picnic for a whisky smuggler plying his illicit trade by moonlight.

From such romantic notions it was a short step to turning the haggis into a wee wild beastie, one with longer legs on one side that was thus condemned to run round and round whichever hill it lived on. In 2003, a poll of American tourists in Scotland found that one in three of them believed they might encounter such a confused creature on a Caledonian vacation.

Bourdain, a native New Yorker, may have qualified as haggis’ biggest admirer since Burns, but his compatriots at the US Department of Agriculture remain unconverted to offal-filled paunch. Haggis imports into the United States were prohibited in 1971 as part of a ban on the consumption of all livestock lungs. Authentic versions of old school haggis remain culinary contraband in the US, as hard to lay your hands on as Cuban cigars.

Across the rest of the world, it’s a different story. According to leading producer Simon Howie, haggis is more widely appreciated and consumed now than it has been since Burns improvised his “Address to a Haggis” for the entertainment of well-to-do Edinburgh acquaintances.

Firmly tongue-in-cheek, the poem lauds the “Great chieftain o’ the pudding race,” as exactly the kind of unpretentious, hearty fare required to nourish a nation of braveheart warriors.

In comparison to the enfeebling foreign muck enjoyed by the capital’s claret-quaffing elites of the time – the olio, fricassée or ragoût that would “sicken a sow” – Burns urges his readers to wonder at the magical impact of haggis on his fellow sons of Scotland’s soil.

As the English translation of the original Scots language version puts it:

These days synthetic casings have largely replaced stomach but ovine and porcine innards remain at the core of most of the haggis produced in its homeland, said Howie, who estimates that his company Simon Howie Butchers, accounts for around 60% of the roughly two million haggises produced every year.

For Howie, versatility, value for money and convenience explain why this staple of the Scottish larder is thriving. Typically haggis retails in Scotland, which accounts for half of global consumption by volume, for around £6, or $7.70 per kilogram ($3.36/pound). That’s around half the price of less expensive cuts of beef or a third of the price of Scotch lamb while enjoying a fairly similar nutritional and calorific profile.

“You can give your kids a meal that is not full of things you don’t want to feed them – for a few pounds you can feed three strapping lads,” Howie said.

“From a kitchen perspective, it is very simple because when it leaves our factory it is already cooked. So when you or a restaurant owner gets it into the kitchen all you have to do is heat it up to be piping hot. It couldn’t be more basic: a student with no cooking skills or a Michelin-starred chef do exactly the same thing to put it out on the plate.”

Its texture means haggis can also be usefully deployed in fine dining alongside leaner meat like venison or as a stuffing for poultry and game birds. Its spicy intensity means it is also finding uses in canapés and as a crouton-borne garnish for soups.

Buoyant sales are also underpinned by the increasing consumption of haggis in forms inspired by Scotland’s ethnic minorities.

Glasgow’s Sikh community pioneered haggis pakora in the 1990s and samosas, spring rolls and quesadillas have followed in its wake, often using a vegetarian version of the protein in which the offal is replaced by a mix of vegetables, pulses and mushrooms.

Such dishes are more than culinary twists. They are badges of belonging, and an indication that, two centuries after Burns grabbed it for the nation, haggis is as intimately entwined with Scots identity as ever.

Just ask Ross O’Cinneide, a promising 14-year-old fly-half in the junior section of Stirling County rugby club.

“Most of my friends and I like haggis,” he says. “Mum makes it for us sometimes after rugby and it’s got a very nice warming feeling. And it’s nice because it’s purely Scottish.”

#280. US now "comfortable" with children dying of measles as death toll hits 10

International authorities will announce US lost its elimination status Tuesday.

Health officials in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin announced two more measles deaths late last week, bringing the national tally of confirmed measles deaths this year to 10. The total includes the deaths of at least four infants: two in Pennsylvania, one in New York, and one in Wisconsin.

Wisconsin health officials said the latest measles death—the second for the state—was in a child. Pennsylvania’s health department did not reveal the age or other details of the latest death—the state’s seventh—besides revealing it was of an unvaccinated resident in Montour County. Overall, the seven deaths in Pennsylvania include two in Jefferson County, three in Lancaster County, and one in Mifflin, in addition to the new death in Montour. An eighth death was reported in Franklin County, but state health officials have not confirmed it.

For all the states with deaths so far, health officials have noted that they’re the first deaths in decades. Multiple outbreaks are underway across the country, pushing the national tally of cases to nearly 5,500 across 47 states and jurisdictions, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Pennsylvania’s case count alone is over 1,500, and Wisconsin is reporting nearly 650.

With outbreaks that have been smoldering and flaring since last year, the US has reportedly lost its measles elimination status—as medical and public health experts have widely expected it would. A panel of experts for the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional branch of the World Health Organization, convened last week to review US measles data and assess its elimination status. The PAHO is set to announce its conclusion and the review’s other findings on Tuesday, November 17. But sources broke the news to The Wall Street Journal on Friday that the panel had found that the US had indeed lost its status.

An elimination status is determined by international health authorities after a country has gone more than 12 months without continuous spread of a virus. The status is lost when epidemiological and laboratory data indicate that a chain of transmission involving a viral strain with an identical genotype and lineage has continued uninterrupted for 12 months or longer.

The US earned its elimination status in 2000 after hard-fought vaccination campaigns over several decades. But US vaccination rates have slipped below protective levels in recent years, fueled by the rise of anti-vaccine rhetoric and vaccine misinformation from fierce anti-vaccine advocates, including current US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. As vaccination rates slipped, measles cases skyrocketed. The current case tally is the highest seen since 1991.

In reporting the PAHO’s determination, the Journal quoted Noel Brewer, chair of an independent US committee who presented findings about the country’s measles outbreaks to PAHO, on the country’s lamentable status: “Runaway measles outbreaks in the United States, as well as the needless deaths, are all due to low measles vaccination coverage. We’ve gotten comfortable letting children be stopped by a deadly disease and die from it.”

The US Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to requests to comment about the loss of the elimination status or to answer a question about how anti-vaccine rhetoric and misinformation, including that from Kennedy, has contributed.

Medical and public health experts continue to sharply criticize Kennedy’s and the Trump administration’s poor handling of the ongoing severe outbreaks. The CDC has not held press briefings in efforts to halt the vaccine-preventable illness and promote vaccination. Instead, Kennedy reportedly ordered the CDC to remove measles death data, and the CDC director declined to approve an urgent health alert about the life-threatening risks of measles during pregnancy.

#278. The important Gmail security settings you should be using

Having your Google account compromised can be a huge deal.

Gmail is no longer just an email service. Plenty of websites and apps let you log in with your Google account, and many people use that one login for almost everything they do online. It makes signing in a lot easier. It also means that whoever holds the keys to your account holds a lot more than just your private emails.

Start with Security Checkup; it's a page in your Google Account that gives you personalized recommendations, like adding a recovery phone number and email. Those might sound like very basic steps, but they matter more than you might think: Google uses them to alert you to suspicious activity and to help you get back in if someone locks you out. From google.com, click your profile icon in the upper right, then click Manage your Google Account. Click Security & sign-in. At the top of the page, you'll see an icon. A green shield means nothing needs your attention right now. A blue, yellow or red exclamation mark means there's something to fix.

The single biggest fix is two-step verification, also known as two-factor authentication. With it on, a stolen password isn't enough, because signing in also takes something you physically have on you, like your phone or your own computer. To switch it on, go to Security & sign-in, find the How you sign in to Google section, select Turn on 2-Step Verification and follow the prompts.

Then there are passkeys, which let you sign in with your fingerprint, face scan or screen lock instead of a password. A passkey can't be shared, copied or written down, so it holds up against phishing. To create one, go to your account's passkey page and select Create a passkey. Only do it on devices you own; once a passkey exists, anyone who can unlock that device can get into your account.

Locking the front door doesn't help if someone already has a key, so check who and what is connected. Go to myaccount.google.com, open Security & sign-in and scroll down to the linked apps section, then select See all linked apps. You'll see the apps and sites you use Sign in with Google for, plus anything that has been given access to your account data. Anything you don't recognize or no longer use can go: select Remove access, then Confirm.

Next, look at Gmail itself. An attacker who gets in often changes a few quiet settings so they can keep reading your mail later. Open Gmail on your computer, click the gear icon in the top right and select See all settings. Then check for anything unfamiliar under automatic forwarding, filters, labels, scheduled emails, your vacation responder, and IMAP or POP access. Mail delegation, which lets someone else read, send and delete email in your account, has its own spot: go to the Accounts and Import tab and look under Grant access to your account. If a name is there that you didn't add, click Delete next to it. You can't manage delegates from the Gmail app, only on the desktop site. Automatic forwarding is the nasty one. It sends a copy of every new message, except spam, to another address, and you'd never notice. If you find a forwarding rule you didn't set up, change your password right away and turn it off.

The devices page is the other place to look. It lives in your Google Account, not in Gmail's settings: go to myaccount.google.com, open Security & sign-in (on a computer it may show up as just Security in the left-hand menu), find Your devices and select Manage all devices. You'll see everywhere you're signed in or have been in the last few weeks. Watch for a device you don't recognize, a location you weren't in or a browser you don't normally use. Take a moment to think about it, though: an airport, a library computer or a phone you recently reset can all look odd. If something really isn't yours, select the device and tap Sign out.

Once the settings are in place, a few habits keep them working. Keep two-step verification on, and never share a verification code with anyone. Google guarantees it won't call you to ask for one. Run Security Checkup again every now and then, since recommendations change and old devices and apps pile up.

In general, keep an eye out for any suspicious activity, or even lack of activity. For example, you stop receiving mail, friends tell you they got spam from you, there are emails sent that you didn't write or messages vanish from your inbox without landing in Trash. If any of that sounds familiar, change your password first, then work through the devices, apps and Gmail settings above.

#277. Meta is testing Direct, a standalone messaging app for Instagram

It’s only available in Turkey and Thailand for now.

Meta is working on a dedicated messaging app for Instagram that could also expand the reach of the app's DMs. The company is starting to test Direct, a new standalone app that brings Instagram's inbox to a separate app, but doesn't require an existing Instagram account to use. Direct will only be available in Thailand and Turkey for now, Meta said in an update.

Direct looks pretty similar to Instagram's inbox at first glance. It has an almost identical layout, with existing chats carrying over from the main app if you log in with your Instagram credentials. It even has some of the same personalization features, like the ability to set custom backgrounds for individual threads and Instagram's status update feature, Notes.

But while Instagram users can log in with their existing accounts, Direct doesn't actually require an Instagram login. People can also sign up for Direct with their email address or phone number, and they'll still be able to message friends in the app. However, it sounds like messaging without a linked Instagram account won't be quite as convenient. Meta notes that users without Instagram credentials will need to manually add contacts to the app via their Instagram username or a QR code in order to start conversations.

Meta says it's also bringing some of Instagram's safety features to Direct. The app won't allow people to start chats with accounts they aren't already connected with via their contacts. And parents will be able to monitor who their teen is chatting with and how much time they spend in the app if they use the company's parental control features. Additionally, Meta says it will "use technology to detect and act on potentially inappropriate interactions with young people," though it's vague about what exactly that will entail.

The test of Direct is an interesting move for Meta. Instagram head Adam Mosseri often notes that messaging is Instagram's most-used feature. But he was also reluctant to give Threads its own inbox because it seemed "redundant" to use multiple apps to reach the same people when Meta briefly considered bringing Instagram's inbox to Threads. He said at the time that mirroring the Instagram inbox could cause "notification routing weirdness" and generally seemed like a less than ideal experience for most people.

The app also raises questions about whether Direct would compete with WhatsApp in the countries where it's rolled out. It's unlikely an Instagram-centric app would replace WhatsApp for many people, but it could eat into that app's engagement if non-Instagram users can use Direct to message friends instead.

That may also be why Direct seems fairly limited for now. Meta describes it as a test that will only be available to people in Turkey and Thailand for the time being. But if the app is a success, it's likely the company will consider expanding it to more places.

#276. African Miss Universe Contestants Struggle to Get U.S. Visas

A crackdown on entry by some citizens of African countries by the U.S. immigration officials means that some contestants might not get visas in time to attend the pageant in Puerto Rico this month.

At least two African contestants for Miss Universe said they were in danger of missing the pageant in Puerto Rico this month because they had not secured U.S. visas amid a crackdown by the Trump administration.

One contestant, Miss Zambia, Mubanga Pamela Hatyoka, said she would not travel to the annual event on Nov. 24 because she had not received her visa, according to Arm Model Management, which said it was the franchise holder of Miss Zambia 2026.

Her nonattendance is “linked to the United States presidential travel restrictions affecting Zambia and other African nations,” the agency said in a statement on social media. “She earned her crown, she earned her title, and she deserves the opportunity to represent the nation she proudly serves.”

The contestant from Zimbabwe, Roseanna Hall, said on social media that she, too, had not received a U.S. visa. “I will not give up,” she said. Contestants from South Sudan and the Republic of Congo also faced delays, according to news reports.

The Miss Universe organization did not immediately reply to a request for comment. The Department of Homeland Security also did not respond to a similar request. It was unclear why the contestants had not received visas.

The social media page of the Miss Universe organization listed 20 African countries among its contestants for the pageant to held in the U.S. territory.

The Trump administration has curtailed several avenues to legal migration to the United States as part of a crackdown, including visa bans and restrictions that have hit African countries hard. The administration in January imposed full or partial travel bans and visa restrictions on 36 countries, and 29 of those are in Africa.

In December, the Trump administration widened travel restrictions to additional countries, including Zambia and Zimbabwe, while keeping in place full restrictions for citizens of the Republic of Congo and adding them for South Sudan.

Homeland Security has said it was “slamming the door shut on the foreign invaders who have undermined our national security.”

Citizens of African countries have for decades complained of draconian visa rules imposed by the governments of the United States and European countries. Governments say the restrictions aim to control migration and prevent fraud, but many Africans say they impede legitimate professional, business and study opportunities and stop family members from attending occasions such as births, weddings and funerals.

Those restrictions have become more severe since public attitudes in many Western countries have turned against immigration over the past decade.

Matthew Mpoke Bigg is the East Africa bureau chief for The New York Times, based in Nairobi, Kenya.

#275. US moves to cut China’s remote access to AI chips

Trump bets China won’t mind US blocking remote access to AI chips.

On the heels of the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training.

In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.

US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop “more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.”

Now, the rules have been tightened up so much that the South China Morning Post reported that, “as a result, any advanced chips made for a Chinese firm are assumed to be restricted, and factories must ask the US government for a license before shipping them.”

The rule change takes effect 90 days after it’s posted to the Federal Register. Moving forward, companies headquartered in any of those countries deemed to “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to China, Russia, and Iran must apply for a license with strict know-your-customer controls when transferring high volumes of advanced chips. If a license is granted, companies will have to “perform robust due diligence,” submitting monthly reports on transactions that thoroughly detail all parties involved, as well as their parent companies, and the final destination for chips sold.

In a press release Sunday, the Commerce Department described the rule change as “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.” An exception was carved out for companies providing computing power “exclusively used for commercial recommender systems.” The Department said it was acting to “prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.”

Without the intervention, officials fear that China could develop a military or economic edge, The New York Times reported.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, suspected of serving as a Chinese spy. Congress is probing if Alice Huang used her personal relationship with Jensen Huang to help her former company, Megaspeed, become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, then used that position to smuggle Nvidia’s restricted AI chips into China. China has denied that Alice Huang was a spy, and Megaspeed has denied that smuggling occurred, while launching its own internal probe.

Megaspeed is a Singaporean data center firm whose primary business is cloud computing and AI infrastructure. Prior to the rule change, selling remote access to AI servers to customers in China was perfectly legal, NYT noted. But now, the Commerce Department has given firms like Megaspeed 90 days to either obtain licenses or face future export restrictions.

Whether or not to add more chip curbs has been a polarizing debate in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly butted heads with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. When the Megaspeed news broke, Bessent pushed for curbs, but Lutnick reportedly appeared “too cozy” with Nvidia to move. Instead, Lutnick initially favored looser controls that Nvidia claimed would ensure global dominance of US technology. (A Commerce Department spokesperson told NYT that Bessent has never confronted Lutnick over his handling of Megaspeed.)

Any companies found violating the rules could face a “range of consequences,” the Commerce Department said after reportedly bending to Bessent’s pressure campaign. Those include possibly facing new import restrictions, stricter license requirements, downgrading their status in the US export control regime, or other changes to their company’s or their base country’s entity-list designations.

Although the summary of the rule change said that “Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion” of the anti-diversion policy, it’s unclear how aggressively the Commerce Department might enforce the rule, NYT noted.

Bessent has publicly criticized Lutnick for failing to sanction Megaspeed, and NYT reported that ultimately, enforcement of the stricter rules—which Bessent helped draft—“would be up to the Commerce Department.”

“The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent said on a CNBC appearance. “I think it’s important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.”

There’s even a push to oust Lutnick over his position on chips, but The Guardian reported that Donald Trump confirmed he has no plans to replace the AI industry-friendly commerce secretary. On Monday, Trump told reporters that Lutnick was right to delay blacklisting Megaspeed, because “if you didn’t delay it… you could have a blow-up with China.”

At the press gaggle, Trump aligned with China in saying that there’s no evidence yet that Alice Huang was a spy. He also joined a band of prominent tech leaders calling for Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, saying that it wasn’t a “bad idea.”

“Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” Trump said. “She may not be a spy.”

However, US investigators have alleged that they found “Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China,” CBS News reported.

China is unlikely to welcome the new rules, as it has consistently accused the US of fabricating the spying claims to justify imposing additional chip restrictions.

However, a senior Trump official, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive policy matters, told the NYT that Trump “did not expect countermeasures from China in response.”

Trump will be in China for an economic summit this week, including a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The new curbs could potentially disrupt those talks, according to Hong Yuan, a researcher and secretary-general of the Center for American Military Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Hong told the People’s Daily that China will likely view the rule change as politically motivated.

“Before any judicial causality was established, Washington handed down a political conviction, substituting suspicion for proof, espionage for personal contact, and an industrial embargo for private conduct,” Hong said. “The issue is not the cause of tighter controls, but a political catalyst.”

The new policy could hurt the US, experts told the Chinese outlets. Analysts told the South China Morning Post that the policy could “accelerate Chinese companies’ shift to domestic AI chips.” Other experts told the People’s Daily—which is the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist Party—that “the cost of switching back to US platforms will rise” over time. If that happened, it could potentially lock in Chinese technology over America’s in “the world’s largest single consumer market for chips,” experts said.

Sun Chenghao, senior fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, told the People’s Daily that “what US companies stand to lose could be customers and technological influence for years to come.”

#274. Kwame Brathwaite, photographer of 'Black is Beautiful' movement, dies at 85

Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.

Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.

His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, announced his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”

Brathwaite’s work has been the subject of resurgent interest from curators, historians and collectors in recent years, and his first major institutional retrospective, which was organized by the Aperture Foundation, made its debut in 2019 at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles before touring the country.

Brathwaite was born in 1938 to Barbadian immigrants, in what he referred to as “the People’s Republic of Brooklyn” in New York, though his family moved from there to Harlem and then to the South Bronx when Brathwaite was 5 years old. He attended the School of Industrial Art (now the High School of Art and Design) and, according to profiles of Brathwaite in T Magazine and Vice, was drawn to photography by two moments. The first was in August of 1955, when a 17-year-old Brathwaite encountered David Jackson’s haunting photograph of a brutalized Emmett Till in his open casket. The second was in 1956, when — after he and his brother Elombe co-founded the African Jazz Arts Society and Studios (AJASS) — Brathwaite saw a young man taking photos in a dark jazz club without the use of a flash, and his mind became alight with possibility.

Using a Hasselblad medium-format camera, Brathwaite attempted to do the same, learning to work with limited light in a manner that enhanced the visual narrative of his imagery. He would soon also develop a darkroom technique that enriched and deepened how Black skin would appear in his photography, honing the practice in a small darkroom in his Harlem apartment. Brathwaite went on to photograph jazz legends performing throughout the 1950s and ’60s, including Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Thelonious Monk and others.

“You want to get the feeling, the mood that you’re experiencing when they’re playing,” Brathwaite told Aperture Magazine in 2017. “That’s the thing. You want to capture that.”

A 106-year-old from the Philippines is Vogue's oldest ever cover model

By the early 1960s, alongside the rest of AJASS, Brathwaite began using his photography and organizing prowess to consciously push back against whitewashed, Eurocentric beauty standards. The group came up with the concept of the Grandassa Models, young Black women whom Brathwaite would photograph, celebrating and accentuating their features. In 1962, AJASS organized “Naturally ’62”, a fashion show held in a Harlem club called the Purple Manor and featuring the models. The show would go on to be held regularly until 1992. In 1966, Brathwaite married his wife Sikolo, a Grandassa Model whom he had met on the street the year prior when he asked if he could take her portrait. The two remained married for the rest of Brathwaite’s life.

By the 1970s, Brathwaite’s focus on jazz shifted to other forms of popular Black music. In 1974, he traveled to Africa with the Jackson Five to document their tour, also photographing the historic “Rumble in the Jungle” boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman in what’s now the Democratic Republic of Congo that same year. Commissions in this era also saw Brathwaite photographing Nina Simone, Stevie Wonder, Sly and the Family Stone, Bob Marley and other music legends.

Creating for community: The Black designers placing identity and heritage at the center of their brands

Throughout the ensuing decades, Brathwaite continued to explore and develop his mode of photography, all through the lens of the “Black is Beautiful” ethos. In 2016, Brathwaite joined the roster of Philip Martin Gallery in Los Angeles, and he was continuing to photograph commissions as recently as 2018, when he shot artist and stylist Joanne Petit-Frère for The New Yorker.

T Magazine’s 2021 profile, published on the occasion of Brathwaite’s retrospective traveling to the Blanton Museum of Art in Austin, Texas, noted that the photographer’s health was failing such that he was unable to be interviewed for the article. A separate exhibition, “Kwame Brathwaite: Things Well Worth Waiting For,” is currently on view at the Art Institute of Chicago, where it will remain until July 24.

#273. Buying a used phone? Make sure to check the IMEI first

A phone's IMEI number can reveal whether the device has sketchy history, what networks it can connect to and more.

Smartphones are no exception to soaring tech prices and the pre-owned market has become a necessary respite for many. However, whenever you're buying a refurbished or generally pre-owned phone, you need to take a few precautions. In particular, you need to look out for the red flags of a potential scam and every mobile device has a special number that can help you.

Buying a pre-owned phone from eBay, Facebook Marketplace or a physical repair shop requires a good deal of prep work. You should properly clean and sanitize the secondhand phones you find while also making sure the phone you're getting doesn't have any obvious defects. When you're asking the seller about the device's condition and history, you should also ask about the phone's IMEI number — which can reveal whether a phone has sketchy history, what networks it can connect to, and more.

Every mobile device has a unique 15-digit number associated with it known as an International Mobile Equipment Identity (IMEI) number. This number is used to register your phone with your network provider and can subsequently be used by that provider to identify your phone. If your phone is lost or stolen, you can contact your provider and have them blacklist your phone via that IMEI number.

If you want to find your phone's IMEI number, it can typically be found in the device's packaging or on any physical or digital receipts, as well as on your network provider account. Additionally, while you can generally find your IMEI number in your phone's settings, dialing *#06# into the keypad of any phone will reveal its unique IMEI code. You can also contact your provider's support team about finding this number if all else fails.

If you're in the position of buying a new phone, the device's seller should provide its IMEI code to you upon request — and you should definitely ask for this code. The IMEI number will help you confirm whether it's been stolen or whether it's compatible with certain cellular networks.

There are all too many scams to avoid when buying refurbished tech online and in person, so be on the lookout for sellers that refuse to provide the IMEI number as they may be selling fenced goods. An IMEI number can't be used to hack or track phones by itself but sellers should only share it with serious buyers through private messaging and buyers should keep screenshots of the conversation just in case.

Upon being provided with an IMEI number, you should proceed with checking its validity and whether it's been reported stolen or lost. There's quite the smorgasbord of sites to use if you want to check an IMEI number, many of which will ask for a small fee before checking the number. While many of the options are free, research whichever site you use first to make sure you're not about to fall for a phishing scam.

#272. Meet the new James Bond: Robert Pattinson

Producers cite “his fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit” and continual reinvention as factors.

The Internet has been abuzz for months about which actor would replace Daniel Craig as British agent 007 James Bond in the franchise. We finally have the answer: Robert Pattinson, who built on his 2005 role as the doomed Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire into an illustrious career mixing roles in franchises and Hollywood blockbusters with daring arthouse fare.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

The choice will reunite Pattinson with Denis Villeneuve, who recently worked with him on the forthcoming Dune: Part III and will direct the next (as yet untitled) Bond installment. “I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey,” Villeneuve said in a statement. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.”

Not everyone is happy with the casting choice; some have never forgiven Pattinson for the Twilight franchise, despite the actor’s impressive recent films. Pattinson has played darker roles in recent years, often as a villain. And at 40, Pattinson is a bit older than the actors he beat out, most notably Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden (Slow Horses), Josh O’Connor (Wake Up, Dead Man), and Callum Turner (Fantastic Beasts).

But Pattinson is a logical choice for Bond; heck, he’s already played a secret agent in Christopher Nolan’s Tenet (2020). In fact, he originally topped the list of longtime Bond franchise steward Barbara Broccoli’s and Michael G. Wilson’s choices to take over from Craig. They shelved that idea when Pattinson was cast in Matt Reeves’ The Batman. But Broccoli and Wilson no longer have creative control over Bond, having sold the rights to Amazon MGM for $20 million.

Pattinson’s box office record this year probably didn’t hurt either: He played central roles in The Drama, Primetime, and The Odyssey, all of which made back their production costs and then some, with Dune: Part III still to come. It’s unclear how his Bond commitments will affect Pattinson’s future as Batman; The Batman: Part 2 has faced production delays (and a director change) and is slated for a 2028 release. Should there be a third installment—not assured in the wake of James Gunn and Peter Safran’s departure from DC Studios—Reeves will likely work around Pattinson’s Bond schedule.

“James Bond is one of the most beloved, inspiring, iconic and yet enigmatic characters in literature and movies,” producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman said in a statement. “The legacy of this character is in great hands with Robert Pattinson. His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times.”

#270. Study finds slightly higher risk of autism diagnosis in areas with more lithium in drinking water, but experts say more research is needed

A new study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.

About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder. Genetics may be a factor, but some have been looking at potential environmental causes, too.

Autism diagnosis has become more common, but pandemic disrupted early detection, CDC says

Cases may be on the rise, but that is also unclear. One study published this year on cases in the New York-New Jersey area found that autism diagnosis rates tripled among certain age groups between 2000 and 2016. A 2021 report found similar increases in cases, but the CDC says the increased number of cases is most likely linked to more doctors screening for the condition.

Lithium is an alkali metal that can be found naturally in some food and ground water. It’s used in batteries, grease and air conditioners, as well as in the treatment of bipolar disorder and some blood disorders. Its levels in US drinking water are not regulated, according to the US Geological Survey.

A new study, published Monday in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, found a small association between lithium and autism diagnosis in Denmark, where the researchers say the level of lithium in drinking water is similar to that in American water systems.

The researchers checked a database of people with psychiatric disorders for children born between 2000 and 2013 to find information on 8,842 cases of ASD and 43,864 participants who did not have ASD. They then measured the concentration of lithium in 151 public waterworks that served more than half of the Danish population and mapped out where pregnant people lived in relation.

For many neurodiverse people, 'The Sims' has been a lifelong comfort

As lithium levels in water increased, there was a modest increased risk of an ASD diagnosis. Specifically, compared with people at the lowest exposure level, those who had the second and third highest exposure during pregnancy had a 24% to 26% higher risk of ASD diagnosed in children. The group with the highest exposure had a 46% higher risk than those at the lowest level of exposure.

The researchers could not tell how much water the pregnant people drank, but they picked Denmark in part because residents there consume some of the lowest amounts of bottled water in Europe.

Experts say it’s important to note that the research can’t show that lithium exposure leads directly to an autism diagnosis.

Further study is required, said study co-author Dr. Beate Ritz, a professor of neurology in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and a professor of epidemiology and environmental health at the UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

“Any drinking water contaminants that may affect the developing human brain deserve intense scrutiny,” Ritz said in a news release. She added that the research would need to be replicated in other countries to look for a similar connection.

The implications of the findings are complex as far as public health policy is concerned, according to an editorial published alongside the study. Lithium levels in water, at concentrations that the study associated with a potential ASD risk, have also been linked with health benefits such as lower rates of hospitalization for psychiatric disorders and suicide.

“If all these of associations are valid, the wisdom of Solomon will be required to develop guidelines for lithium in drinking water that are maximally protective of the entire population,” wrote Dr. David C. Bellinger, a professor of neurology and psychology at Harvard Medical School. “Until the basic biology of ASD is better understood, it will be difficult to distinguish causal from spurious associations.”

'Heartbreaking' delays in autism diagnosis and treatment got even worse during pandemic

Dr. Max Wiznitzer, director of the Rainbow Autism Center at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies and Children’s Hospital in Cleveland, points to other research on the effects of lithium on pregnant people who take it for mental health disorders. Those studies – which look at people exposed to much higher levels than are found in drinking water – do not show a connection with autism spectrum disorder.

“It’s an interesting association, but causation is definitely not proven,” said Wiznitzer, who was not involved in the new research. “We have to see if there’s a viable and biologically plausible mechanism by which a small amount of lithium in the water supply can somehow do this, yet pharmacologic dosing of lithium in women with bipolar disorder has not been reported to be causing increased risk of ASD.”

Other studies have also suggested connections between ASD and environmental exposures to things like pesticides, air pollution and phthalates. But none of them points to any of these factors as a direct cause of the disorder.

Sign up here to get The Results Are In with Dr. Sanjay Gupta every Tuesday from the CNN Health team.

A link between environmental exposure and ASD is hard to prove, Wiznitzer said. With research showing that increased exposure to air pollution raises the risk of giving birth to a child with ASD, for example, he often wonders whether pollution is the determining factor or if it’s just the populations who live in more polluted areas.

“There’s a lot of speculation about about environmental factors, but how many of them are truly causally associated?” Wiznitzer said. “We are bombarded with a variety of environmental stressors in our everyday lives. We have to figure out how to basically safely navigate them, and this is probably not one that’s high on our list.”
