#197. Island is a new screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game

A new startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content.

This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel, Databricks, and Microsoft.

Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.

Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying.

“Once we were in YC, I think there’s a big mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be.

“So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.”

With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves.

“A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj said.

What’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping users meet their goals, the startup’s early data shows. After early testing and an October launch, the team says that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning.

Island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into users’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks.

The idea to encourage users to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience, which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps.

Similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch, Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj.

Island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer.

The startup says Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active users-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed.

The app is currently free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The company hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but plans to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year.

#196. Asia’s Eurovision Contest Is Missing China, India, Pakistan, Indonesia and Japan

China, India, Pakistan, Indonesia and Japan didn’t join the singing contest in Bangkok. That left some of the region’s best-known musical cultures out of the mix.

For a competition meant to introduce the diversity of Asian pop music to the world, the lineup for the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia on Saturday had several notable absences.

For starters, the continent’s four most populous nations — China, India, Pakistan and Indonesia — were not there. Even Japan, a country globally considered a cultural powerhouse, was absent.

That left some of the region’s best-known musical cultures out of the mix. India has Bollywood hits. China has produced both Mandopop and Cantopop, the genre associated with Hong Kong pop stars. JPop was once huge across Asia.

As a result, the only large pop powerhouse in this contest was South Korea.

China’s absence is relatively simple to explain. Performers are entered by local broadcasters, and Eurovision has long had a messy relationship with China’s, which are heavily regulated and try to reflect the government’s social and political values. Mango TV once had a deal to broadcast the high-camp Eurovision to Chinese viewers, but Eurovision abruptly canceled it in 2018 after Mango TV censored acts whose performances featured gay themes. It also blurred rainbow flags in the performance arena.

Frank-Dieter Freiling, a former Eurovision official, said in an interview that such censorship was against Eurovision’s values and that the show’s organizers had historically barred broadcasters from airing the competition with delays.

It’s less clear why broadcasters from India, Pakistan, Japan and Indonesia did not participate. Assaf Blecher, Eurovision Asia’s executive producer, said that conversations with Chinese, Japanese and Indian broadcasters had not concluded in time. But he insisted that they “are knocking on our door.”

Not participating saved those countries the potential embarrassment of being the regional power that comes in last.

Just look to Europe, where Britain and Germany often perform badly at Eurovision. In this year’s show, Britain’s Look Mum No Computer placed last, scoring only one point, while Germany finished third from last. Whenever that happens, political commentators give interviews suggesting that the results reflect those countries’ poor standing across Europe.

Alex Marshall is a Times reporter covering European culture. He is based in London.

Francesca Regalado is a Times reporter covering breaking news.

#195. Trump says ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy did not threaten national security

U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he does not believe the country’s national security was put at risk as a result of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

“It was not put at risk,” Trump said when asked by reporters in light of his own friendship with Huang. “Our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China.”

Trump went on to contradict previous findings from U.S. officials by doubting that Huang’s paramour, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy.

“He probably shouldn’t have been doing on a personal basis what he did … That’s a different story,” Trump added. “But nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.”

Last year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw the production of an internal memo, circulated among top policymakers, which warned that Alice Huang was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump was reportedly briefed about these intelligence findings at least twice, including once in May aboard Air Force One, shortly before the former Nvidia CEO joined him on a trip to China. But Trump has maintained that he was not aware of these claims.

The U.S. regulates the exports of Nvidia’s top chips to China as a way of maintaining a competitive advantage. But prior to news of Huang’s affair publicly emerging, both the U.S. and Singaporean governments had been investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Huang has since stepped down from the role he has had for 33 years at Nvidia after more reporting revealed that he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees, at least one of whom was a direct report.

Given Huang’s importance to Nvidia, some prominent figures in the industry — including Elon Musk, Y Combinator president and CEO Garry Tan, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney — have signed a public letter calling for Nvidia to reinstate Huang.

“A lot of people are asking Jensen — they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” Trump said. Referring to the former Apple chief executive, Trump added: “I recommended Tim Cook.”

#191. Apple adds ‘face unlock’ to the iPhone Duo, but it’s not Face ID

One of the top complaints from tech reviewers about Apple’s new foldable, the iPhone Duo, has been its reliance on Touch ID, a technology that’s been largely replaced by Face ID across the company’s iPhone lineup.

With Monday’s release of iOS 27.3 beta for developers, Apple is addressing that complaint with a new “face unlock” feature that lets iPhone Duo users unlock their phones using the front camera, rather than waiting for a future hardware upgrade.

To be clear, this feature is not Face ID.

Due to hardware constraints, the iPhone Duo shipped without support for Face ID technology primarily because its thin, foldable design doesn’t offer enough space for the TrueDepth sensor array that Face ID requires. A recent report from Bloomberg suggests that the company is working to change that in a future version of the iPhone Duo. In the meantime, the Duo uses Touch ID for unlocking, authentication, and Apple Pay.

The new face unlock feature, however, will allow users to quickly unlock the device using the front camera when the phone is closed. It only works if users have recently authenticated with Touch ID or a passcode. Apple notes that Apple Pay and passwords will still require Touch ID, and users will have to authenticate with Touch ID again after 45 minutes of inactivity.

The move is meant to make it easier for people to use the Duo in the way they’re accustomed to, after years of unlocking an iPhone just by looking at it.

Apple isn’t going so far as to allow face unlock to work across the entire device, though, because the technology isn’t as secure as Face ID. The latter uses Apple’s TrueDepth 3D sensing hardware, which includes a flood illuminator and a dot projector that casts over 30,000 invisible infrared dots onto the user’s face to build a unique 3D map of the face. The system combines this map with attention-awareness checks, making it resistant to attempts to fool it with photos or other 2D images.

The software update addresses another complaint by incorporating one of the “hacks” iPhone Duo early adopters were using to force their phone to lock when they shut it. That involved creating a shortcut that would automatically run when the phone was closed. Now, Apple says users can enable this feature directly in Settings, under Display and Brightness.

Alongside the software update, Apple announced that more than 200,000 apps are now optimized for the iPhone Duo, up from over 100,000 earlier this month.

Other new features in this latest software release include an option to ask Siri questions about the content of a web page, even portions that aren’t visible without scrolling. Apple is also introducing video podcasts in Apple Podcasts in the Apple TV app, catching up with rivals like YouTube and Spotify.

The iOS 27.3 software update is currently available to developers and will soon arrive for public beta testers. It will roll out more broadly to all users after further testing is complete.

#189. Germany news: Merz, Söder aim to revisit electricity tax cut

The Christian Democrats are in Munich, pushing to revive some tax relief that didn't make it into the budget after talks last week. And Manuela Schwesig faces a vote on a new term as regional leader. Follow DW.

Stay tuned for more on these stories and anything else in or concerning Germany on November 16, 2026.

We'll be back with the latest headlines out of Germany tomorrow. Bis dann!

Germany dominated neighbor and historic rival the Netherlands in their Nations League quarterfinal match-up at Berlin's Olympic Stadium on Monday evening.

It was the team's sixth game under head coach Jürgen Klopp and the 50th ever between the two sides.

Germany's 5-0 shellacking of the Oranje was their most lopsided victory since 1959, when they won 7-0. In all, Germany have now won 19 of those matches, the Netherlands have won 12, and 18 ended in a draw.

Speaking to German broadcaster ARD after the game, attacking midfielder Florian Wirtz — who scored twice in the fixture — said: "We hope that we can make it fun for the fans. It was definitely fun for us, especially in the second half."

Despite the loss, Xavi Hernandez's Dutch side will reach the final eight alongside Germany.

Prior to the match, Klopp had made it clear that he and his team were approaching Monday's showdown as a final after having lost to Greece 1-0 in his first home game in the job on September 27.

By night's end, Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck each scored once and Brajan Gruda scored once and added two assists on top of Wirtz's double.

Klopp has been high on Wirtz, who has come under fire for not delivering at Liverpool since his arrival there in June 2025, and his bet seems to be paying off with the 23-year-old now scoring four goals in his last four games for Germany.

"We don't care who we play. We want to play attacking football. We want to score goals and dominate the opponent. And I think we did that perfectly," said Wirtz on Monday evening before adding: "We want to keep going next year. We want to get better. I think we've taken some great steps in our development as a team."

A group of five EU member states, including Germany, have entered talks over a scheme to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.

The plan to set up so-called return hubs in a non-EU country had been announced by the group — which also includes Austria, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark — had first been announced back in September.

Tesla has earmarked some €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its factory in Germany, near to Berlin.

The Grünheide complex will be expanded to start producing the electric car company's driverless Cybercabs, with output expected to eventually reach 1 million units.

The Elon Musk-owned company said construction would begin in 2027, with the first Cybercabs rolling off the line in 2029.

"With this, we are laying the foundations for the world's most technologically advanced Tesla factory here in Grünheide," Tesla said.

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has joined the chorus of football figures critical of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. But with time running out, there are few who seem willing to run against him.

Matt Pearson on our sports desk breaks down where the power struggle currently stands, with the deadline for candiates just a matter of hours away now.

Lawmakers in the state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have voted in Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier.

The 52-year-old has been in the role since 2017 and is heading into a third term.

The vote was a secret ballot, but it can still be assumed who voted and how.

She received 39 of the 68 votes cast in the chamber, exactly as many as commanded by Schwesig's three-party coaliton of her Social Democrats (29), the ecologist Greens (5), and the socialist Left Party (5).

While Söder's comments in Munich focused in particular on the policy the coalition in Berlin had not delivered, Merz initiatlly focused on talking up the efficacy of his federal coalition.

"We are aware of the situation. We know that we now need to deliver. And we also know that we face difficult talks within the coalition. But I would also say from the experiences of the last weeks that there are solutions to the problems which we have in Germany," Merz said.

Merz said that in the 18 months since last year's election, the coalition "has already successfully implemented many things, not 'set them into motion' as people like to say, but actually implemented."

He noted a total of 17 bills going through the second and third reading process in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, last week, "including the most comprehensive reforms of our intelligence and security services that we have ever done in [post-war] Germany."

Among others, he thanked Bavarian Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, a senior member of the Bavarian CSU sister party to Merz's own conservative CDU, for his contribution to this.

Merz also touted the support given to CSU politician Ilse Aigner, not just from his CDU but from the Social Democrat coalition partners and the Greens, to become the next president, calling her a person who would "represent our country very well at home and abroad."

After hailing these accomplishments, Merz then turned to electricity tax cuts, saying he anticipated talks on the matter on Tuesday that would be "very short."

He said that over the weekend, coalition leaders had revisited the figures, and now believed they would be able to "completely" reduce electricity taxes to the minimum European levels in 2027 "also for private households."

Bavarian state premier Markus Söder has appeared with Friedrich Merz at a press conference during the chancellor's trip to Munich.

It seems Söder, Merz and the CDU/CSU believe they have unfinished business after the budget was finalized in the Bundestag late last week.

Merz had pledged in the run-up to the decision to provide a reduction in electricity tax for all, but the final agreement did not include this step, with the coalition partners the Social Democrats (SPD) saying it was not adequately costed.

Söder said he and Merz had discussed "backup for the coming days," for Berlin and for a "collective stance, that is really, really important."

He said the coming days were about "demonstrating credibility in politics," seemingly in reference to Merz's promise that the coalition did not ultimately deliver.

"That's why it's really important to us that we do indeed bring about the reduction in electricity tax," Söder said. "This is important for businesses. It would be a relief for citizens. But it's also a matter of credibility and it's written in the coalition agreement."

Söder said that as to the question of "where the money comes from, with a €560 billion (roughly $615 billion) budget, with €200 billion in new debt, nobody can tell me there's no potential within the budgeting process."

A festive piece of merchandise on the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) "fan shop" website has upset some religious leaders in Germany.

Called a "chocolate Nicholas," it appears to depict a semblance of Saint Nicholas in bishop's regalia and the party's colors and holding a book with "AfD" written on the cover where a Bible might be in more traditional iconography.

The Bishop of Essen, Franz-Josef Overbeck, was highly critical of the promotion in Monday's edition of the Bild newspaper.

"The AfD is appropriating Christian symbols for party campaigning," Overbeck said. "Showing the holy Nicholas in a blue coat with mitre, staff and the gospel with an AfD logo is not in order."

Overbeck acknowledged that other organizations like football clubs would sell chocolate Christmas figurines in club colors, but he said they would tend to refrain from including overtly Christian symbols when doing so.

Bild quoted an AfD spokesman as saying that as a "liberal-conservative party that clearly associates itself with Christian values," the item fit "particularly well" with the party image.

The main German protestant church group EKD's cultural representative, Johann Hinrich Claussen, said the offer showed the AfD had "no understanding of traditions and no respect" for Christianity.

He described the action as "embarrassing and revealing," and said that Christianity was "supra-partisan."

"The AfD knows little about what is holy to Christians. Otherwise, it would be aware that Bishop Nicholas of Myra, in what today is Demre in Turkey, stood clearly for uniting the occident and the orient. Beyond that, he is the patron saint of rescues at sea," Claussen said.

The partner of deceased Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger has said that anybody is welcome at his funeral this coming Saturday.

Aiwanger was the economy minister in Bavaria's state government as the leader of the junior coalition partners to the center-right CSU.

"Hubert was a man of the people and so it stands to reason that anyone who liked or treaasured him is allowed to come to his funeral," Tanja Schweiger wrote on her Instagram profile overnight.

She was posting after a requiem in the state capital Munich paying tribute to the leader of the Free Voters (Freie Wähler) party over the weekend. Around 1,100 people attended this ceremony.

Aiwanger died suddenly and unexpectedly on November 4 during a working visit to Berlin, aged 55.

Prosecutors have since said he died of natural causes, after he was found dead in his hotel room.

Germany's national men's football team will play neighbors and rivals the Netherlands for the 50th time on Monday night.

And there's quite a lot at stake for Jürgen Klopp's team in the last group stage game of the Nations League competition at Berlin's Olympiastadion.

If Germany win, they will qualify for the knockout stages, but a defeat could lead to potential relegation into the second tier of Nations League football.

Klopp was upbeat in the pre-match press conference at the prospect of playing the Netherlands, who he said play "Xavi football," in the image of the skillful Spanish playmaker and World Cup winner coaching the team.

"I've always loved playing against teams like this. For all my coaching career," Klopp said. "When someone says, 'hey they can really play football,' then in my mind the party's already started."

A full house with some 71,000 fans is expected in the capital when the game kicks off. Klopp played on the Dutch reputation for liberal use of bicylces in his comments to reporters, saying he wanted to "put a stick in their spokes" and dislodge them from the saddle.

The notion of a bridge over the valley between Ratingen and Heiligenhaus to the east of Düsseldorf in western Germany as part of the A44 highway is more than half a century old. And the physical bridge itself has stood, complete, ever since 2022.

Yet still the crossing is not connected to any roads at either end.

A construction project to build the last 4.4 kilometers of highway and link the bridge to the A44 highway will formally start on Monday.

State premier Hendrik Wüst, as well as the regional transport and traffic ministers will attend the ground-breaking ceremony.

A project first conceived some 55 years ago has faced repeated delays because of lawsuits, environmental protection studies and onerous planning and permit procedures.

The bridge across the Angerbachtal (Angerbach Valley) should improve the road connection between the North Rhine-Westphalia state capital of Düsseldorf, the Bergisches Land mountain range and the industrial cities in the Ruhr Valley. It's also meant to help remove some strain from the perenially busy A3 highway and to improve the road connections to Düsseldorf International Airport.

The last stretch of highway is expected to cost around €200 million (roughly $220 million), or roughly the annual costs incurred each year by forcing traffic to divert around it, according to estimates from Düsseldorf's IHK industry and trade association.

Construction is expected to take several years, no formal end date has yet been set.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz heads to Munich early on Monday, for a meeting with the leadership of the Bavarian Christian Social Democrats (CSU), the sister party to his conservative  Christian Democrats(CDU).

No concrete details about the talks were made public ahead of time, except for the CSU saying it would serve as a general exchange that had been planned for some time.

The trip comes a week after Merz nominated Ilse Aigner as the next German president, likely paving the way for her to become the first woman and first CSU politician to assume the role.

It also follows soon after the 2027 federal budget cleared a marathon meeting of the parliamentary budget committee in Berlin. This serves as one of the more conspicuous examples of the frictions and difficulties in the grand coalition between the Christian Democrats and the center-left Social Democrats — with the compromises it contains a point of frustration among the CSU and for state premier Markus Söder.

The northeastern state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will likely vote in Social Democrat (SPD) Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier early in the afternoon.

The 52-year-old, who first stepped into the role in 2017, plans to lead a new coalition of the SPD, the environmentalist Greens and the socialist Left Party after state elections in September.

The right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) emerged as the largest single party in the sparsely populated state.

But still, the political calculus that emerged was arguably simpler than in Berlin — where the socialist Left Party is the largest party but could struggle to lead a coaltion — and in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD was by far the largest party but short of an outright majority.

Schwesig's SPD claimed 29 seats, with the Greens and the Left each taking 5, meaning that when combined, they hold a fairly clear majority over the AfD with its 32 seats.

The SPD's relatively successful performance in the state, at least compared to its national struggles, has also led to Schwesig being linked with a possible return to federal politics. The SPD plans to elect a new leadership duo early next year.

Schwesig has already had a spell in Berlin as the federal minsiter for families, pensioners and women, and briefly led the SPD on an interim basis in 2017, but after this she returned to her home state to seek the top regional job instead.

#187. Uber says hackers stole information on close to 150,000 driver’s licenses during data breach

Uber is notifying close to 150,000 drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers.

In notices filed this week with several U.S. attorneys general, including California and Iowa, the ride-hailing giant said it was notified on October 9 by the provider that hackers broke in and stole internal credentials, which were used to access Uber’s data.

The company said it subsequently began notifying affected drivers that their personal information was stored with the provider.

The stolen data includes affected drivers’ names, addresses, dates of birth, and driver’s license numbers.

TechCrunch has learned that the provider is Fireworks AI, which lets developers access and use open-weight AI models. Fireworks reported a data breach last month in which hackers stole its customers’ information, including billing data and some private AI datasets.

Online productivity startup Notion and AI coding startup Cursor have both confirmed that they had data stolen during the Fireworks hack.

In Uber’s case, the company said it had alerts enabled to detect unauthorized access to its Fireworks environment, but because the hackers used Fireworks’ own internal credentials, “no alerts were triggered.”

When reached for comment, an Uber spokesperson told TechCrunch: “The notices to drivers are in relation to a security incident impacting one of our third-party vendors, Fireworks.ai, which had access to some Uber data,” and deferred our questions to Fireworks.

A spokesperson for Fireworks confirmed that the company identified a security issue involving unauthorized access to some of its systems, which affected customer data, but the spokesperson did not address our questions about the incident.

Fireworks attributed its breach to a financially motivated cybercriminal group whose goals are to sell stolen tokens for accessing large language models, or LLMs. No known cybercriminal group has taken credit for the data theft.

In a notice filed with Oregon’s attorney general, Uber said it notified 149,346 people in total that their information had been taken in the breach at Fireworks.

TechCrunch previously reported that Uber has notified drivers in California, Illinois, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and South Carolina. We’ve also seen data breach notices filed in Texas and Vermont.

When asked by TechCrunch, Uber’s spokesperson did not say how many drivers are affected by the breach, nor how many drivers it was notifying about the incident.

It’s unclear if the number of affected drivers is expected to rise, and Uber did not respond to a follow-up email sent Monday.

This is Uber’s second known data breach this year. The company reported a security incident at its Uber Freight truck shipping unit, for which an extortion gang took credit for stealing data.

First published on November 13, and updated with a response from Fireworks, and again with a new updated figure of affected individuals from Oregon’s attorney general.

#186. Micron Technology: China probes US chip maker for cybersecurity risks as tech tension escalates

China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe announced new restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.

The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.

It came on the same day that Japan, a US ally, said it would restrict the export of advanced chip manufacturing equipment to countries including China, following similar moves by the United States and the Netherlands.

Washington and its allies have announced curbs on China’s semiconductor industry, which strike at the heart of Beijing’s bid to become a tech superpower.

Last month, the Netherlands also unveiled new restrictions on overseas sales of semiconductor technology, citing the need to protect national security. In October, the United States banned Chinese companies from buying advanced chips and chipmaking equipment without a license.

Micron told CNN it was aware of the review.

“We are in communication with the CAC and are cooperating fully,” it said, adding that it stands by the security of its products. “Micron’s product shipments, engineering, manufacturing, sales and other functions are operating as normal.”

Shares in Micron sank 4.4% on Wall Street Friday following the news, the biggest drop in more than three months. On Monday, they closed another 1.2% lower. Micron derives more than 10% of its revenue from China.

In an earlier filing, the Idaho-based company had warned of such risks.

“The Chinese government may restrict us from participating in the China market or may prevent us from competing effectively with Chinese companies,” it said last week.

Japan joins the US and Europe in chipmaking curbs on China

China has strongly criticized restrictions on tech exports, saying last month it “firmly opposes” such measures.

In efforts to boost growth and job creation, Beijing is seeking to woo foreign investments as it grapples with mounting economic challenges. The newly minted premier Li Qiang and several top economic officials have been rolling out the welcome wagon for global CEOs and promising they would “provide a good environment and services.”

But Beijing has also exerted growing pressure on foreign companies to bring them into line with its agenda.

Last month, authorities closed the Beijing office of Mintz Group, a US corporate intelligence firm, and detained five local staff.

Days earlier, they suspended Deloitte’s operations in Beijing for three months and imposed a fine of $31 million over alleged lapses in its work auditing a state-owned distressed debt manager.

CNN’s Michelle Toh, Junko Ogura, Sandi Sidhu and Chris Lau contributed to the article.

#184. California state AG sues OpenAI over rogue agent incidents

OpenAI is facing a new lawsuit from the California Attorney General’s office, alleging that the company’s training practices and lax security pose an ongoing danger to the public.

At the center of the case is the July 2026 Hugging Face compromise, in which a pre-release model within OpenAI compromised both companies’ security systems to complete a training benchmark. In its official report on the incident, OpenAI called it “an outlier scenario involving a rare and unexpected confluence of events.”

The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts by a government regulator to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident, with significant implications for both OpenAI’s competitors and its clients.

The complaint centers on the Hugging Face incident, but also cites similar incidents involving RubyGems, DseWiki, the Wikimedia Foundation, and Australian government websites as evidence that the underlying behavior is ongoing.

The complaint also alleges that dozens of similar incidents have occurred without public disclosure.

“OpenAI has recently sent notices to dozens of additional third parties whose websites or internal systems have been infiltrated by OpenAI agents,” the complaint reads. “In some cases, OpenAI agents were able to access sensitive personally identifiable information, such as employee records containing names, birth dates, addresses, and more. The vast majority of these incidents have not been disclosed or discussed publicly by either OpenAI or by the affected third parties.”

The central allegation is that OpenAI’s ongoing testing practices constitute a public nuisance because the lack of safety controls present an ongoing risk to the public. A secondary claim alleges unfair competition stemming from the marketing of an unsafe product. If the lawsuit succeeds, OpenAI could face an injunction “to abate the ongoing public nuisance,” leaving broad discretion in the hands of the court.

It’s the first regulatory case targeting OpenAI specifically over rogue agent incidents, although public endangerment claims have been considered by other states. In June, the Florida attorney general sued the company over allegedly harmful effects on users, particularly children and teenagers. In August, the Alabama attorney general launched a probe into deceptive practices related to the breach, but no case has been filed.

In a statement to the press, California Attorney General Rob Bonta presented the case as an effort to maintain public safety in the face of a powerful new technology.

“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society. The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in the statement. “The law is simple: Don’t do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place.”

In a statement, OpenAI emphasized the company’s extensive effort to investigate the Hugging Face incident and improve its systems in the aftermath.

“This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” OpenAI said. “We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

#183. South Sudan’s National Election, Its First, Will Be Delayed

Analysts had warned that the vote, originally set for December, faced a legitimacy crisis. South Sudan has not held a national election since gaining independence in 2011.

Officials in South Sudan, the world’s youngest state, said on Saturday that its first national election would be postponed, raising new questions about a vote that analysts had already said could not yield a credible result.

The National Elections Commission said in a statement that the presidential and legislative elections, which had been scheduled for Dec. 22, would be held on Feb. 11 instead. The country’s information minister, Ateny Wek Ateny, said the postponement would allow more time to register voters and educate them about the process.

South Sudan has never held a national election. Since gaining independence from Sudan in 2011 after decades of war, it has been ruled by President Salva Kiir, and it has faced seemingly intractable political difficulties.

In 2013, civil war broke out between the government and forces loyal to the main opposition leader, Riek Machar. Under a peace agreement to end the conflict in 2018, Mr. Machar became the vice president in a transitional government.

The upcoming election was supposed to underwrite that agreement. But the peace deal has unraveled since March 2025, when Mr. Machar was placed under house arrest in the capital, Juba, and charged with treason. In recent months, the government has replaced opposition lawmakers with its own supporters and dissolved the unity government.

With Mr. Machar effectively sidelined, there are no credible challengers to Mr. Kiir, who is widely expected to win the presidential election. He has a broad national following, and his party controls state institutions and the news media.

The election faces stark logistical challenges. Civil servants have not been paid in more than a year, and parts of the country are controlled by armed groups, including Mr. Machar’s forces. Thousands of people have died in fighting and attacks on civilians. In March, more than 200 people were killed in a massacre in Unity State near the border with Sudan, according to human rights groups.

“The conditions for credible polls are not currently in place,” the International Crisis Group said in a briefing for the U.N. Security Council this week. “Rushed elections could be a decisive final blow to the 2018 framework and would open the door to a return to sustained large-scale violence.”

Mr. Ateny, the information minister, acknowledged that the government could not gain access to “small parts” of the country, but said the election would be credible.

“It’s not always 100 percent, but it can be good for the sovereignty of the country and it’s good for the mandate of the state,” he said in an interview.

In addition to the violence and civil unrest, South Sudanese have been faced with soaring food prices, drought and flooding. Of the country’s roughly 12 million people, more than 8 million are in need of food assistance, according to the Famine Early Warning Systems Network, a globally recognized monitor of hunger.

Matthew Mpoke Bigg is the East Africa bureau chief for The New York Times, based in Nairobi, Kenya.

#182. Apple reveals new Mac security controls as AI agents raise privacy risks

As promised last month, Apple on Monday announced changes to Mac security controls designed to protect users’ data from the growing popularity of AI agents and their apps’ demand for “full disk access.”

“Before granting an app such extraordinary access, users should understand that it puts all of the data on their Mac at risk,” Apple warned in its blog post aimed at app developers.

Unlike AI chatbots that simply answer questions, agents run on a user’s device where they can take actions across the operating system, files, and apps on the user’s behalf.

To balance these competing interests, Apple said in October that it would revise some of its security settings around Mac apps. The announcement followed two notable incidents involving AI agents. In one, a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app read their private messages without consent; a separate report from Wired cited a flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac app that could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data.

Now, Apple is sharing the changes it’s making.

For starters, it’s splitting up Device Control and Data Access into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. The changes are designed to help users better understand that selecting the first option means overriding built-in security protections.

To streamline configurations, Apple says there will now also be a single method for granting permissions that involves selecting the requested app from a list. The company will also introduce new guidance encouraging users to grant access only to the specific apps that need it when they enable the System & App Protection Override setting. Similar guidance will appear when users enable Full Disk Access to allow an app to access their folders.

The company will also provide users with “increased visibility into the wide range of data apps will receive access to or control over if full permissions are granted,” the blog post notes.

Another change will give users more granular control over when an AI agent or app can gain access by allowing users to configure their apps to ask for permission every time access is needed. While arguably tedious and a potential obstacle to true automation, the feature could allow users to experiment with local AI without giving the agent carte blanche.

There will also be a new transparency indicator that appears when an app is controlling another app through the System & App Protection Override option.

The changes, which are arriving with macOS 27.3, don’t appear to prevent Mac users from installing and running AI agents or other apps that ask for higher levels of access. Instead, they give users more nuanced options, control, and information about the choices they’re making.

Apple advises app developers to adjust their onboarding processes to account for the new changes and suggests that their apps learn to “gracefully handle having access to only a limited set of folders or apps.”

Developers of apps that request Full Disk Access for disk backup or to provide assistive technologies can request exceptions to the new rules (which Apple calls “entitlements”) to preserve the same functionality they offered before the macOS 27.3 update.

#177. All the questions Nvidia should answer on Tuesday — but probably won’t

Nvidia interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress is about to have one of the biggest days of her career on Tuesday when the company reports its third-quarter results.

For the first time, Kress will be running through the numbers and sharing guidance without Nvidia’s charismatic but now-disgraced founder Jensen Huang.

Huang was forced to resign last week after he admitted to having an affair with an exec of a customer, Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and he was accused of having two more affairs with Nvidia employees.

Now, the company is facing questions about its restricted chips allegedly being smuggled into China, especially by Huang’s mistress’ company. Nvidia promised to conduct an internal investigation. Meanwhile, Huang was commanded to answer questions to Congress in a closed-door joint session with three Republican-led committees. Plus, top Democrats have also vowed to investigate the company.

Given the turmoil Nvidia is in, there are a number of questions that Kress should answer.

Huang’s role now and going forward. Huang ran Nvidia with an iron fist, having some 60 direct reports and his fingers in everything. No one knows the company better than him.

An internet petition signed by 180,000 and growing is calling for the board to reinstate him. Huang may also have been mounting an attempt to return, Financial Times reported. However, CNBC is reporting, citing unnamed sources, that the company is not in talks to reinstate Huang.

So, we’ll be looking for language from the interim CEO about Huang’s ongoing involvement with the company, its search for a new CEO, and any talks to bring him back.

China and Singapore. As Huang vehemently argued in favor of easing export restrictions for Nvidia chips to China, Huang said that he’s seen no evidence that its powerful semiconductors were being diverted from legit buyers to China.

But in October 2025, The New York Times reported that the U.S. was investigating Huang’s mistress’ company, Megaspeed, over allegations it was doing just that. Nvidia at the time vouched to CNBC that Megaspeed was legally using the chips for its cloud. However, Nvidia recently told The Wall Street Journal that it had voluntarily blocked Megaspeed from receiving more chips way back in June 2025.

Last year, Nvidia said that Singapore, the region where Megaspeed is located, was one of its fastest-growing, accounting for 22% of its total revenue for its second quarter of that year. After the investigation into Megaspeed came to light, Nvidia changed how it reported revenue. It now reports based on a company’s headquarters, instead of its shipping address. That completely hid sales to Singapore and Megaspeed’s impact.

So we’re listening to what Kress says about the future of sales to the China region and the cloud business in Singapore that was once 20% of sales. We’re especially listening for what she says about Nvidia keeping track of where its restricted chips wind up.

China sales policy. Huang’s argument was, essentially, that the U.S. can’t stop China from developing advanced AI models, so the West is better off selling them less powerful Nvidia chips and keeping them dependent, he said on the Dwarkesh Podcast last summer. Notably, that’s a position that would make Nvidia a lot of money.

The China hawks counter that selling an adversary any powerful chips at all will help them, and U.S. companies shouldn’t do that. So we’re listening for any indications that Kress is reversing Nvidia’s goals with China.

Bankrolling the AI build-out. The expectation is that Kress, the CFO who reportedly had unsuccessfully tried to push back against Huang’s extreme AI dealmaking, will be conservative on such deals going forward. We’ll be listening for what she says about the impacts of existing deals on the books. (Will she subtly try to throw Huang under the bus for those controversial deals?) We’ll also be listening for her future plans.

Governance. With the ousting of Huang and more fallout sure still to come, has the board learned its lesson about too much power in the hands of one person? We’ll be listening for information about how Nvidia might restructure itself.

#176. A Mexican Artist Sang Some of His Hits. Authorities Stopped the Show, Then Arrested Him.

A concert by the singer Gabito Ballesteros was suspended after he sang songs that supposedly glorify cartel culture. The action has renewed a debate over culture and free speech.

A popular Mexican singer’s concert was halted on Friday night because he performed songs considered to be glorifying cartel culture, making him the latest and most high-profile artist to be ensnared in a government crackdown on the genre known as narcocorridos.

He was later arrested by the federal authorities in relation to an unrelated investigation.

Gabito Ballesteros, 27, whose songs have billions of streams, was performing at a fair in Querétaro State in central Mexico when authorities escorted him off the stage.

Before the show, his set list was reviewed and approved by state officials and event organizers, according to a statement issued by the fair. Songs that glorified criminal activities were explicitly excluded, in accordance with state regulations, the fair said.

Last year, the state joined several other states and municipalities throughout Mexico that effectively prohibit the public performance of so-called narcocorridos, a version of traditional Mexican ballads that celebrate drug cartels instead of historic events and everyday life. Violations were punishable with fines or even jail time.

The actions — and the genre itself — have sparked much debate in Mexico, which has been wrestling with both the effects of organized crime, particularly amid pressure from the Trump administration to crack down on cartels, and its identity as defined through popular culture. The discussion also has became a referendum on free speech.

On Friday night, Mr. Ballesteros performed an unauthorized song and local authorities took him offstage to remind him of his prior agreement, the fair said. When he returned, the fair said Mr. Ballesteros started to perform another unauthorized song, “AMG.” The 2022 hit, which references the luxurious lifestyles and fancy cars of cartel members, has nearly one billion streams on Spotify.

#175. Cyber giant Infoblox confirms security incident after hackers access ‘company information’

Cybersecurity and automation giant Infoblox has confirmed a cybersecurity incident, during which hackers accessed company information through one of its technology vendors.

Infoblox is a privately held cyber giant that provides companies cybersecurity and networking services, such as domain name resolution and identity and user access management.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Infoblox told TechCrunch that the company is “investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor.”

“We immediately activated our incident response procedures, took steps to contain the incident and are working with leading outside cybersecurity experts to investigate the facts, understand the scope and address any confirmed risks.”

TechCrunch has learned that the data breach involves a vendor that provides SharePoint data migration services, according to a notification sent by Infoblox about the breach, two people with knowledge of the incident told TechCrunch.

One of the people said sensitive customer data was taken in the breach.

According to public internet records seen by TechCrunch, Infoblox hosts much of its files, emails, and infrastructure with Microsoft, including a SharePoint server, which TechCrunch confirmed is accessible through Infoblox’s single sign-on provider. SharePoint is web-based software that companies use to share and host internal files and documents.

Infoblox has not named the third-party migration vendor that was hacked, but one person with knowledge of the incident said that Infoblox has terminated its work with the vendor.

The company’s spokesperson did not comment on this, but added that the company has “no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved” in the breach.

Infoblox would not say how many customers were affected by the incident, or if the company is aware at this time. The company also did not say, when asked, if it had been contacted by the hackers and if they had made any demands.

#174. Erdogan's political fate may be determined by Turkey's Kurds

Editor’s Note:  A version of this story first appeared in CNN’s Meanwhile in the Middle East newsletter, a three-times-a-week look inside the region’s biggest stories. Sign up here.

Turkey’s persecuted pro-Kurdish party has emerged as a kingmaker in the country’s upcoming election, playing a decisive role that may just tip the balance enough to unseat two-decade ruler Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

In a key setback to the Turkish president and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AK Party), the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) last month announced that it would not put forward its own presidential candidate, a move analysts say allows its supporters to vote for Erdogan’s main rival.

“We are facing a turning point that will shape the future of Turkey and (its) society,” said the HDP in a statement on March 23. “To fulfill our historical responsibility against the one-man rule, we will not field a presidential candidate in (the) May 14 elections.”

It is a twist of irony for the Turkish strongman, who spent the better half of the past decade cracking down on the party after it began chipping away at his voter base. Its former leader Selahattin Demirtas has been in prison for nearly seven years and the party faces possible closure by a court for suspected collusion with the militant Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and affiliated groups. But its influence may nonetheless determine the course of Turkey’s politics.

The HDP’s decision not to field a candidate came just three days after head of the Republican People’s Party (CHP) Kemal Kilicdaroglu, Erdogan’s main rival, visited the party’s co-chairs. He told reporters that the solution to Turkey’s problems, “including the Kurdish problem” lies in parliament,” according to Turkish media.

Kilicdaroglu, who represents the six-party Nation Alliance opposition bloc, is the strongest contender to run against Erdogan in years. And while the HDP hasn’t yet announced whether it will put its weight behind him, analysts say it is the kingmaker in the elections.

Erdogan's 'polar opposite' wants to replace him as president of Turkey

“It was a carefully crafted political discourse,” Hisyar Ozsoy, deputy co-chair of the HDP and a member of parliament from the predominantly Kurdish province of Diyarbakir, told CNN. “We are not going to have our own candidate, and we will leave it to the international community to interpret it the way they wish.”

Experts say the crackdown on the HDP is rooted in the threat it poses to Erdogan politically, as well as its position as one of the main parties representing Turkey’s Kurds, an ethnic minority from which a separatist militant movement has emerged.

The party and the Kurdish people have had a complicated relationship with Erdogan. The leader courted the Kurds in earlier years by granting them more rights and reversing restrictions on the use of their language. Relations with the HDP were also cordial once, as Erdogan worked with the party on a brief peace process with the PKK.

But ties between Erdogan and the HDP later turned sour, and the HDP fell under a sweeping crackdown aimed at the PKK and their affiliates.

Kurds are the biggest minority in Turkey, making up between 15% and 20% of the population, according to Minority Rights Group International.

It is unclear if the HDP will endorse Kilicdaroglu, but analysts say that the deliberate distance may be beneficial for the opposition candidate.

The accusations against the HDP place it in a precarious position during the elections. It currently faces a case in Turkey’s Constitutional Court over suspected ties to the PKK, which is designated as a terrorist group by Turkey, the United States and the European Union. Knowing it may be banned at any moment, its candidates are running under the Green Left Party in parliament.

If the opposition is seen as allying with the HDP, Erdogan’s AK Party may use its influence in the media to discredit it as being pro-PKK, said Murat Somer, a political science professor at Koc University in Istanbul and author of Return to Point Zero, a book on the Turkish-Kurdish question in Turkey.

The HDP’s threat to Erdogan’s hold on power became apparent after the June 2015 election, the first general election it participated in. It won 13% of the seats, denying the ruling AK Party its majority for the first time since 2002. Erdogan, however, called a snap election five months later, which led to a drop in the HDP’s support to 10.7%, as well as the restoration of the AK Party’s overall majority.

“They are a kingmaker in these elections because the HDP gets about half of the votes of the Kurdish population in Turkey,” said Somer, adding that the other, more conservative Kurdish voters have traditionally voted for Erdogan’s AK Party. And last month, the Free Cause Party (HUDA-PAR), a tiny Kurdish-Islamist party announced support for Erdogan in the elections. The party has never won seats in parliament.

Erdogan's political fate may rest on his response to the earthquake

The HDP knows that its position is key to the outcome of next month’s vote, but that it’s also in a delicate situation.

“We want to play the game wisely, and we need to be very careful,” said Ozsoy, adding that the party wants to avoid a “contaminated political climate” where the elections are polarized “between a very ugly ultra-nationalist discourse against Kilicdaroglu and others.”

The party was founded in 2012 with a number of aims, said Ozsoy, one of which was “peaceful and democratic resolution of the Kurdish conflict.”

Somer said that the party was seen to be “an initiative” of the PKK, which later led to a heavy government crackdown on it in the name of counterterrorism.

Its former leader Demirtas remains an influential figure.

The Turkish government has been trying to link the HDP to the PKK but has so far failed to prove “a real connection,” said Asli Aydintasbas, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution in Washington, DC.

A post-Erdogan Turkey may give some breathing space to the Kurds and Kurdish-dominated parties in Turkey, Aydintasbas told CNN, noting that many Kurdish voters have recently left Erdogan’s camp. “For HDP, this is more than just an ideological choice,” she said. “It’s a matter of survival.”

Ozsoy says his party understands what’s at stake, not only for Turkey’s Kurds but for all its minorities.

“We are aware of our responsibility here. We are aware of our role. We know we are in a kingmaker position,” the HDP lawmaker said.

#170. In Banff, a Grizzly Bear Known as ‘the Boss’ Rules the National Park

Bear 122 has survived a train, cars and rival bears. Some fear the biggest threat to his life now is his own fame.

“The Boss,” the near mythical grizzly bear king of Banff National Park.Credit...All in the Wild Photography

Reporting from Banff National Park, Canmore and Dead Man’s Flats, Alberta.

To the scientists and wardens of Banff National Park he is grizzly bear 122. But to everyone who lives in or near Canada’s oldest national park, and many of its 4.5 million annual visitors, he is the Boss.

He has been struck by a freight train without apparent ill effect. He has shrugged off being hit by cars. Scientists have confirmed that he killed and snacked on a black bear at least once, and he is believed to have fathered many, if not most, of the bears in his 2,000-square-kilometer territory.

Most of all, the Boss has become Canada’s 700-pound celebrity bear king. When he strolls along the Trans-Canada Highway looking for dandelions, “bear jams” swiftly follow. His battles with a rival bear known as Split Lip are legendary. (He caused the split lip.) His annual awakening from hibernation, usually in March, is reported by news outlets across Alberta.

Galleries in Banff and neighboring Canmore ship giant photos of him worldwide. His image appears on fridge magnets, T-shirts and tote bags. A local restaurant is named for him, its main dining room dominated by a scrap metal sculpture of the bear.

But despite his fearsome demeanor, enhanced by four-inch claws, few bear experts consider the Boss a threat to park visitors or residents. Rather, they fear his celebrity and the legions of fans it have created, may be the biggest threat to his life and his dominance.

#168. Israeli military veterans, a backbone of protest movement, vow to keep demonstrating

In a sea of Israeli flags, Yiftach Golov holds one that looks a little different.

Among the hundreds of thousands of protesters who took to the streets for the 13th week in a row on Saturday, Golov hoists a brown flag that represents a group called “Brother and Sisters in Arms.”

They are veterans – many, like Golov, from elite forces – who now feel they are fighting on a new battlefield: To save Israeli democracy.

“We believe this is our responsibility to go once again called to the flag of the nation to stop this madness to defend Israel,” Golov said, as he weaved his way through the protesters on Tel Aviv’s Kaplan street, between the high-rises that house many of Israel’s high tech companies.

During the second intifada, in the early 2000s, Golov served in a special forces reconnaissance unit. He was never before particularly political, focusing more on getting his PhD in biophysics from Tel Aviv University.

But when the protest movement against the Israeli government’s judicial overhaul plan began in January, Golov attended one a demonstration and soon became one of thousands of veterans, and now military reservists, who have taken up the cause as their new mission.

Some, including elite Air Force reservists, have taken it a step further, threatening not to heed the call to train or even serve in protest of the government’s plans planned judicial changes, which would give the governing parties more control over Israel’s judiciary.

Others have taken to becoming some of the most active organizers and demonstrators. Last week, a group from Brothers and Sisters in Arms protested by carrying a figure wrapped in the Israeli flag on a stretcher, the way they would carry a wounded comrade off the field.

While Golov says he has not taken the drastic step to refuse service, he understands the motivation.

“We’re fighting for justice and liberty, just like the American story, that’s the values that that are being represented symbolized back when we look at our flag, that’s something that was lacking lacking for the last few decades. So basically, we reclaim the flag,” he said.

Palestinian taxi driver recounts surviving attack by right-wing protesters

Fellow members of the group, all wearing brown shirts with the organization’s logo, come up and say hello. They’re sprinkled all throughout the protests. One is even leading the “Pink Front,” a group of coordinated drummers who look like they are dressed for a rave, and often lead the chants at the protests.

They’re using skills they learned in the military – how to organize, how to mobilize – now for the protests. But more importantly, they say they have the same type of motivation.

“The very deep feeling that you are part of something bigger than yourself, that (you’re) allowed to sacrifice anything that is needed, whether it’s your career, health, seriously mental health,” Golov said. “We all have a mission, you’re willing to do it at any cost. You’re very determined, you know that you are on the right side, you’re carrying the torch of light. That keeps us being highly motivated despite the fact that we’re not sleeping for days.”

Israel’s protest movement is made up of many disparate groups, but the pressure from Israel’s much vaunted veterans has been seen as a key to moving the needle.

Last Monday, after weeks of sustained protests and the largest general strike in Israeli history, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a pause to the legislation, to allow time for negotiations with the opposition.

But despite the announcements, protesters are still out in the streets in large numbers. CNN affiliate Channel 12 in Israel estimated the size of Saturday’s demonstration in Tel Aviv at about 150,000 people. Organizers claimed it was 230,000.

Last week’s mass protests and widespread strike action came after Netanyahu said he had decided to fire Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for advocating a delay in passing the legislation – a move that Netanyahu has since delayed, sources told CNN, due to “the present security situation.”

In his televised speech calling for a delay, Gallant had said the pause in the legislation was needed “for the security of Israel,” citing the refusal of some Israel Defense Forces reservists to train in protest of the government plans. He said pressing ahead with the proposals could threaten Israel’s security.

Under pressure at home and from allies abroad, Netanyahu said he would delay votes on the remaining legislation until after the Knesset’s Passover recess in April “to give time for a real chance for a real debate.”

“Out of the responsibility to the nation, I decided to delay … the vote, in order to give time for discussion,” he added.

But Netanyahu indicated that the delay was only temporary. He insisted that the overhaul was necessary, and reiterated criticism of refusal to train or serve in the military in protest at the planned changes. “Refusing is the end of our country,” he said.

Many protesters don’t believe that the pause is real, or say it’s simply a stalling tactic to give Netanyahu some breathing room and get the protesters to go home before he plows on with the reforms.

“We will start doing deactivation only when we will know 100% that Israel state will stay a functional democratic country. Whatever needs to be done for that,” Golov said.

#161. Band of baby sea turtles swims into ocean after historic California nesting

Hatchlings emerge after discovery in September of first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on US west coast

Two months after the discovery of the first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on the US west coast, the eggs have hatched – and California’s first group of 75 native-born olive ridley sea turtles have been released into the Pacific.

The eggs incubated at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach after the historic discovery of two separate nests in September at southern California beaches, a shift likely driven by this year’s El Niño conditions.

On Saturday, the Aquarium of the Pacific announced the turtles’ first emergence in a social media post: “The hatchlings are here! We are excited to share that some of the olive ridley sea turtle eggs from Seal Beach successfully hatched after a 58-day incubation period. Working with our partners, we carefully released them from the beach in the dark early hours of this morning.”

A day later, the Aquarium added: “Even more egg-citing news! A second group of olive ridley sea turtle hatchlings, this time from the Huntington Beach nest, was released into the ocean early Sunday morning.”

In total, 54 turtles were released from the Seal Beach nest and 21 from the Huntington Beach nest.

On 16 September, an olive ridley sea turtle was observed digging a nest and laying eggs on Seal Beach in the first-recorded instance of any sea turtle nesting on the west coast. Three days later, a second turtle was spotted nesting on Huntington Beach.

Typically a tropical species, the olive ridley sea turtle normally resides in the Pacific, Indian and Atlantic oceans, but has been known to nest on the southern tip of Baja California.

“It is not known why these turtles chose southern California beaches as nesting sites, but it indicates an important historical change that could have long-term implications for the species and for local sea turtle management and protection,” the Aquarium of the Pacific said in a social media post.

“The behavior of these turtles was probably influenced, at least in part, by the incoming El Niño, along with the recent tropical storm, range expansion, or perhaps navigational mistakes. The species is also known for its behavioral flexibility.”

As Hurricane Polo began to form in late September, researchers with the aquarium and its federal and local partners relocated the 204 eggs from the two nests to incubate in the safety of the aquarium’s animal care facility.

“As animals adapt in unexpected ways to changes in their natural world, humans will need to adapt and make space to ensure endangered and threatened species are given a fighting chance,” said Jeffrey Flocken, president and CEO of the Aquarium of the Pacific.

“If they successfully hatch, these baby turtles will likely one day return to nest to carry on future generations on these very same beaches, giving us a remarkable opportunity to help a species expand its range and thrive.”

Even as the Huntington Beach and Seal Beach turtles have begun hatching and returned to the ocean, researchers are continuing to advise the public to be on the lookout for more nests. On 1 November, a third nest was recorded in Ventura county although those eggs were swept away by unusually high tides – likely also caused by El Niño.

#158. A new approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine shows early promise

Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.

In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.

WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk

Although this vaccine has several more hurdles to clear before it gets to a doctor’s office or drug store, other nasal vaccines are in use or are nearing the finish line in clinical trials.

China and India both rolled out vaccines given through the nasal tissues last fall, though it’s not clear how well they may be working. Studies on the effectiveness of these vaccines have yet to be published, leaving much of the world to wonder whether this approach to protection really works in people.

The US has reached something of a stalemate with Covid-19. Even with the darkest days of the pandemic behind us, hundreds of Americans are still dying daily as the infection continues to simmer in the background of our return to normal life.

As long as the virus continues to spread among people and animals, there’s always the potential for it mutate into a more contagious or more damaging version of itself. And while Covid infections have become manageable for most healthy people, they may still pose a danger to vulnerable groups such as the elderly and immunocompromised.

Researchers hope next-generation Covid-19 vaccines, which aim to shut down the virus before it ever gets a chance to make us sick and ultimately prevent the spread of infection, could make our newest resident respiratory infection less of a threat.

China approves its first mRNA Covid-19 vaccine

One way scientists are trying to do that is by boosting mucosal immunity, beefing up immune defenses in the tissues that line the upper airways, right where the virus would land and begin to infect our cells.

It’s a bit like stationing firefighters underneath the smoke alarm in your house, says study author Emanuel Wyler, a scientist at the Max Delbruck Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association in Berlin.

The immunity that’s created by shots works throughout the body, but it resides primarily in the blood. That means it may take longer to mount a response.

“If they are already on site, they can immediately eliminate the fire, but if they’re like 2 miles away, they first need to drive there, and by that time, one-third of the house is already in full flames,” Wyler said.

Mucosal vaccines are also better at priming a different kind of first responder than injections do. They do a better job of summoning IgA antibodies, which have four arms to grab onto invaders instead of the two arms that the y-shaped IgG antibodies have. Some scientists think IgA antibodies may be less picky about their targets than IgG antibodies, which makes them better equipped to deal with new variants.

The new nasal vaccine takes a new approach to a very old idea: weakening a virus so it’s no longer a threat and then giving it to people so their immune systems can learn to recognize and fight it off. The first vaccines using this approach date to the 1870s, against anthrax and rabies. Back then, scientists weakened the agents they were using with heat and chemicals.

The researchers manipulated the genetic material in the virus to make it harder for cells to translate. This technique, called codon pair deoptimization, hobbles the virus so it can be shown to the immune system without making the body sick.

“You could imagine reading a text … and every letter is a different font, or every letter is a different size, then the text is much harder to read. And this is basically what we do in codon pair deoptimization,” Wyler said.

In the hamster studies, which were published Monday in the journal Nature Microbiology, two doses of the live but weakened nasal vaccine created a much stronger immune response than either two doses of an mRNA-based vaccine or one that uses an adenovirus to ferry the vaccine instructions into cells.

The researchers think the live weakened vaccine probably worked better because it closely mimics the process of a natural infection.

The nasal vaccine also previews the entire coronavirus for the body, not just its spike proteins like current Covid-19 vaccines do, so the hamsters were able to make immune weapons against a wider range of targets.

As promising as all this sounds, vaccine experts say caution is warranted. This vaccine still has to pass more tests before it’s ready for use, but they say the results look encouraging.

Health officials consider another round of bivalent boosters for the most vulnerable Americans

“They did a very nice job. This is obviously a competent and thoughtful team that did this work, and impressive in the scope of what they did. Now it just needs to be repeated,” perhaps in primates and certainly in humans before it can be widely used, said Dr. Greg Poland, who designs vaccines at the Mayo Clinic. He was not involved in the new research.

The study began in 2021, before the Omicron variant was around, so the vaccine tested in these experiments was made with the original strain of the coronavirus. In the experiments, when they infected animals with Omicron, the live but weakened nasal vaccine still performed better than the others, but its ability to neutralize the virus was diminished. Researchers think it will need an update.

It also needs to be tested in humans, and Wyler says they’re working on that. The scientists have partnered with a Swiss company called RocketVax to start phase I clinical trials.

Other vaccines are further along, but the progress has been “slow and halting,” Poland said. Groups working on these vaccines are struggling to raise the steep costs of getting a new vaccine to market, and they’re doing it in a setting where people tend to think the vaccine race has been won and done.

In reality, Poland said, we’re far from that. All it would take is another Omicron-level shift in the evolution of the virus, and we could be back at square one, with no effective tools against the coronavirus.

“That’s foolish. We should be developing a pan-coronavirus vaccine that does induce mucosal immunity and that is long-lived,” he said.

At least four nasal vaccines for Covid-19 have reached late-stage testing in people, according to the World Health Organization’s vaccine tracker.

The nasal vaccines in use in China and India rely on harmless adenoviruses to ferry their instructions into cells, although effectiveness data for these has not been published.

Two other nasal vaccines are finishing human studies.

Covid vaccine maker Novavax says it may not survive

One, a recombinant vaccine that can be produced cheaply in chicken eggs, the same way many flu vaccines are, is being put through its paces by researchers at Mount Sinai in New York City.

Another, like the German vaccine, uses a live but weakened version of the virus. It’s being developed by a company called Codagenix. Results of those studies, which were carried out in South America and Africa, may come later this year.

The German team says it’s eagerly watching for the Codagenix data.

“They will be very important in order to know where whether this kind of attempt is basically promising or not,” Wyler said.

They have reason to worry. Respiratory infections have proved to be tough targets for inhaled vaccines.

FluMist, a live but weakened form of the flu virus, works reasonably well in children but doesn’t help adults as much. The reason is thought to be that adults already have immune memory for the flu, and when the virus is injected into the nose, the vaccine mostly boosts what’s already there.

Sign up here to get The Results Are In with Dr. Sanjay Gupta every Tuesday from the CNN Health team.

Still, some of the most potent vaccines such as the vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella use live attenuated viruses, so it’s a promising approach.

Another consideration is that live vaccines can’t be taken by everyone. People with very compromised immunity are often cautioned against using live vaccines because even these very weakened viruses may be risky for them.

“Although it’s strongly attenuated, it’s still a real virus,” Wyler said, so it would have to be used carefully.

#156. Is Italy the Model for Europe’s Future?

Over more than a quarter-century, I’ve watched Europe’s politics become more like Italy’s, with all the resulting instability, as the far right came in from the cold.

Jason Horowitz, previously bureau chief in Rome, is now bureau chief in Madrid. This article is adapted from his recent book, “The Italian Job: A Memoir of an American Reporter in Rome.”

When I first moved to Rome, I spent my time living in the past.

At the turn of the century, I drifted through a vintage postcard of postwar Italy: old women sitting around tables they had dragged into the street, old men playing cards in caps, cats arching their backs on the hoods of snub-nosed Fiats.

As newspapers filled with talk of Silvio Berlusconi, a media mogul with ambitions and appetites worthy of a Roman emperor, my meanderings inevitably took me toward Tiber Island, a sliver of land in the middle of the river that divides Rome.

An ancient bridge on the island’s left bank had a strange statue of weather-beaten faces positioned back-to-back as if they couldn’t stand one another. The heads rose out of the shared torso of a square pillar and represented Janus, Rome’s god of the past and future, the deity of transitions and change.

Back then, I didn’t see the change around me, but now, more than a quarter-century later, after spending decades reporting on Italian politics and changes across Europe, I have come to understand that I was living in the future.

In the time since, I have seen an Italianization of politics all around the continent, with coalitions of small parties resulting in instability, with fed-up voters desperate for new saviors. But more than anything, I have seen — in Britain, France, Germany — countries following the Italian model by allowing the far right into the political mainstream.
