#152. The $500 billion beauty industry's 'green' ambitions are a patchwork at best. And they're falling short

The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.

'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, new report shows. Here are the key takeaways

Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an important purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.

This shift in consumer preferences has propelled many beauty brands to set environmental goals: to move away from single-use and virgin plastics, provide recyclable, reusable and refillable packaging and offer more transparency around products’ ingredients so customers can ascertain how “green” their purchase is.

However, consumers still struggle to understand the sustainability credentials of many products, according to the British Beauty Council. This is because the industry’s clean-up efforts have been inconsistent, and fall short of making a recognizable impact in the absence of collective goal-setting, global strategy and standardized regulations.

There is no international standard for the beauty industry on how much product ingredient information to share with customers — or how to do so. Brands can set their own rules and goals, giving rise to confusion and “greenwashing,” where sustainability claims are often touted but not substantiated.

Companies often use marketing language like “clean beauty” to make it seem like their products are natural, for example, when they may not actually be organic, sustainable or ethically made.

After rebranding in the West, many beauty companies are still offering to 'whiten' skin elsewhere

“The term ‘clean beauty’ has become quite dangerous. It’s used to sell more products,” according to British Beauty Council CEO Millie Kendall, who added that such buzzwords are losing traction in the UK as British customers wise up to their shortcomings. “Customers need better marketing information and certification information.”

In a 2021 report calling on the industry to have “the courage to change” their business practices, the British Beauty Council wrote that, all too often, even natural ingredients involved in manufacturing products give way to “over-consumption, non-regenerative farming practices, pollution, waste and neglect.”

“The only way out of this is transparency,” Kendall told CNN.

Jen Lee, chief impact officer at US-based brand Beautycounter, said she continues to see confusion over ingredients among consumers. (In 2013, the company launched and published “The Never List,” which currently cites more than 2,800 chemicals — including heavy metals, parabens and formaldehyde — it claims to never use in its products.)

“Natural vs. synthetic ingredients has been a conversation. People think natural is safer, but it’s not always the case,” Lee explained. “Natural ingredients formulated in the industry can have toxic load. Heavy metals can occur in natural components of the earth.”

Mother loses peripheral vision from apparent exposure to mercury in beauty creams. Toxic levels in her home put family at risk, say experts

“We used to be more natural and organic,” added Sasha Plavsic, founder of makeup brand ILIA Beauty. “What was challenging is (that) raw materials were difficult to source or would come in inconsistently or products wouldn’t perform.”

Most makeup is created and molded at high temperatures, Plavsic explained. Purely organic materials often fall apart in this heat, leading to inconsistent results and subpar product performance. “Not every synthetic is bad,” Plavsic said. “Sometimes, it helps create the best in class formula.”

The industry’s plastic packaging is a particular sustainability challenge — 95% is thrown away and the vast majority is not recycled, according to the British Beauty Council.

The cosmetics business is the fourth biggest plastic packaging user globally — after food and beverage, industrial packaging and pharmaceuticals — and plastic is about 67% of the industry’s packaging volume, according to Vantage Market Research. Beauty giant L’Oreal used 144,430 metric tons of plastic in its packaging material in 2021, for example, according to the Ellen Macarthur Foundation (EMF). Estee Lauder Companies reported its brands produced 71,600 metric tons of plastic in product packaging that same year.

And only 9% of the global plastic waste is recycled, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The United States only recycles 4% of its plastic waste.

Single-use plastic is wreaking havoc on the planet. Here's what you can do to minimize your impact

Many brands are trying to phase out harmful plastics from their operations and adopt post-consumer recycled (PCR) plastic. (L’Oreal has set a target of 50% PCR plastic usage by 2025, while Estee Lauder is targeting 25% “or more” PCR plastic — but both are far from achieving their targets.)

“Between 60-70 major global brands have made unprecedented progress” in PCR plastic usage across industries, EMF’s Plastic Initiative Lead Sander DeFruyt told CNN. But DeFruyt stressed that PCR plastic must be adopted in conjunction with brands removing single and virgin plastics from their usage cycles to truly make a difference.

However, PCR plastic is not easy to find — low recycling rates around the world mean there is limited supply. Meanwhile, demand for it is growing demand across industries, DeFruyt said. This competition hikes up its price, which is already higher than virgin plastic.

Hair care brand FEKKAI claims that it used up to 95% PCR content in its packaging, but pricing and supply issues posed a challenge, forcing it to currently aim for containers and packaging that feature at least 50% PCR in its packaging.

“PCR plastic is more expensive than stock plastic. The cost is hard and then sourcing it is too,” founder Frédéric Fekkai told CNN. “PCR is close to our heart, but there is a massive demand, so finding recycled plastic is difficult.”

Beauty retailers plays a pivotal — and under-utilized — role, with control over stocking decisions and supply chains. But many vary when it comes to the standards they set for brands they sell.

“Smaller businesses do more, full stop,” said Jessi Baker, founder of the technology platform Provenance, which helps brands display their sustainability credentials for customers. “They move more nimbly. Some of them are born-good brands — climate friendliness was part of their setup. They don’t need to restructure their entire supply chain. Their culture already has it compared to the larger brands who need to work hard to change.”

A history of beauty trends -- and the standards that shaped them

Sephora launched its “Clean + Planet Positive” initiative in 2021, which labeled products that met its set criteria. (This is separate from the French retailer’s “Clean at Sephora” program, which is currently facing a consumer lawsuit alleging it carries a significant percentage of products understood by customers to be harmful.) Target launched a similar program in 2022, featuring a “Target Zero” icon for both online and in-store offerings that either have reusable, recyclable, compostable or reduced plastic packaging, or feature waterless or concentrated products.

Still, many steps taken by brands and retailers do not even begin to touch on the waste and pollution generated throughout supply chains, manufacturing and shipping, all huge problems for the industry to grapple with.

The gaps in standardization in the beauty ecosystem can, to some extent, be filled by certifications such as the US-born B Corporation, or B Corp. This accreditation, one of the most well-known in the beauty space, is issued by the non-profit B Lab, which scores a company on a variety of criteria around ethics and sustainability. However beneficial it may be among eco-conscious consumers, though, it is currently completely voluntary for brands to apply for.

Governments and multinationals enforcing regulations and setting a base line for brands to operate from when making sustainability claims would go a long way to making change, many experts and business leaders believe.

Susanne Kaufmann, founder of her namesake beauty brand, says her efforts in Austria would reap better results if more countries around the world had stricter, more uniform garbage disposal laws.

A trash heap 62 meters high shows the scale of India's climate challenge

“I package our product in a recyclable material,” Kaufmann said. (Her products’ packaging, which is refillable and reusable, is made from 75% recycled plastic — and is 100% recyclable.) If I send this to the US, the garbage is not separated… and it’s not recyclable,” she explained, referring to inconsistencies in recycling laws across the United States.

And when it comes to ingredients, the European Chemicals Agency lists 2,495 substances banned from use in cosmetic products marketed for sale or use in the bloc. But the US Food and Drug administration only lists 11, making it more challenging for American consumers to find safer, greener options. The Environmental Working Group, a non-profit watchdog, studied lab tests of 51 sunscreen products in 2021 and found that only 35% of products met the EU standard, compared with 94% that passed the US standard.

However, while government can set minimum requirements, Mia Davis, vice president of sustainability and impact at beauty retailer Credo Beauty, says the needle will move in the private sector.

Sustainable ships: The world's most eco-conscious cruises

“Regulation can raise the floor a bit. A person who doesn’t know about any (sustainability issues) should still be able to walk into a bodega and get clean products… But that’s never going to be what the market can do,” she said. “Market leadership is key.”

In the absence of bold regulations or global standards on sustainability practices, this “leadership” — undertaken both by brands and customers in the beauty marketplace — is likely to be the most immediately impactful vector for addressing the industry’s climate shortcomings. It will take continued collective advocacy and initiative to see meaningful climate-conscious change.

#150. Israel Kidnapped Iranian Generals in Hunt for Ron Arad

Israeli officials were convinced that Tehran was to blame for the airman’s disappearance. Alternative theories got little attention, until now.

Israeli officials were convinced that Tehran was to blame for the airman’s disappearance. Alternative theories got little attention, until now.

At a protest in 2025 in Tel Aviv, supporters of Israeli hostages held captive by Hamas held pictures of the hostages and of Ron Arad, who has been missing since 1986.Credit...Itai Ron/Reuters

By Adam GoldmanRonen BergmanFarnaz Fassihi and Hwaida Saad

Ronen Bergman, Farnaz Fassihi, Adam Goldman and Hwaida Saad have spent years investigating the disappearance of the Israeli airman Ron Arad.

Gen. Abdullah Saberi, an Iranian commander, stepped out for a jog early one morning in an upscale diplomatic quarter of Syria’s capital. Israeli intelligence officers waited nearby. Posing as movers, they had slipped past the neighborhood’s security checkpoints.

As he headed for a nearby park, General Saberi passed two men who carried an oversize refrigerator box. In a flash, the men restrained the general, drugged him, threw the box over his head, shoved him into a white van and left as if nothing had happened.

He was whisked to Israel for interrogation, according to numerous officials in the Middle East, including senior Iranian officials close to General Saberi and a Syrian official who reviewed video of the September 2021 kidnapping.

As a veteran of Iran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, General Saberi knew many secrets. But his interrogators were interested in only one.

Mr. Arad, an Israeli airman, vanished decades ago, and the Israeli military says he is the only service member classified as missing in action. The government’s long search for him has captivated the public and has come to symbolize Israel’s commitment, rooted in Jewish tradition, to bringing its soldiers home, dead or alive. Articles, books and documentaries have been produced about the hunt for Mr. Arad.

The Israeli government was so determined to find him that, even four decades after his disappearance, it took the risk of kidnapping General Saberi in the shadow of his own embassy.

#148. Fiona the hippo under veterinary care after eating hat at Cincinnati zoo

Knit hat caught in ceiling fan and flung into enclosure eaten by Fiona, who is being closely monitored by zoo staff

The Cincinnati zoo says Fiona, its beloved hippo who became a global celebrity after her premature birth nearly a decade ago, is undergoing veterinary care after swallowing a knit hat that got into her enclosure.

Zoo veterinarians and staff are monitoring Fiona and working to help her pass the hat, the zoo said in a statement Monday.

“Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self,” the zoo said. The zoo said she received fluids and an enema Sunday to help move things through her system.

The cap got into Fiona’s habitat after it was tossed into the air by a visitor and caught by a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening above the area’s viewing windows, said zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley.

“We probably couldn’t make [it] happen again if we tried,” zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley told Axios in a statement, emphasizing it was an accident. Fiona will be off the exhibit until she is in better health.

Fiona was born six weeks premature in January 2017, and her fight to survive grabbed international attention.

She initially could not stand on her own and weighed just 29lbs (13.2kg) at birth, 25lbs (11.3kg) less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species.

Fans followed her progress online, and she became so popular that books were written about her. She also inspired a line of beer, all sorts of clothing and an ice cream flavor.

One couple even got engaged in front of her exhibit, with Fiona getting into the picture while underwater in the background.

Other zoos contacted Fiona, showing concern for her health. Timothy, the hippo at the San Antonio zoo sent well wishes via Instagram. “I know you’ve got some amazing people looking after you. We’re sending lots of love from Texas to the most beautiful hippo in the world. Hope you’re feeling more like yourself soon!”

The zoo said in a social media post it will share more information as they get it, also reminding visitors to be careful when near habitats and to secure belongings.

“If something falls into a habitat, please notify a zoo staff member immediately,” the zoo said.

#147. Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million users a month.

But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass users’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.

And once installed, it’s tough to remove.

In a detailed investigation, CNN spoke to half a dozen cybersecurity teams from Asia, Europe and the United States — as well as multiple former and current Pinduoduo employees — after receiving a tipoff.

Multiple experts identified the presence of malware on the Pinduoduo app that exploited vulnerabilities in Android operating systems. Company insiders said the exploits were utilized to spy on users and competitors, allegedly to boost sales.

“We haven’t seen a mainstream app like this trying to escalate their privileges to gain access to things that they’re not supposed to gain access to,” said Mikko Hyppönen, chief research officer at WithSecure, a Finnish cybersecurity firm.

“This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.”

This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.

Malware, short for malicious software, refers to any software developed to steal data or interfere with computer systems and mobile devices.

Evidence of sophisticated malware in the Pinduoduo app comes amid intense scrutiny of Chinese-developed apps like TikTok over concerns about data security.

Some American lawmakers are pushing for a national ban on the popular short-video app, whose CEO Shou Chew was grilled by Congress for five hours last week about its relations with the Chinese government.

The revelations are also likely to draw more attention to Pinduoduo’s international sister app, Temu, which is topping US download charts and fast expanding in other Western markets. Both are owned by Nasdaq-listed PDD, a multinational company with roots in China.

While Temu has not been implicated, Pinduoduo’s alleged actions risk casting a shadow over its sister app’s global expansion.

There is no evidence that Pinduoduo has handed data to the Chinese government. But as Beijing enjoys significant leverage over businesses under its jurisdiction, there are concerns from US lawmakers that any company operating in China could be forced to cooperate with a broad range of security activities.

The findings follow Google’s suspension of Pinduoduo from its Play Store in March, citing malware identified in versions of the app.

An ensuing report from Bloomberg said a Russian cybersecurity firm had also identified potential malware in the app.

Pinduoduo has previously rejected “the speculation and accusation that Pinduoduo app is malicious.”

CNN has contacted PDD multiple times over email and phone for comment, but has not received a response.

Pinduoduo, which boasts a user base that accounts for three quarters of China’s online population and a market value three times that of eBay (EBAY), wasn’t always an online shopping behemoth.

Founded in 2015 in Shanghai by Colin Huang, a former Google employee, the startup was fighting to establish itself in a market long dominated by e-commerce stalwarts Alibaba (BABA) and JD.com (JD).

It succeeded by offering steep discounts on friends-and-family group buying orders and focusing on lower-income rural areas.

Pinduoduo posted triple digit growth in monthly users until the end of 2018, the year it listed in New York. By the middle of 2020, though, the increase in monthly users had slowed to around 50% and would continue to decline, according to its earnings reports.

It was in 2020, according to a current Pinduoduo employee, that the company set up a team of about 100 engineers and product managers to dig for vulnerabilities in Android phones, develop ways to exploit them — and turn that into profit.

According to the source, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, the company only targeted users in rural areas and smaller towns initially, while avoiding users in megacities such as Beijing and Shanghai.

“The goal was to reduce the risk of being exposed,” they said.

By collecting expansive data on user activities, the company was able to create a comprehensive portrait of users’ habits, interests and preferences, according to the source.

This allowed it to improve its machine learning model to offer more personalized push notifications and ads, attracting users to open the app and place orders, they said.

The team was disbanded in early March, the source added, after questions about their activities came to light.

PDD didn’t reply to CNN’s repeated requests for comment on the team.

Approached by CNN, researchers from Tel Aviv-based cyber firm Check Point Research, Delaware-based app security startup Oversecured and Hyppönen’s WithSecure conducted independent analysis of the 6.49.0 version of the app, released on Chinese app stores in late February.

Google Play is not available in China, and Android users in the country download their apps from local stores. In March, when Google suspended Pinduoduo, it said it had found malware in off-Play versions of the app.

The researchers found code designed to achieve “privilege escalation”: a type of cyberattack that exploits a vulnerable operating system to gain a higher level of access to data than it’s supposed to have, according to experts.

“Our team has reverse engineered that code and we can confirm that it tries to escalate rights, tries to gain access to things normal apps wouldn’t be able to do on Android phones,” said Hyppönen.

The app was able to continue running in the background and prevent itself from being uninstalled, which allowed it to boost its monthly active user rates, Hyppönen said. It also had the ability to spy on competitors by tracking activity on other shopping apps and getting information from them, he added.

Check Point Research additionally identified ways in which the app was able to evade scrutiny.

The app deployed a method that allowed it to push updates without an app store review process meant to detect malicious applications, the researchers said.

They also identified in some plug-ins the intent to obscure potentially malicious components by hiding them under legitimate file names, such as Google’s.

“Such a technique is widely used by malware developers that inject malicious code into applications that have legitimate functionality,” they said.

In China, about three quarters of smartphone users are on the Android system. Apple (AAPL)’s iPhone has 25% market share, according to Daniel Ives of Wedbush Securities.

Sergey Toshin, the founder of Oversecured, said Pinduoduo’s malware specifically targeted different Android-based operating systems, including those used by Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi and Oppo.

CNN has reached out to these companies for comment.

Toshin described Pinduoduo as “the most dangerous malware” ever found among mainstream apps.

“I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive,” he said.

Most phone manufacturers globally customize the core Android software, the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), to add unique features and applications to their own devices.

Toshin found Pinduoduo to have exploited about 50 Android system vulnerabilities. Most of the exploits were tailor made for customized parts known as the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) code, which tends to be audited less often than AOSP and is therefore more prone to vulnerabilities, he said.

Pinduoduo also exploited a number of AOSP vulnerabilities, including one which was flagged by Toshin to Google in February 2022. Google fixed the bug this March, he said.

I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive.

According to Toshin, the exploits allowed Pinduoduo access to users’ locations, contacts, calendars, notifications and photo albums without their consent. They were also able to change system settings and access users’ social network accounts and chats, he said.

Of the six teams CNN spoke to for this story, three did not conduct full examinations. But their primary reviews showed that Pinduoduo asked for a large number of permissions beyond the normal functions of a shopping app.

They included “potentially invasive permissions” such as “set wallpaper” and “download without notification,” said René Mayrhofer, head of the Institute of Networks and Security at the Johannes Kepler University Linz in Austria.

Suspicions about malware in Pinduoduo’s app were first raised in late February in a report by a Chinese cybersecurity firm called Dark Navy. Even though the analysis didn’t directly name the shopping giant, the report spread quickly among other researchers, who did name the company. Some of the analysts followed up with their own reports confirming the original findings.

Soon after, on March 5, Pinduoduo issued a new update of its app, version 6.50.0, which removed the exploits, according to two experts who CNN spoke to.

Two days after the update, Pinduoduo disbanded the team of engineers and product managers who had developed the exploits, according to the Pinduoduo source.

The next day, team members found themselves locked out of Pinduoduo’s bespoke workplace communication app, Knock, and lost access to files on the company’s internal network. Engineers also found their access to big data, data sheets and the log system revoked, the source said.

Most of the team were transferred to work at Temu. They were assigned to different departments at the subsidiary, with some working on marketing or developing push notifications, according to the source.

A core group of about 20 cybersecurity engineers who specialize in finding and exploiting vulnerabilities remain at Pinduoduo, they said.

Toshin of Oversecured, who looked into the update, said although the exploits were removed, the underlying code was still there and could be reactivated to carry out attacks.

Pinduoduo has been able to grow its user base against a backdrop of the Chinese government’s regulatory clampdown on Big Tech that began in late 2020.

That year, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology launched a sweeping crackdown on apps that illegally collect and use personal data.

The Personal Information Protection Law stipulates that no party should illegally collect, process or transmit personal information. They’re also banned from exploiting internet-related security vulnerabilities or engaging in actions that endanger cybersecurity.

Pinduoduo’s apparent malware would be a violation of those laws, tech policy experts say, and should have been detected by the regulator.

“This would be embarrassing for the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, because this is their job,” said Kendra Schaefer, a tech policy expert at Trivium China, a consultancy. “They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.”

Pinduoduo did not appear on any of the lists.

They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.

CNN has reached out to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Cyberspace Administration of China for comment.

On Chinese social media, some cybersecurity experts questioned why regulators haven’t taken any action.

“Probably none of our regulators can understand coding and programming, nor do they understand technology. You can’t even understand the malicious code when it’s shoved right in front of your face,” a cybersecurity expert with 1.8 million followers wrote last week in a viral post on Weibo, a Twitter-like platform.

CNN’s Kristie Lu Stout and Sean Lyngaas contributed reporting.

Vivian Nereim reported from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and Aaron Boxerman from Jerusalem.

Iran launched a drone attack against Bahrain on Sunday for the second time in days, as peace talks with the United States have faltered.

The Revolutionary Guards said that Friday’s attack was retaliation for a previous American strike on a telecommunications tower in Iran.

The attacks were the first to target Bahrain in about two months. After the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in February, Iran launched thousands of retaliatory missile and drone attacks at Gulf Arab countries that host American military installations. But those attacks had largely petered out as the two sides entered a stalemate.

#143. How Milburn won over Labour on tackling rising youth unemployment

Labour grandee seems to have assuaged MPs’ nerves on need for welfare reform to tackle youth unemployment crisis

In a boxing gym in Peterborough almost a year ago, Alan Milburn, freshly appointed to run a government review into the nearly 1 million young people out of work and education, said he would be “unafraid to shine a light on uncomfortable truths”.

The Labour grandee, who held three cabinet jobs under Tony Blair, warned there was a “downward escalator” taking young people into a “world of benefits” and vowed to provide radical solutions.

Many Labour MPs bristled. Just six months earlier, they had mounted a successful rebellion to kill off the government’s planned £5bn cuts to health and disability benefits, significantly damaging Keir Starmer’s political authority by forcing him into a U-turn on his flagship welfare bill.

That day in the gym, Milburn knew he would have to win over a party suspicious of his motives and anxious about the impact of changes on vulnerable people, even if some acknowledged that the growing welfare bill was unsustainable.

On the eve of publishing his report on Tuesday, early signs are that he has assuaged backbench nerves, succeeding where Starmer failed in moving the Overton window within the Labour party on the welfare debate around young people.

Milburn’s strategy was clear from the off: make the moral argument for change, make it loudly and make it often. His favourite – and oft-repeated – statistic has been that the government spends 25 times as much on benefits for young people as it does on supporting them into work.

In a series of interviews and MP engagement sessions over the following months, he described the projections – that numbers could reach 1.25 million by the early 2030s without major intervention – as a “national failure” that would result in a “catastrophic” generational fault line.

After his interim report in May, he gradually signalled that overhauling health and disability benefits for young people would be a central outcome of his review, suggesting the welfare system in its current form had failed them and was exacerbating inactivity.

Labour MPs were given time to get used to the idea and to air the arguments in public, with controversial elements of the report released early – the abolition of health benefits for under-25s, including existing claimants, among them.

“Alan didn’t want any nasty surprises,” said one government source. “He wanted to engage fully with MPs and charities and anybody else with concerns. The government can’t move forward on this unless it’s able to bring people with them.”

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

He had several factors working in his favour. As his days in No 10 ran out, Starmer was so weakened that Milburn was able to “bulldoze” Downing Street into supporting his proposals, according to another source, especially as Pat McFadden, the welfare secretary, was already onboard.

Secondly, several of the leading figures in the welfare rebellion were now inside government – most notably Louise Haigh, who is now Andy Burnham’s number two, and Anneliese Midgley, the chief whip.

Meg Hillier, the moderate chair of the Treasury select committee who had fronted that rebellion, last week indicated the proposals should get a “fair wind”, although she also acknowledged the difficulty of the choices ahead.

Thirdly, the drip-drip of pitch-rolling came alongside a wider sense of alarm in the UK over the prospects of the next generation, amid concerns over rising mental ill health, social media and AI upending the jobs market.

Burnham has said he wants to cut the welfare bill “as soon as we possibly can” but has warned against “crude cuts” (which the government would struggle to get past Labour MPs anyway) in the push for “sustainable” employment.

His approach has echoes of Tony Blair, who talked of “a hand up, not a hand out”, actively pursuing a policy of reforming and investing in welfare specifically to bring down what he termed the “bills of social failure”.

The big difference now is that the fiscal backdrop is more challenging, though Milburn will recommend that ministers spend hundreds of millions on back-to-work support in the short term in return for welfare savings, increased tax receipts and a fairer, happier country over the long term.

The rather clunky symbolism of choosing a boxing gym for his first promotional visit last year wasn’t lost on anybody. Since then, Milburn – a former chair of the Social Mobility Commission – has been clear this is a fight he thinks the government needs to have.

His recommendations, along with those from the Timms review into health and disability benefits, which will be published in the coming weeks, will form the basis of a white paper next spring that will then become a new welfare bill, voted on by Labour MPs.

So, for now, the campaign to win them over continues. Standing alongside Milburn at a meeting of the parliamentary party on Monday night, McFadden said: “What is proposed is a new settlement for young people. This is not last year’s proposal with better PR.”

#141. Leave.EU and Vote Leave veterans launch rival campaigns to defend Brexit

Andy Wigmore says there will be no animosity this time between his Enough Official group and Michael Gove-backed Stay Out movement

The Brexit wars were a bitter period in political history, fraught with tension and badmouthing – and that was just between the different leave campaigns.

Now as a new incarnation of Dominic Cummings’ Vote Leave looks set to re-enter the political fray, so too does a rival anti-EU campaign from the team behind Leave.EU, who ran their own unofficial campaign backed by Nigel Farage.

This time, both have vowed to be cordial with each other, but in 2016 there were significant creative differences.

Many of the names are the same. Oliver Lewis, a veteran of Vote Leave who was a Brexit negotiator under Boris Johnson, will chair Stay Out, a new campaign group backed by the former cabinet minister Michael Gove and under the interested eye of Cummings, though he has no formal role.

The launch of the campaign video – which claimed the costs of rejoining the EU would be £750m a week, and featured footage of recent riots in France and Spain and warnings about unchecked migration – caught No 10 off-guard.

On Monday they were joined by the launch of a parallel campaign from Andy Wigmore’s Leave.EU, which will be called Enough Official. Wigmore told the Telegraph he wanted to work with Lewis’s group. “There’s no split camps this time,” he said. “We’re all going to support each other, and we will support anyone who’s going to fight this.”

A number of high-profile political figures seem to be willing to re-enter the fray from retirement, including Johnson. The former prime minister and leave campaigner told the Telegraph it would be “madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority … [Andy Burnham] won’t win – because the reality is that people are not fools.”

Johnson hinted to the paper that he would be willing to be part of a campaign to stay out of the bloc. “There are plenty of people who are only too happy to make the points I’ve made – but I will of course make the points that I’ve made,” he said.

One senior campaigner said it was an irresistible opportunity for many former political advisers who were now out of Westminster politics. “They’re very effective guys that have been sitting around waiting for a chance to make themselves useful. A lot of talent on the right is currently off making money or kicking their feet. Rejoining is the one thing that will bring them back,” they said.

Veterans of both Vote Leave and Leave.EU are split between those who are willing to campaign to stay out and others who believe the political landscape is now far more uncertain.

One senior figure said they “had PTSD” from the Brexit period and vowed to steer clear. “I think that is exactly the reason why the prime minister should not be reopening this debate, but I don’t think anyone should be under any illusion it would be an easy win for either side.”

Another campaign veteran said both pro- and anti-EU campaigns would find it more difficult to get businesses to pick a side or to get public figures involved. “I think that many are scarred from previous involvement, but this would work in both directions,” they said.

Several of those involved in the campaigns said they expected serving politicians to be kept at arm’s length – including Farage.

At a press conference on Monday, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said she would not engage with campaigning on Brexit. “We need to stop obsessing about Europe and whether to be in or out, and actually get on with doing the things that we are elected to do,” she said.

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

“Sort out the economy, fund our defence, cut welfare, get jobs for people, make sure that businesses can create those jobs. We don’t need to be in the EU to do any of that.”

Badenoch said she believed that voters would decide to stay out of the EU, but added: “I’m not interested in engaging in this debate. They [Labour] want to distract us by making us talk about Brexit, because if we’re talking about that then we’re not talking about the government’s failures. I’m not falling for that trick.”

Launching the campaign over the weekend, Lewis said Stay Out would make the argument on the economics and on immigration – and on the risk of reopening divisions.

“The bloc is also getting bigger, with Albania, Moldova and the western Balkans all in the queue to join, and Brussels wants Britain back in as one of the few countries rich enough to pay for it,” he said. “The country has had enough of arguing about Europe, and it is time to move on and spend our money on our own priorities.”

Gove, who was a co-convener of Vote Leave, said a move towards rejoining would “commit the country to another decade of fractious negotiations and a return to the divisions we have spent years putting behind us, at the very moment people are desperate for Westminster to get on with delivering on their priorities.”

Speaking on Monday before a crunch EU summit where Burnham hopes to clinch a new deal with the EU on food and drink and emissions trading, as well as a youth mobility deal, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said the government respected the 2016 result.

“What we’re very focused on is actually what’s in front of us, which is this summit and how we can just help the British people in the situation we face,” he told BBC Breakfast.

#138. Ministers to end Palantir’s contract with NHS in England in 2029

DHSC to extend US tech firm’s contract for two more years to allow time to line up British companies to replace it

Ministers will end the NHS’s contract with the controversial tech firm Palantir – but not until 2029, to allow time to line up British companies to replace it.

The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) has decided to extend Palantir’s contract to provide the federated data platform (FDP) – the software that links different healthcare providers – for two more years rather than exercise a break clause that would have let them axe it next spring.

Ministers have come under growing pressure to end the NHS in England’s relationship with Palantir, which is run by the Donald Trump-supporting US tech billionaire Peter Thiel.

James Frith, a health minister, said Palantir’s role would end in 2029 to boost public trust in NHS tech, end its “over-dependence” on one supplier and let UK companies start providing crucial digital infrastructure. The DHSC will in the meantime select UK tech firms to replace it.

However, Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs criticised Palantir being given a further two years.

“My committee has repeatedly called on the government to exercise the 2027 break clause in Palantir’s federated data platform contract with the NHS,” said Chi Onwurah, the chair of the Commons science and technology select committee.

“It’s deeply disappointing to hear that it won’t do so and is instead choosing to extend the contract for two years, during which time it says it will procure a UK-based supplier.

Martin Wrigley, a Liberal Democrat MP, said: “After months of campaigning by the Liberal Democrats, the government has finally admitted that the Palantir contract has to end.

“However, ministers have kicked the can down the road to March 2029. That leaves a company co-founded by Trump ally Peter Thiel, and criticised by human rights groups over its work with ICE [the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency], holding the keys to our health data for years to come.”

Campaign groups such as Amnesty International and Just Treatment have been urging ministers to activate the break clause in February in the contract that NHS England agreed with Palantir in 2023.

Many NHS care trusts have declined to use the FDP, amid widespread doubts in the service that it is as good as Palantir insists. NHS England last week deleted a claim from its website that 137 trusts were benefiting from the FDP after the Guardian disclosed that 29 were using it never or rarely.

“The current contract will remain for two years, before coming to an end,” Frith told MPs. The DHSC will soon invite British tech outfits to bid to be part of whoever replaces Palantir. “A process this important must command public trust as well as clinical confidence,” Frith added in a tacit admission that many hospital bosses and doctors are sceptical about Palantir’s claimed benefits.

Ben Coleman, a Labour member of the Commons health select committee, who last week urged ministers to replace Palantir with a group of British firms, said: “I’m glad the government is ending reliance on a single supplier and shaking off the Palantir albatross. This must be done without disrupting patient care or creating new dependence [on a new single supplier]”.

Amnesty International said the decision was “a victory for healthcare workers, patients and campaigners who refused to give up”.

“Doctors and nurses … should never have to work in a health service that partners with a company supporting a military committing genocide.

“Palantir has openly acknowledged supporting Israel’s military in ‘war-related missions’, while Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. ‘First, do no harm’ should apply not just to NHS staff, but to the companies the NHS contracts with,” said Tom Guha, its crisis campaigner.

#137. Finland's Prime Minister Sanna Marin concedes election

Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.

The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data showed with all ballots counted.

“We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo said in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.

He will get the first chance at forming a coalition to obtain majority in parliament as Marin’s era as prime minister was expected to end.

Popular abroad, at home Marin faces battle to keep her job

“We have gained support, we have gained more seats (in parliament). That’s an excellent achievement, even if we did not finish first today,” the prime minister said in a speech to party members.

Marin, 37, the world’s youngest prime minister when she took office in 2019, is considered by fans around the globe as a millennial role model for progressive new leaders, but at home she has faced criticism for her partying and her government’s public spending.

Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin takes drug test following partying backlash

While she remains very popular among many Finns, particularly young moderates, she antagonized some conservatives with lavish spending on pensions and education they see as not frugal enough.

The NCP has led in polls for almost two years although its lead had melted away in recent months. It has promised to curb spending and stop the rise of public debt, which has reached just over 70% of GDP since Marin took office in 2019.

Orpo accused Marin of eroding Finland’s economic resilience at a time when Europe’s energy crisis, driven by Russia’s war in Ukraine, has hit the country hard and the cost of living has increased.

Orpo has said he will negotiate with all groups to obtain a majority in parliament, while Marin has said her Social Democrats may govern with the NCP but will not go into government with the Finns Party.

Marin called the Finns Party “openly racist” during a debate in January – an accusation the nationalist group rejected.

The Finns Party’s main goal is to reduce what leader Riikka Purra has called “harmful” immigration from developing countries outside the European Union. It also calls for austerity policies to curb deficit spending, a stance it shares with the NCP.

Most notable of Marin’s foreign policy actions has been her push, along with President Sauli Niinisto, for the country to make a watershed policy U-turn by seeking NATO membership in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

That process is now almost complete, with Helsinki expected to join within days after all the Western defense alliance’s 30 members approved the accession.

#134. Refused UK asylum seekers to lose five-day grace period and face immediate removal

Home Office plans will cause unnecessary distress and anxiety, say refugee charities

Asylum seekers who have exhausted the formal appeals process will be stripped of a five-day grace period and become eligible for immediate removal under Home Office plans condemned as “distressing” by refugee charities.

Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will amend a bill currently before parliament to allow immigration enforcement officers to detain and remove people who have unsuccessfully appealed against their asylum or immigration claim being rejected without further notice.

Currently, enforced returns for rejected claimants can only take place after a minimum notice period of five working days, which can allow people to launch other legal interventions or prepare themselves for removal.

Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, condemned the change.

“We must treat people with dignity. Removing people at such short notice will cause unnecessary distress and anxiety,” he said.

“We also need to look at the evidence of what works. The reality is that voluntary removals are far more effective at removing people than enforced returns. If you assist people to return with dignity, many will take that option, at far lower cost to the taxpayer.”

Louise Calvey, the executive director at Asylum Matters, said: “People deserve a fair chance to make their claim for help and sanctuary, but forcibly removing people from the country so they don’t get a chance to make their claims won’t fix that.

“Right now, 63% of the population don’t have access to an asylum legal aid provider. What that means is people are attempting to navigate a horrendously complex and hostile system in a new country, often in a second language. In that environment, many people may not have had the proper advice in initial claims, so many who make further claims are found to have a genuine need for support.

“Expelling people from the country to ensure we never get to hear their legitimate claims is nothing to be proud of – it will lead to real injustices.”

Mahmood has tabled an amendment to the immigration and asylum bill that will scrap the five-day timeframe.

Officials would instead be given a six-month period to remove refused asylum seekers and rejected migrants before further notice is required, the Home Office said.

The changes follow a similar approach to the system that Denmark successfully operates, the Home Office has said.

The number of migrants awaiting removal in Denmark was cut from more than 2,185 cases at the end of 2020 to fewer than 1,000 at the end of 2025.

The UK has increased the number of removals since Labour came to power, but faces huge backlogs in asylum applications. As of 30 June 2026, 40,168 people were waiting for an initial asylum decision in the UK. The number of refused applications hit more than 90,000 in the same month, breaking previous records.

There are currently exceptions to the five-day notice period for removals, such as where the removal was disrupted by the individual or was cancelled due to bad weather. In these scenarios, removal can be attempted again without further notice for 21 days.

This timeframe will now be increased to six months under reforms in the bill, which returns to the House of Commons for report stage and third reading on 17 November.

The bill will also introduce a new immigration appeals authority with the aim of speeding up removals and changes to how human rights and modern slavery laws are applied to asylum applications to root out what the government described as “vexatious” claims.

Ministers hope the bill will bring into force proposals that will create a firm but fair asylum system, and which will reduce the pull factors driving illegal immigration.

Under other reforms, the responsibility to make modern slavery decisions for children will be devolved to local safeguarding partners.

This will ensure professionals who already support the child, and are closest to the child, are making the decisions for their future, the Home Office said.

Anna Turley, the minister for border security and asylum, said: “This government is ramping up removals of those with no right to be here, with over 80,000 illegal migrants and foreign nationals returned since the general election. “Now we are ensuring those migrants who have exhausted their right to appeal can be removed promptly, rather than being given an opportunity to frustrate their legitimate removal from this country.”

The U.S. economy hitched its wagon to Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Now that he has stepped down, the company faces deep uncertainty.

A week ago, we learned the news that Jensen Huang, the rock star C.E.O. of the chip-making company Nvidia, had acknowledged an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy. But why are Huang and Nvidia so irreplaceable — and is anything that cannot be replaced automatically vulnerable? Today I’m writing about power, vulnerability and choke points.

Last week, as it became clear that Jensen Huang’s future at Nvidia might be in jeopardy, a meme began making the rounds on the internet. It showed a complicated, multitiered structure, delicately balanced on a tiny block. The structure was labeled “entire global economy”; the block was labeled “Jensen Huang’s wife.”

The meme is already outdated: Huang has resigned from his role as Nvidia’s C.E.O. (and it never made sense to put any of this on his wife). But the image still captured the idea that so much of the business world somehow came to depend on one man and his — now, it seems, questionable — judgment.

Report on Britain’s youth jobs crisis calls for welfare, education, health and employment policy shake-up

Andy Burnham is being urged to spend billions of pounds on a “new deal” for the next generation that would fund guaranteed jobs support for young people to offset a radical cut in benefits.

In a watershed report on Britain’s youth jobs crisis, Alan Milburn, the Tony Blair-era health secretary, said the country was at a “fork in the road” after a surge in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost a million.

He said ministers had a choice to either carry on down a path of state and market failure or adopt a 10-year plan with an ambition to eradicate long-term youth unemployment.

Publishing a blueprint for change in a highly anticipated review, the report calls on the government to launch a sweeping shake-up of welfare, education, health and employment policy with the aim to ensure every young person has the chance to earn or learn.

If adopted by the government, Britain could halve the number of young people neither earning nor learning, helping about 600,000 more under-25s into education, employment or training each year by 2036, according to the review.

Milburn’s report comes as Britain’s young bear the brunt of rising joblessness as employers freeze their hiring plans amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East. Coupled with the legacies of the Covid pandemic and austerity, and a rise in mental ill-health and as AI upends the jobs market, the UK’s Neet rate has reached 13% – the highest level since 2014. Milburn said that rate could be lowered to 5% by 2036.

However, central to his plan would be a controversial shake-up of Britain’s benefits system to approach the under-25s as wholly separate from the working-age population at large.

Urging the prime minister not to shy away from welfare reform – after Keir Starmer was forced into a humiliating climbdown over a plan to cut disability benefits amid pressure from Labour MPs – Milburn warned the future of the next generation depended on the government making changes.

At a press conference in London on Tuesday to mark the launch of his report, he is expected to say: “It is time for a new settlement that makes work not welfare the future for the next generation.”

But Milburn also warned that crude benefit cuts would not work, arguing that changes would need upfront investment.

Burnham pledged on Sunday to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment. Writing in the Guardian, he promised that changes to benefits he was considering in response to Milburn’s review would only be accompanied by a “root and branch rethink” of youth support.

At the heart of Milburn’s blueprint would be the creation of an entirely new welfare system for young people, involving tougher eligibility criteria than for older claimants. In exchange, however, there would be a drastic step-change in support to help young people find work.

This would involve some young people with health conditions and disabilities losing access to current benefits, although they would be able to apply to a local fund for short-term expenses and equipment. Those with the most profound health conditions who would be unable ever to work would still get more generous financial support.

To counterbalance the changes, Milburn said upfront investment to create a new “youth opportunity service” in England should be created to deliver a drastic boost in support for young people.

Accountable to regional mayors and local leaders, the service would combine employment, careers, health and practical support. Young people would receive a personalised participation plan and a named adviser, with access to support guaranteed by two new legal guarantees.

While education, skills and health policies are devolved in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, Milburn will say at the report launch that the underlying principles in his report should also apply.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

Analysis in Milburn’s report shows that for every £1 spent on helping young people into work or education, the state spent £25 on youth benefits last year. Under his proposals that figure would be rebalanced to £2 to £1, bringing Britain closer into line with the ratios in other European countries.

The changes will, however, raise fears among some Labour MPs as well as charities and campaigners that slashing youth benefits could result in plunging more young people into poverty, particularly for those who require additional financial support to manage health conditions.

As Milburn prepared to launch his review, backbenchers from the left of the party – including Nadia Whittome, Bell Ribeiro-Addy, John McDonnell, Apsana Begum, Clive Lewis and Richard Burgon – warned in a letter that an entire generation risked becoming disconnected from work and wider society.

“What young people need is not more punishment, but more opportunity,” the signatories wrote, warning that an approach relying on benefit cuts “risks further disenfranchising young people who are already struggling”.

They added: “Placing young people under threat of losing essential financial support does not address the shortage of good-quality jobs, the barriers facing disabled young people, or the lack of meaningful routes into employment.”

In a bid to ease concerns among Labour MPs after last year’s welfare rebellion threatened to rupture the party and arguably began Starmer’s downfall, Milburn held meetings with MPs on Monday alongside the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden.

McFadden told backbenchers: “What is proposed is a new settlement for young people. This is not last year’s proposal with better PR. It’s about bringing together the help young people need in one place – treating them as a person not a departmental client.”

Milburn said Britain had faced a Neet problem for 25 years and had never made a plan to end it before. “We are at a fork in the road and half measures will not do. A complete system reset is needed. A lost generation is not inevitable. A work generation is possible.”

Labour has faced fierce criticism from business groups who say its decisions – including tax increases and a rising minimum wage – have added to Britain’s crisis in youth jobs, while the Conservatives and Reform have pushed for a tougher approach on benefits.

Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, said Milburn’s review was “too cautious on reversing that damage and too often his answer is the big and expensive hand of the state”.

“Overall, it fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in government spending and won’t make the slightest difference for young people stuck on welfare now – because nothing will happen for at least three years,” she said. “Even so, there’s a long road ahead to see if it can get past welfare-loving Labour MPs.”

#130. Britain's pound is beating every other major currency this year

The British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget plans by former Prime Minister Liz Truss. Now, it’s enjoying a comeback.

Sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022. The pound, which has advanced about 3.3% versus the greenback since the start of 2023, is the best-performing currency among developed economies this year.

The UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected. Activity is now thought to have expanded 0.1% in the final three months of last year, up from a previous estimate of no growth at all. Gross domestic product growth in January has been estimated at 0.3% after dropping 0.5% in December.

This resilience is bolstering expectations the Bank of England will maintain aggressive interest rate hikes despite concerns about the health of the global banking sector. Rising rates can boost the domestic currency because they help attract foreign investors searching for higher returns.

Inflation in the United Kingdom also jumped to an annual rate of 10.4% in February, underscoring the need for the Bank of England to maintain its tough approach.

The pound plunged close to $1.03 in September 2022 after the Truss government unveiled plans to boost borrowing while slashing taxes, unleashing panic in financial markets that fueled fears of a recession in the United Kingdom.

The International Monetary Fund predicted in January that the UK economy would contract by 0.6% this year, while all other advanced economies would grow, if only slightly.

“There was a lot of pessimism being priced into the pound,” said Francesco Pesole, a currency strategist at ING.

But the sharp pullback in energy prices and China’s reopening have provided some relief about the economic outlook since the start of the year.

“There was a big re-rating of growth expectations around Europe, and that impacted the UK,” Pesole said.

The euro has also been lifted by these dynamics, rising 2.3% against the US dollar in 2023. The pound’s rally has been sharper in large part because its 2022 declines were more severe, according to Pesole.

Both currencies have been aided by the greenback’s sharp drop from highs reached last September as recession fears have percolated in the United States.

A lack of clarity around the Federal Reserve’s next steps has also restrained the dollar in recent weeks. Investor speculation has increased that the Fed could pause or stop rate hikes due to concerns about the economy following the failure of Silicon Valley Bank last month.

Jordan Rochester, a currency strategist at Nomura, said he thinks the pound could rise to $1.30 this year and “potentially higher.” But he still sees risks given the uncertainty surrounding the Bank of England’s plans and how rate rises will feed back through the country’s economy. And Pesole cautioned that currency fluctuations are often overdone when markets are choppy, as they are now.

“In a volatile market environment, moves are exacerbated,” he said.

#128. Environmentalists criticise choice of Earthshot prize venue owned by fossil fuel firm

Mumbai facility is part of Reliance Industries, owner of world’s biggest oil refinery and funder of controversial mega-zoo

The Prince of Wales’s Earthshot prize will host its forthcoming annual awards ceremony at a venue owned by the billionaire Ambani family conglomerate, drawing criticism from conservationists over their fossil fuel businesses and their foundation’s controversial mega-zoo.

A spokesperson for the Earthshot prize, which awards £1m to five winners every year to invest in conservation work, confirmed to the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay that this year’s ceremony will be held at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on 17 November.

The venue is part of Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, which also owns Jamnagar, the world’s biggest oil refinery in Gujarat on India’s western coast. The group’s philanthropic arm funds the 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo Vantara, which was founded by Mukesh’s son Anant Ambani and inaugurated by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, last year. The zoo is embroiled in a long-running controversy over its vast collection of more than 150,000 animals, which reportedly includes some of the world’s most endangered species – from the radiated tortoise, native to Madagascar, to the Spix’s macaw, endemic to north-eastern Brazil but now considered extinct in the wild.

Megan Carr, of the Wildlife Animal Protection Forum South Africa (WAPFSA), warned that using a venue owned by Reliance “could lend an unearned environmental prestige to a corporate group currently under question by the global conservation community”.

Conservation groups, including WAPFSA, have raised concerns about the speed with which Vantara has amassed so many animals, and about how they were sourced. The site, near the family’s oil refinery, houses more than 2,000 species of animals.

This week, the 32-member committee that governs Cites, the UN-administered body that regulates trade in endangered species, requested that India submit another report on the steps it is taking to address concerns relating to its imports of protected species.

The committee also requested the Cites secretariat review 11 cases where there are unresolved questions over how animals were sent to Vantara.

Joanna Swift, the executive director of communications at the Earthshot prize, said it had not sought a philanthropic partnership for its award ceremony venue and that it was paying the standard commercial rate to rent the space.

“The [Jio World Convention Centre] was selected because it allowed us to host the event in Mumbai while meeting the practical requirements of an event of this size. It offers world-class facilities, technical infrastructure and experience of hosting major international events, including environmental ones,” Swift said. “In February this year, JWCC hosted the first ever Mumbai climate week.”

Vantara, Kensington Palace and JWCC have been approached for comment.

Vantara has previously denied allegations of wildlife trafficking and says its purpose is “to rescue wild animals in distress, provide treatment along with lifelong care, and rehabilitate those fit for the wild”.

“With regulatory approval, we also breed select endangered or extinct-in-the-wild species, serving as a modern Noah’s Ark to ensure their survival under human care and restore wild populations through reintroduction,” Vantara says on its website.

Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo of allegations that animals had been acquired illegally or mistreated.

A later Cites fact-finding mission raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.

Susan Cheyne, the vice-chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s small apes section, said that Vantara’s model has not yet been shown to support conservation and “may be driving demand for wild animals in trade”.

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

“For gibbons and other primates, this matters a great deal. Moving animals out of their range countries into a private facility does nothing for wild populations unless there is a transparent, credible plan for those animals: for welfare, for any conservation breeding with clear goals, and for return to range states where that is possible. Real rescue and sanctuary work for primates is done by underfunded centres in range countries,” Cheyne said.

Daniela Freyer, co-founder of the German NGO Pro Wildlife, added: “Our planet is increasingly threatened by the overexploitation of wildlife and by climate change driven by fossil fuels. This week, the Cites Standing Committee, which oversees international wildlife trade, decided to keep India under its compliance procedure, as questions remain about the origin of some of the world’s rarest animals imported to Vantara. A prize whose goals include protecting nature and fixing our climate should be careful not to lend its reputation to these questions.”

Vantara had sought to lobby the UK, the chair of this week’s Cites meetings, attempting to persuade officials to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara, the Guardian and Mongabay reported earlier this month. Ministers were advised not to engage formally with Vantara, internal documents revealed.

The Earthshot prize, founded by Prince William in 2020, is billed as the most prestigious environmental award. William appeared on the BBC’s Graham Norton show last month to promote the prize, saying it was designed to “talk about urgency and optimism together”.

Swift said that it was vital to host an edition of the Earthshot prize in India.

“Mumbai is the sixth largest city on earth. It is home to exceptional environmental solutions and the people behind them, with an impact felt in India and around the world. Spotlighting progress like this, to the largest possible audience, is why the Earthshot prize exists,” Swift said.

This article was amended on 9 November 2026. An earlier version said the Vantara zoo covers 400 hectares; in fact, it is 1,400 hectares.

#126. Grenades, grief and a deepening political divide: five takeaways from Sonia Gandhi’s new memoir

From the assassinations of her husband and mother-in-law to press stonewalling under Modi, Belonging offers an insider’s account of India’s political evolution

Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

Few love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi. The former’s much-awaited political memoir, Belonging, offers a strikingly candid account of her journey from a small town in Italy to the highest echelons of power in India – all for love, she says.

The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world. In Belonging, she opens up for the first time about the extraordinary twists and turns of a life that has largely unfolded in full public view. (The Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Petersen has a rare in-person interview with Gandhi, and you can read an excerpt from the book here.)

Belonging, published today, contains moving glimpses of Gandhi’s private grief. She writes about the loss of her first child, who died shortly after birth, and the chilling discovery of grenades in a room of their house after Operation Blue Star, the 1984 military operation against Sikh separatists at the Golden Temple in Amritsar. She also provides a ringside view of several turbulent chapters in Indian politics, not least the violent assassinations of her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, in 1984 and her husband, Rajiv, in 1991.

Her book also revisits some of the darker episodes that have dogged the Gandhi family and the Congress party, including Indira’s imposition of the Emergency in June 1975, a 21-month period during which civil liberties were suspended, political opponents were jailed and the press was gagged, which caused fear and dismay across the country. In Gandhi’s account, it also caused a rift within the family.

Ultimately, Gandhi’s memoir is a vivid record of six decades of India’s political transformation from the Congress-dominated secular republic she moved to in 1968 until today, when Hindu nationalism has become the dominant political force under Narendra Modi.

Here are five key takeaways from her memoir and what they reveal about the state of Indian politics today.

Gandhi has had no real contact with Modi for the last 12 years

Gandhi’s account offers a glimpse of how deep the political polarisation runs in Indian politics today. In one revealing passage, Gandhi writes that she has had “practically no real contact” with Modi in the 12 years he has led the nation. In fact, at times when the two have been in the same rooms, such as the speaker’s small chamber, Modi “tends to look away, avoiding eye contact”, she says. On occasion, she adds, he has asked briefly about her health after a hospital stay.

For her, this breakdown is a departure from the past, when leaders on opposing sides of the aisle “would treat one another with cordiality”. After the 2001 terror attack on parliament, Gandhi immediately called then-BJP prime minister AB Vajpayee to enquire about his safety, a gesture he appreciated.

Gandhi sees an increasingly authoritarian style of politics, in which those in power seek to “belittle and torment” opponents. For years, Gandhi’s son, Rahul, has been the subject of BJP’s ridicule, which calls him Pappu, a derisive term intended to portray him as inexperienced and naive. She adds that similar things are happening elsewhere in the world, an observation that can be read in the context of US President Donald Trump’s use of personal insults and ridicule against opponents.

It’s lonely at the top for India’s female politicians

India has an illustrious history of women occupying top leadership positions, long before many other democracies. But their rise has often come at a cost – that of loneliness in navigating a male-dominated political world.

In the book, Gandhi describes a 2012 conversation with Hillary Clinton on the countrys’ female leaders and their backgrounds. In her recollections of Indira, she shares that, despite wielding authority, Indira could feel besieged and profoundly alone, and this was particularly acute, Gandhi writes, in the months leading up to the declaration of the Emergency by her mother-in-law.

Gandhi also writes of her own isolation, including when she decided to take on the leadership of the Congress out of a sense of duty to her family’s political legacy.

Those in power are increasingly stonewalling the press

Among the many ways in which Gandhi charts the erosion of India’s democratic conventions in Belonging, one particularly telling shift is the changed relationship between the media and those in power. She recalls a time when journalists had opportunities to question prime ministers directly.

In 12 years in power, Modi has not addressed a single press conference on his own. He has sat in on one press briefing at the conclusion of an election campaign, and appeared alongside US presidents at joint press encounters after bilateral meetings, where they took questions from the press. Modi has consistently avoided facing journalists in an open forum, and his media interactions have largely been one-on-one interviews with sympathetic, pro-government news anchors or in one much publicised exchange with a Bollywood actor who asked him how he liked to eat mangoes.

The book’s publication has brought renewed attention to concerns about the space for free expression in contemporary India, and the extent to which apprehensions about repercussions may influence what can be said, written and published.

Penguin Random House India was to publish Gandhi’s memoir but withdrew from the project in August. Gandhi told the Guardian that it was “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and said it had dropped the book after she declined certain suggested edits. Penguin has disputed her account, saying that the suggestion it decided not to publish the book because of refused editorial changes “does not accurately reflect the circumstances”.

The book, released in the US by Alfred A Knopf, is being published in India by HarperCollins.

In June, Penguin had also pulled out of plans to distribute graphic journalist Joe Sacco’s The Once and Future Riot, about the 2013 Muzaffarnagar communal violence. The publisher cited an inaccurate map of India and unresolved citation issues. Sacco, however, blamed the decision on the “current political climate in India”.

She’s had quiet fallouts with the ‘thoroughly dishonest’

Western political memoirs, particularly by former heads of government or senior politicians, are often forthcoming in naming political adversaries, recounting private exchanges and offering candid assessments of colleagues. David Cameron’s 2019 memoir, For the Record, took aim at his former friend, Michael Gove, describing him as “mendacious” and a “foam-flecked Faragist”.

Niha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern India

Gandhi, in contrast, is restrained. She writes warmly of the closeness between the Gandhi family and that of Bollywood superstar Amitabh Bachchan, whose parents she lived with when she first moved to India, but she makes no mention of the subsequent estrangement between the two families. In another instance, she does not name the political leader she describes as “thoroughly dishonest” and who she says she trusted in 1999, when Congress unsuccessfully attempted to form a coalition government.

Art | Art Mumbai runs from 12-15 November at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse. Among the highlights of this year’s edition is artist Baaraan Ijlal’s collaboration with the celebrated lyricist Javed Akhtar, turning his evocative Urdu couplets into paintings. The two will be in conversation with curator Ranjit Hoskote on Friday.

Government | The official bungalow of Andhra Pradesh’s chief minister, N Chandrababu Naidu, was renovated by a government-owned enterprise for Rs 6.5 crore (£518,000), according to the Indian Express (£). The renovation work on the Delhi property included was said to have had a major makeover.

Film | Bollywood’s ambitious rendering of Hindu epic Ramayana, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Sai Pallavi, was released on 5 November. Touted as the most expensive Indian film ever made, it earned praise from the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw, who described it as “thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular”.

It’s hard to take one’s eyes off Muhammed Riswan when he’s at work. The 23-year-old football freestyler from Areekode in Kerala’s Malappuram district conjures tricks with the ball in a delicately choreographed dance. It glides between his feet, next it is rolling on to his back right before he leaps into the air to catch it with one hand.

#125. Jordan Sentences 3 to Death Over Greek Orthodox Church Attack

The Jordanian military said that the men, who were arrested after a shooting at a Greek Orthodox church last month, had been convicted of terrorism charges.

A military-run court in Jordan sentenced three men to death on Sunday after they were convicted in connection with an attack at a church last month that killed nine people, the Jordanian Armed Forces said in a statement.

The shooting at a Greek Orthodox church, which also wounded about three dozen people, was one of the deadliest militant attacks in the country in years, and King Abdullah II vowed that it would be met with “the harshest retaliation.”

The three men were sentenced after being convicted of violating antiterrorism laws, according to the Jordanian military. They were found guilty of carrying out deadly terrorist acts, possessing weapons and ammunition with the intent to commit terrorism, and promoting the ideas of a terrorist group.

That group was not named in the armed forces statement.

The sentences are subject to appeal, the military statement noted.

The three men were arrested in late October in Jordan after a shootout with security forces during a predawn raid on their hide-out in an abandoned house in the southern province of Karak, where the church attack took place. Karak is home to a sizable Christian community.

King Abdullah praised the arrests on social media. “No proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” he wrote.

Jordanian officials have not said what motivated the shooting at the church. Shortly afterward, Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said it was “the result of terrorist takfiri ideology,” using an Arabic phrase that often describes Islamist extremists who declare other Muslims heretics.

The sentencing on Sunday came a weeks after Jordan retaliated for the church attack with deadly airstrikes on Islamic State targets in southern Syria, a Jordanian government spokesman said at the time. The Jordanian military said it had been “targeting hide-outs of terrorist organizations,” without naming any specific group.

The airstrikes in Syria killed at least seven civilians, including three children, according to the Syrian civil defense rescue service, and the attack was condemned by Syrian officials.

Muslims make up more than 97 percent of the population in Jordan, and Christians make up about 2 percent, according to United States government estimates. The country’s Constitution declares Islam the state religion but safeguards the free exercise of religion and bars discrimination on religious grounds. Christian Jordanians are guaranteed seats in Parliament and have long served as cabinet ministers and ambassadors.

The Christian presence in Karak dates back more than 1,500 years, and there are multiple churches there to this day. Jordan also has important biblical and Christian pilgrimage sites, including one along the Jordan River where Jesus was said to have been baptized.

In June, Jordan hanged six men convicted of terrorism-related or drug-trafficking charges. The executions came after a nine-year hiatus in executions and were condemned by the European Union and human rights groups, including the Death Penalty Information Center and Human Rights Watch.

Ephrat Livni is a Times reporter covering news around the world. She is based in New York.
