#121. Disgraced former leader Sheikh Hasina plans return to Bangladesh from exile

Former prime minister faces death penalty upon return after being sentenced in absentia over deaths in 2024 uprising

Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party, after the disgraced former prime minister applied for a new passport this week.

Hasina has been living in self-imposed exile since August 2024 when she was toppled from power by a mass uprising against her authoritarian rule. She crossed the border to India, where she has since been allowed to live freely in Delhi.

Last November, a tribunal in Bangladesh found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity and sentenced her to death over her crackdown on a student uprising that left an estimated 1,400 people dead.

Her return to Bangladesh is likely to be disruptive for the country where Hasina’s party, Awami League, is still banned and thousands of its members are in jail. Should she be allowed to return, she is likely to be arrested immediately.

Hasina first raised the prospect of going back to Bangladesh in August. Speaking to the Guardian this week, several exiled Awami League leaders also living in India confirmed that Hasina was serious and “confident” about returning by next month. They confirmed that several other party figures had already returned in anticipation.

On Monday, a British lawyer acting on behalf of Hasina wrote to the Bangladesh high commission in Delhi requesting a new passport and national identity card to be issued “in a timely fashion”, in a letter seen by the Guardian.

“The reason our leader Sheikh Hasina has applied for a passport is that she genuinely wants to return,” said a party leader based in the Indian city of Kolkata, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he is not authorised to speak to the media on the party’s behalf.

Hasina has rejected the charges against her and claimed the tribunal that convicted her was illegitimate. “She is confident about her return, which is why she has applied for a new passport and a national identity card. If the authorities do not issue her a passport, she will apply for a travel pass to make her return to Bangladesh possible,” said the Awami League leader.

Since Hasina’s conviction, the Bangladesh government has put pressure on the Indian authorities to extradite the former prime minister. However, the Indian government, which was close to Hasina while she was in power, has ignored the demands, straining ties between the two countries.

This week, the Bangladesh government said that, as a “terrorist”, Hasina would only be allowed to return via an “acceptable prisoner exchange” under the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty.

Aminul Islam, the chief prosecutor of the tribunal that sentenced Hasina, said there was “no legal scope” for her to be issued a new passport as she was a “convicted fugitive”.

Islam emphasised that Hasina would be hanged if she returned, as the deadline for her to appeal against her conviction had passed. “Sheikh Hasina has no option but to face the execution of the verdict,” he said.

Despite the abuses and oppression that mired her 15 years in power and subsequent conviction for crimes against humanity, Hasina still commands significant popularity among the thousands of Awami League cadre still in Bangladesh, many of whom have been driven underground.

Some senior party figures have returned in recent months, including the former MP Mustaque Ahmed Ruhi. He was immediately arrested on his return in September and faces prosecution over an alleged murder during the 2024 uprising.

Exiled Awami League leaders have continued to meet in Kolkata, where many of them are living, and are routinely summoned to Delhi to meet Hasina.

Speaking over email this week, Hasina told the Associated Press: “If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people.”

#115. World’s top court to rule if Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya

International court of justice has never before found a state guilty of genocide, and ruling will have implications for case against Israel

The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this week on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, in a landmark case that will set a critical 21st-century benchmark for the gravest of all international crimes.

The closely watched judgment could become one of the most significant moments in international law since the end of the second world war.

The international court of justice (ICJ) has never found a state responsible for genocide, a crime defined after the Nazi-led Holocaust. The ruling will have implications for a separate high-profile genocide case against Israel.

Nearly a decade after a military campaign forced hundreds of thousands of Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border, the ICJ in The Hague will deliver its judgment on Thursday morning.

“The ICJ ruling will be historic for Rohingya survivors and their families around the world,” said Yanghee Lee, a former UN rights investigator to Myanmar.

“The international community failed to prevent Myanmar military atrocities against the Rohingya nine years ago. It must seize this opportunity to finally secure justice for the Rohingya and begin to reckon with these failings.”

ICJ judges have spent seven years weighing accusations by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, that Myanmar’s repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN genocide convention.

A key issue in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Antonia Mulvey, the founder of Legal Action Worldwide (Law), a group that represents hundreds of Rohingya survivors, said she was “cautiously optimistic” the court would hold Myanmar fully accountable.

Government actions showed “patterns of conduct” that proved clear attempts to destroy the group, she said.

“The attacks on the villages took place the same way,” she said. “They would attack the civilians, burn the villages, separate men and women, conduct sexual violence … and then as they fled, they would continue to kill them.”

Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the Balkans fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent the genocide at Srebrenica.

Mulvey said a key part of the upcoming judgment will be how it handles the issue of rape and sexual violence as an act of genocide. Her team has collected accounts of soldiers mutilating women’s genitals and biting their faces. “That’s to mark people, to brand them … it is also to stop reproduction,” she said.

“Yes, we would say sexual violence is a critical part to show their intent to destroy the group,” she added.

“You don’t need to gang-rape people. You don’t need to kill their children in front of them. You don’t need to mutilate them. You don’t need to do it in public. What is the purpose of that? The purpose is to destroy the group.”

In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear directly from Rohingya survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. One witness said her child was taken from her arms, stabbed and thrown into a fire, according to Law, while another described seeing piles of bodies in a mass grave.

During hearings, Gambian justice minister Dawda Jallow told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”.

“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”

Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents.

For decades, Rohingya people have been stripped of their citizenship and targeted by increasing discrimination, amid a backdrop of communal violence with Buddhists in the country’s western Rakhine state.

The crisis reached a climax after a Rohingya militant group conducted guerrilla-style attacks in the summer of 2017. The Myanmar army responded with massive “clearance operations”.

Refugees who fled into Bangladesh in 2017 told the Guardian of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, including the drowning of children in a river.

This testimony from Tula Toli – which satellite footage later showed had been razed – added to dozens of witness accounts collected over the years to build a case for genocide.

A ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would add international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-2017 attacks and later overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead.

The former general is separately b​eing investigated by the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals and not states like the ICJ, on allegations of crimes against humanity. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely condemned as a sham, and has made efforts to rebuild diplomatic ties.

For many onlookers, the ICJ decision will hold relevance far beyond Myanmar, as it will provide the strongest hint of how judges might assess the seminal genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its campaign in Gaza.

The cases have much in common, with an ethnic group targeted by a powerful military, although Israel has far stronger diplomatic backing from the US.

The judgment comes as Washington has been on the offensive against international human rights bodies, including sanctioning the ICC. Washington technically already considers the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration.

However, Trump’s UN ambassador, Mike Waltz, warned that the ICJ “must not be allowed” to establish a standard for genocide that could be used against “allied soldiers”, a statement that will be relevant for Israeli troops.

Supporters of the Myanmar case say the judgment should compel states to block arms transfers and jet fuel supplies. While the court does not have the means to enforce its decisions, they have been respected in the past, and the UN security council could give it strength, although divisions, especially between the US and China, make this unlikely.

More than 1 million Rohingya remain in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement. Fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Myanmar.

A displaced Rohingya living inside Myanmar told the Guardian he hoped the judgment would “help end decades of persecution and discrimination”.

“We are not asking for sympathy alone,” he said. “We are asking for justice, recognition, equal rights and a future in which our children can live safely and with dignity in their own homeland.”

#112. ‘I saw a picture of a two-year-old girl buried in mud. I knew we had to do something’ – This is climate breakdown

When the floods hit Pakistan he went out to help. Then the water reached his own family. This is Imran Lodhi’s story

Please enable Javascript to fully experience this interactive article.

Disaster: Pakistan intense monsoon rainfall

Imran Lodhi is a university lecturer with a doctorate in climate change and sustainable development. The 41-year-old was living in Dera Ghazi Khan, a city in south-western Punjab, when floods devastated provinces across Pakistan. Climate change made the monsoon rainfall that caused the floods more intense.

In 2022, I was living in an area that had less risk of flooding. I had a small child and my PhD thesis was just a few weeks away. I tried to avoid flood news on social media until I saw a picture of a two-year-old girl who was buried in mud. It was probably her last breath. She died after that. That was the turning point.

I immediately called my friends, six to seven people, in a mosque. I talked to them: “We don’t know what to do, but at least we can start from somewhere.” Initially, it was food. We hired some commercial cooks.

We planned to work only in villages close to our city. A lot of people were taking refuge in nearby high places, high enough that the water did not reach them. On the first day we went with some food to the nearest village.

When the rain is over, the sun comes out. Usually, it’s a good sign. But, in those areas, it didn’t feel good. It felt like it opened a scar. The pain that was hiding somehow had become open. It was like being naked. I could see trolleys, tractors, vehicles and homes all drowned in the flood. There was nothing from the government, nothing from any development sector. There was no camp. People were just living under open skies.

Men felt that their women being in an open place was a kind of emotional damage for them. It was not normal for most of the people here. Many women never came out. They came out for their work, the agriculture work, but not sitting that openly among the public. Their hair was full of dust and dry mud. Their clothes had a heavy layer of dry mud; no shoes on their feet. Mothers were not breastfeeding. Babies crying for milk, and the milk was not there. Mothers trying to soothe them with fake sounds.

The cows did not have feed and were not giving milk. Many of the animals were lost, their bodies wide open, decomposed. Then the water, which stayed there for a week, started to smell very bad. There was no good smell.

We prepared food in the morning. Then we prepared food at lunchtime. We generally finished distributing food around 8pm. One night it was 11pm and we thought some people might not have food. So we just cooked some food late at night and went to every camp.

One old woman started to laugh. I was surprised. I asked her: “It’s OK, we have food, but why are you laughing?” And she said: “I was just complaining, ‘Lord, that you left me with an empty stomach today.’ And suddenly you appeared.”

It was a very strange experience for her. For us also. People, when they are in tough conditions, are attached to their beliefs. And, when things like that come up, they establish a spiritual connection with the people who are helping out.

We posted on social media. We tried to mobilise. A lot of people contacted us who were from other parts of Pakistan. Money poured in and we kept expanding the team. From two or three villages, we started to cover the entire district, and then almost the entire region.

The government protocols were to not go into certain areas that looked dangerous or were not safe for a boat. Families were trapped, many, many kilometres into the water. There was no land in one village. Small wooden cupboards were hung on trees so stuff could be saved from the water. The immediate shelter was a big tree near them. The whole family was in the tree. The elders were lying on the branches. They somehow made a swing for the kids. They spent days in those trees.

A few villages were completely destroyed. Not a single home was standing. Everything was in shock, even the trees. One old woman who was living with her married kids was not ready to leave that rubble. She was so attached to that home that she felt like there was no life after it. She had a small cupboard in which she kept some small things to sell, for her independence. She was so concerned about that small cupboard. When I reached there, that cupboard was all broken.

One day I had a fever and my wife stopped me: “Don’t go out – you are not well enough to help other people.” But I still went out to a village to help people. When we reached there, I got news that the city we were living in – which I thought was safe – suddenly was a source of threat. There was water coming toward the city. Within hours, the water would be in the city. My family was there. And I was almost 100km away.

So I rushed back. But the road toward the city was cut off by the flood. There was no way I could go back to my family. I called my wife and I asked them to stay vigilant and look out for water in the city. I gave them some suggestions: how they could save themselves and evacuate. That was a very, very tough call.

Eventually, the city was saved. Next day, we took a boat to get past the road that was cut off. Sitting in that boat, I was thinking about my family. Once I reached the other side, I called some people to take me home.

When I reached home, I had a very strong fever and I spent that day at home. I tried to behave normally, but everybody knew I was not feeling well. I took one day off from community work.

The next day I wanted to stop. But the problem was, I was in the middle of that network. If I stop, this whole process will stop. This whole network of relief work will stop.

The next day, even with a high fever, I left for the field because I didn’t want that to stop. When I grew up, the community fabric was very strong. It was common practice that whenever people got sick, got in an accident, hospitalised, people would visit the person and share some money.

This was the kind of culture I observed happening around me.

I went back to those areas where the flood came. There was still some water standing so there were remains of that devastation. But there’s a very common sweet in that area we call jalebi. I can smell that sweet in those villages. I see shops open. I see farmers, labourers. I felt good watching people working again. It looked like life was coming back.

There was an annual poetry event happening three months after the flood. Saraiki culture is very rich, one of the oldest. I was consulted by one of my friends who is the organiser of that event. Should we suspend this year’s events or not?

I said you should never suspend the event. Let people believe the normalisation, let people believe in the spirit of survival. They organised the poetry event.

This is climate breakdown was put together in collaboration with the Climate Disaster Project at the University of Victoria, Canada. Read more.

#111. American Global Health Aid Isn’t Dead. It’s Changing.

The Trump administration promised to make aid programs more “America First.” Some countries are balking.

Americans might have assumed that their country was out of the business of promoting global health. On his first day in office, President Trump announced the United States’ withdrawal from the World Health Organization and abruptly “paused” foreign aid. Over the following weeks, Elon Musk took a chain saw to the U.S. Agency for International Development.

In the wake of these actions, reporters documented shortages of tuberculosis, malaria and H.I.V. drugs, widespread clinic closures and the abandonment of patients enrolled in medical trials. Many programs never resumed, and researchers predicted that hundreds of thousands of avoidable deaths would occur in the first year alone. Assessing whether this came true is complicated by the fact that programs tracking health outcomes were among those the U.S. ended.

Congress had originally allocated about $10 billion to the government’s main global health programs, or roughly $30 per U.S. resident, to run one of the world’s most effective foreign aid efforts. But even after the wave of staff terminations and grant cancellations, Congress still wanted that money to be spent. To direct the funds, last September, the U.S. State Department released a new plan: the America First Global Health Strategy.

This plan endorsed some goals that experts have long championed regardless of political fealty, such as having recipient countries take more responsibility for running and funding the programs.

But it also had a distinctly Trumpian element that seemed shocking to observers of the foreign aid world: The money had significant — and unusual — strings attached. Countries that receive aid were invited to negotiate “America First” agreements with the United States “that promote our national interests while saving millions of lives,” according to a letter from Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

#109. The four astronauts NASA picked for the first crewed moon mission in 50 years

Sign up for CNN’s Wonder Theory science newsletter. Explore the universe with news on fascinating discoveries, scientific advancements and more.

Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.

The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.

Wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009. A native of Baltimore, Maryland, he’s completed one prior spaceflight, a 165-day trip to the International Space Station that had launched aboard a Russian Soyuz rocket in 2014. Most recently, Wiseman served as chief of the astronaut office before stepping down in November 2022, making him eligible for a flight assignment.

Wiseman will serve as commander of the Artemis II mission.

Hansen, 47, is a fighter pilot who was selected by the Canadian Space Agency for astronaut training in 2009. From London, Ontario, Hansen is one of only four active Canadian astronauts, and he recently became the first Canadian to be put in charge of training for a new class of NASA astronauts.

He will be the first Canadian ever to travel to deep space.

Glover is a 46-year-old naval aviator who returned to Earth from his first spaceflight in 2021 after piloting the second crewed flight of SpaceX’s Crew Dragon spacecraft and spending nearly six months aboard the International Space Station.

“It’s so much more than the four names that have been announced,” Glover said during the Monday announcement at NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston. “We need to celebrate this moment in human history. … It is the next step in the journey that will get humanity to Mars.”

Glover, born in Pomona, California, served in several military squadrons in the United States and Japan in the 2000s, and he completed test pilot training with the US Air Force. When he was selected for the NASA astronaut corps in 2013, he was working in the US Senate as a legislative fellow. All told, Glover logged 3,000 flight hours in more than 40 aircraft, over 400 carrier arrested landings and 24 combat missions.

Glover’s first mission to space was as part of the SpaceX Crew-1 team, which launched to the International Space Station in November 2020 for a six-month stay on the orbiting laboratory.

Koch, 44, is a veteran of six spacewalks — including the first all-female spacewalk in 2019. She holds the record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman, with a total of 328 days in space. Koch is also an an electrical engineer who helped develop scientific instruments for multiple NASA mission. Koch, a native of Grand Rapids, Michigan, also spent a year at the South Pole, an arduous stay that could well prepare her for the intensity of a moon mission.

The Artemis II mission will build on Artemis I, an uncrewed test mission that sent NASA’s Orion capsule on a 1.4 million-mile voyage to lap the moon that concluded in December. The space agency deemed that mission a success and is still working to review all the data collected.

If all goes to plan, Artemis II will take off around November 2024. The crew members, strapped inside the Orion spacecraft, will launch atop a NASA-developed Space Launch System rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

The journey is expected to last about 10 days and will send the crew out beyond the moon, potentially further than any human has traveled in history, though the exact distance is yet to be determined.

The “exact distance beyond the Moon will depend on the day of liftoff and the relative distance of the Moon from the Earth at the time of the mission,” NASA spokesperson Kathryn Hambleton said via email.

After circling the moon, the spacecraft will return to Earth for a splashdown landing in the Pacific Ocean.

Artemis II is expected to pave the way for the Artemis III mission later this decade, which NASA has vowed will put the first woman and person of color on the lunar surface. It will also mark the first time humans have touched down on the moon since the Apollo program ended in 1972.

The Artemis III mission is expected to take off later this decade. But much of the technology the mission will require, including spacesuits for walking on the moon and a lunar lander to ferry the astronauts to the moon’s surface, is still in development.

NASA is targeting a 2025 launch date for Artemis III, though the space agency’s inspector general has already said delays will likely push the mission to 2026 or later.

The space agency has been seeking to return people to the moon for more than a decade. The Artemis program was designed to pave the way to establishing a permanent lunar outpost, allowing astronauts to live and work deeper into space long term as NASA and its partners map a path to sending the first humans to Mars.

Vanessa Wyche, the director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, declined to provide details to CNN about the selection process. But she emphasized the diversity of the Artemis II crew, which includes men and women rather than only a staff of White male test pilots as has been the case for historic missions of the past.

“I can tell you, they still all have the right stuff,” Wyche said. “We have requirements different than we did (when we) just had test pilots” on inaugural missions.

Koch said in an interview with CNN’s Ed Lavandera that the group found out they were selected a few weeks ago.

“We were all sent to a meeting that was on our calendars under a different pretext that didn’t sound as lofty as the one it was going to be,” Koch said. “And accidentally two of us were very late to that meeting.”

She said the offer rendered her “speechless.”

“It truly is an honor,” she added. “It’s an honor — not to get myself in the space — but because it’s amazing to be a part of this team that’s going back to the moon and on to Mars.”

An interview with the four astronauts will air on “CNN This Morning” on Tuesday, which starts at 6 am ET.

CNN’s Kristin Fisher contributed to this story.

#106. Iran launches drone attacks against US military base in Bahrain

Strikes cast further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington with increasing risk of escalation

Iran has launched drone attacks against a US military base in Bahrain, casting further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington and raising the spectre of escalation.

Blasts sounded over the Gulf nation on Sunday in the second Iranian drone attack in three days in retaliation for US strikes in Iran.

Meanwhile, in Yemen, Iran’s Houthi allies advanced against pro-government forces in the south, opening a potential route to Aden. Iran also claimed that a mine sank an oil supertanker in the strait of Hormuz.

The developments deepened gloom about the chances of any diplomatic breakthrough in the region.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said they launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in retaliation for “hostile US actions”. Authorities in Bahrain said air defences intercepted the drones before they reached their targets.

At a press conference in Tehran the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Iran would continue to respond to any military aggression by the US or other states. Asked if the latest strikes indicated a change in Iranian direction as negotiations with the US have stalled, he said Iran was “not waiting for anyone” and was focused on its security.

US forces have conducted a series of strikes against Iranian targets in recent weeks, including Qeshm Island in the strait of Hormuz.

Donald Trump last week called them minor strikes and said Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states had cautioned him against large-scale combat operations.

However, the president also said Washington was no longer seeking a deal with Iran and that he had instructed the vice-president, JD Vance, to switch his focus to alleged corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.

Vance – who blamed the Republicans’ loss of Congress in midterm elections on the Iran war – had requested a personal meeting with Iranian negotiators to discuss peace terms.

A conflict that began with joint US and Israeli attacks against Iran in February remains at an impasse, with the US maintaining a naval blockade and Iran its chokehold over the strait of Hormuz.

In a separate development, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed that two ships hit mines in the strait of Hormuz and that one, an oil supertanker with 2m barrels of oil, sank. The ships suffered “massive explosions and fire”, said the statement.

There was no immediate independent verification. The US military recently claimed it had cleared all mines from main routes through the waterway.

The strikes against Bahrain suggested Iran has decided on a tit-for-tat response to US attacks.

Bahrain hosts significant US bases, including a forward base that was home to the US Fifth Fleet and US Naval Forces Central Command, operating as a central support hub for military operations in the Middle East.

Tehran repeatedly targeted the kingdom until September, when there was a lull in attacks. That ended on Friday when Iran launched drones against a US radar facility. US Central Command said it shot down two drones without any injury or damage.

The attacks on Sunday prompted sirens and alerts from Bahrain’s authorities urging residents to seek shelter.

“It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them,” resident Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told Agence France Presse.

Bahrain’s foreign ministry called the resumption of attacks “heinous aggression” and a flagrant violation of international law.

The kingdom rejected Tehran’s “flimsy pretexts and baseless claims” to target its territory, it said in a statement. “The kingdom also rejects the transformation of its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks and their consequences.”

Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar condemned the attacks and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.

In Yemen, Saudi Arabia’s campaign against the Iranian-aligned Houthi rebels reeled when forces fighting on behalf of the Yemeni government retreated from the Bab el-Mandeb strait to defend ⁠Aden on the southern ​coast.

“The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of ‌a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate,” the main military force fighting for Yemen’s government in the south said in a statement.

The admission signalled the apparent failure of a six-week government counteroffensive to drive the Houthis from the mouth of the Red Sea to secure a key oil route.

A Houthi missile strike near Aden killed people and wounded 12 near Aden, AFP reported, citing military and government sources.

#105. American Roosters Fight in the Philippines Despite U.S. Crackdown

It’s illegal in the United States to transport game fowl for fighting. But investigators say breeders are sending birds to the Philippines, where cockfighting is legal and lucrative.

It’s illegal in the United States to transport game fowl for fighting. But investigators say breeders are sending birds to the Philippines, where cockfighting is legal and lucrative.

Men preparing roosters for a cockfight at an arena in Talisay, Philippines, in July.Credit...Ezra Acayan for The New York Times

Francesca Regalado reported from Bacolod City in the Philippines.

Jerry Jalandoni navigated hundreds of chickens running loose on his farm in the Philippines before stopping at a row of tall cages that held his latest acquisitions: a dozen cockfighting roosters from the United States.

On top of one cage was a cardboard box, poked with holes that had allowed a hen to breathe during her solitary journey from Texas to Bacolod City. “She’s been through a lot,” Mr. Jalandoni said.

The hen arrived alone, he said, because her mate had been held back by exporters wary of attracting the attention of animal rights groups. Such birds come from game fowl breeds developed in the United States that are renowned internationally for their sturdiness and aggression — qualities valued in cockfighting, a legal and highly profitable industry in the Philippines.

Those birds were not supposed to be on Mr. Jalandoni’s farm, according to U.S. federal laws. But they are part of a trade in which breeders in the United States send fighting roosters to the Philippines.

While the trade has long been an open secret, the channels through which American fighting birds arrive in Asia are drawing fresh scrutiny from U.S. officials.

Cockfighting — the practice of tying metal blades, or gaffs, to the legs of roosters that fight each other to the death — has been illegal in the United States since 2008, when Louisiana became the last state to outlaw it. Transporting animals across state lines or out of the country for the purpose of fighting was banned in 1976.

#104. Revealed: Israel uploaded millions of photos to Amazon’s facial recognition platform to track Palestinians

Upload came as the Israeli military was increasing its reliance on Amazon’s cloud platform to meet the technological demands of its bombardment of Gaza

The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal.

Leaked documents show the expansive catalogue of images was moved into Amazon’s cloud in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza.

The images were uploaded by a department of the Israeli military that holds a vast collection of photos covering the Palestinian populations in Gaza and the West Bank.

The department informed Amazon of the decision to upload the images in early 2024 so it could use Rekognition, the company’s AI-powered image analysis platform for a facial recognition project.

The documents obtained by the Guardian form part of an investigation into the Israeli military’s reliance on the technology and infrastructure of Amazon’s cloud computing business to monitor Palestinians.

According to the files and interviews with military sources, Israel has in recent years migrated huge volumes of data – including sensitive intelligence material and information about Palestinians living under occupation – into Amazon’s datacentres.

The large set of images was moved into an Amazon datacentre near Tel Aviv by a department commonly known as Rolling Stone, which sits within a military software unit.

The department takes its name from a system widely used by the Israeli military that serves as a central repository of information about Palestinians living in Gaza and the West Bank.

At the time, the department was exploring using facial recognition technologies to analyse the extensive catalogues of images of Palestinians it holds, several sources with knowledge of its work said.

After Israel’s ground invasion of Gaza in October 2023, its military routinely collected images of Palestinians as they passed through checkpoints, often after they had been forcibly displaced by the bombing campaign.

It’s not clear whether the 3.5m images uploaded to Amazon’s Rekognition were captured at these checkpoints, which effectively served as pop-up surveillance posts.

However, a military source familiar with facial recognition efforts at the checkpoints said Amazon’s cloud infrastructure was used due to the “very large scale” of images collected at the sites.

Israel has long used facial recognition technology, particularly in its occupation of the West Bank. Face scanning is routine at checkpoints, while Israeli soldiers use custom-built smartphone apps to collect images of people living in the Palestinian territory.

In the early stages of its campaign in Gaza, Israel used Rekognition to identify hostages captured by militants in the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023. The military also deployed facial recognition technology to identify people it suspected were militants.

The New York Times has previously reported how the military experimented with commercially available technology in Gaza to detect faces in crowds and in drone footage, at times wrongly flagging civilians as militants.

The new documents reveal the Israeli military’s use of Amazon technology, both for experiments with facial recognition and for a more far-reaching project to move its data on to the servers of the computing arm of the conglomerate founded by billionaire Jeff Bezos.

They also shed light on what the Israeli military is moving into the cloud and how it uses Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure to support the collection and processing of Palestinians’ personal data, typically gathered indiscriminately, through intrusive means and without their consent.

The files suggest the ties between AWS and the Israeli military deepened during a period in which Israel has been accused of committing grave crimes in Gaza, including genocide – a charge denied by Israel, but supported by a UN commission of inquiry, Israeli human rights groups and genocide experts.

In early 2024, a small group of Israeli soldiers worked from AWS’s offices in Tel Aviv, located on the 28th floor of one of Israel’s tallest skyscrapers.

The soldiers were exploring ways to use the company’s cloud infrastructure to more effectively operate a facial recognition programme underway in Gaza, several military sources said.

It’s not clear whether their work was made operational or if it related to the 3.5m images uploaded to Rekognition. The presence of the group at AWS’s offices, however, underscores the close relationship between the Israeli military and the cloud provider.

An AWS spokesperson said its customers “regularly visit our offices for briefings and meetings”. They added: “Any suggestion that these visits are anything other than routine customer engagement is wrong and unsubstantiated.”

The foundation of Israel’s relationship with Amazon is a sweeping 2021 contract known as Project Nimbus. Under the multibillion dollar deal, AWS and Google provide cloud services to a wide range of government and military clients.

The Guardian revealed last year that the Nimbus contract contains unusual terms that prohibit the US companies from restricting or suspending Israeli government and military use of their cloud services, even if Israel breaches their terms of service.

This would prevent the kind of unilateral action taken by Microsoft last year when it disabled the Israeli military’s access to technology used to operate a mass surveillance system uncovered by the Guardian and +972 Magazine.

As part of the Nimbus deal, AWS opened new datacentres in Israel in early 2023, allowing the Israeli government and military clients to migrate data from their own servers, according to documents. A large proportion of data was also moved from AWS datacentres in Ireland.

A central component of the Nimbus contract, files show, was an obligation on AWS to provide the Israeli military with access to a segregated area within its Tel Aviv datacentres, fortified with enhanced digital and physical security measures.

This isolated area within the AWS cloud – used to store sensitive material relating to military operations and intelligence collection – was described by the company and its client as a “walled garden”.

The Israeli military’s reliance on AWS reflects its embrace in recent years of leading US tech companies to meet the technological demands of war with rapidly scalable storage, computing power and AI-driven services.

The role of AI in Israel’s offensive in Gaza has come under fresh scrutiny particularly after the release of NAZA, a Guardian-produced documentary about the remote surveillance and killing of Palestinian civilians.

The Rolling Stone department is among AWS’s most significant Israeli military clients, documents suggest. Its use of Rekognition in early 2024 to analyse 3.5m images came after it had expanded its use of AWS products and services to store and analyse its data.

Files show the department migrated significant volumes of the data it holds into the so-called “walled garden” in AWS’s cloud throughout 2023. A military source involved in this effort said it had planned to move all of its databases from the military servers into AWS’s cloud.

The source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said: “The plan [at Rolling Stone] was to migrate pictures, videos, all the confidential intelligence information – everything.”

A spokesperson for the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said it “does not intend to comment on engagements or services related to operational needs”.

The Rolling Stone department oversees several expansive databases that collate data on Palestinians, including the system from which the branch takes its name.

Used by the military for decades, the Rolling Stone system is constantly updated and includes data such as basic personal and family details, property holdings, and information on checkpoint crossings, work permits, and criminal activity.

A soldier who provided testimony to Breaking the Silence, an Israeli NGO, in 2016 described Rolling Stone as “a computerised system where all the information relevant to the control of the Palestinian civilian population is centralised”.

As a result of Israel’s control of the population registries covering Gaza and the West Bank, the Rolling Stone department has amassed millions of Palestinians’ photographs taken for the identity cards issued to every resident when they turn 16 years old.

Sources familiar with its work said the images were routinely used for facial recognition programmes. These include Blue Wolf, a smartphone app Israeli soldiers use in the West Bank to scan Palestinians’ faces and access information about them, including whether they’ve been flagged as suspects for arrest.

In Gaza, at temporary Israeli checkpoints established after the ground invasion, cameras trained on Palestinian people were used to capture their images as they approached the sites. Facial recognition was then used to match people to images held in Rolling Stone’s systems, sources said.

The checkpoints became notorious in Gaza as places where people were pulled aside and detained. Many were taken into Israeli custody and held incommunicado, amounting to enforced disappearances, according to several UN bodies and rights groups.

Documents suggest AWS’s cloud technology was used at times during 2024 to support the work of the checkpoints. Military insiders said the checkpoints were referred to by Israeli soldiers as Nakaz – a Hebrew word for drainage.

#103. France's Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency

Philippe Diallo is the second candidate to stand against incumbent Gianni Infantino. He is backed by European football's governing body UEFA, known to be critical of Infantino.

French Football Federation (FFF) President Philippe Diallo has received UEFA backing to be a candidate in FIFA's presidential election, which will take place in March in Morocco, with criticism against current chief Gianni Infantino growing.

UEFA, European football's governing body, said it has backed Diallo "unanimously" in a bid to replace Infantino, putting it's "full support" behind the Frenchman.

Veteran Japanese official Kohzo Tashima has also announced his candidacy, with the deadline for candidates to stand for election being November 18.

Potential candidates for the post must show letters of support from five of FIFA's 211 member associations before going through eligibility and integrity checks.

Diallo, the 63-year-old head of the FFF, is the son of a Senegalese boxing champion.

He was appointed the federation's president in 2023 after being elected with a large majority. He was reelected for another four-year term in 2024.

Back in September, Diallo said the FFF had withdrawn its support for Infantino ahead of the March 2027 election, saying trust in the FIFA president had "been betrayed."

"The way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us," the French football head said of the decision.

If elected, the Frenchman would become FIFA's first black president, as well as it's third French leader after Robert Guerin and Jules Rimet, who served as the organization's first and third presidents.

Gianni Infantino has been in charge of world football's governing body since 2016.

He has been facing growing criticism since pitching a plan of sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors. The criticisms were led by UEFA and its President Aleksander Ceferin.

Infantino ended up scrapping the plan but UEFA went ahead and took FIFA to court in the US trying to gather evidence ahead of potentially lodging a criminal complaint with Swiss authorities about alleged "mismanagement" by Infantino.

FIFA's headquarters are located in Zürich, Switzerland.

Infantino was also criticized after creating a peace prize and awarding it to US President Donald Trump last year.

The connection between Infantino and Trump came under criticism once again during the World Cup, after United States forward Folarin Balogun was allowed to take part in the round of 16 game against Belgium despite being shown a red card in the previous game.

The US president admitted to having personally intervened through a conversation with Infantino.

#100. Saudi Arabia strategy challenged by anti-Houthi forces in Yemen

Accusations of incompetence follow retreat of Riyadh-backed forces in effort to relieve siege of Taiz and protect Aden

Saudi Arabia has been accused by anti-Houthi forces over its military strategy after its Yemeni allies withdrew troops from the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and pulled back forces from parts of Marib in the central part of the country.

The Saudi-backed government explained the repositioning by saying the strategic priority was to break the attritional siege on Taiz, Yemen’s third city, and to protect Aden, the southern port city in which the Saudi-backed and UN-recognised government is now based.

Many blame the Houthi advance on the absence of a consolidated military command and control among the disparate forces backing the Aden-based government. Saudi Arabia responded to the setback by sidelining the commander of its Yemen coalition, Lt Gen Fahd bin Abdulaziz al-Salman, and replacing him with the chief of staff, Gen Fayyad bin Hamed bin Ruqad al-Ruwaili.

The Houthis’ steady advance towards the areas surrounding Bab al-Mandab, the narrow strait linking the Red Sea with the Indian Ocean on Yemen’s west coast, culminated on Sunday with a formal withdrawal of Yemen government forces, including some in the Southern Giants Brigades that had always been reluctant to defend territory outside the old southern Yemen. In 1990 Yemen had been divided in two, and many in the south want to return to a separated state.

The Saudi-backed government launched a fresh military campaign 42 days ago to drive the Houthis from Yemen but so far it has backfired.

The forces redeployed on Sunday have moved along the coast to al-Suqyah, 95 miles west of Aden, and inside the old Southern Yemen.

The retreat seems to be acknowledgment of Houthi resilience and is all the more remarkable given the Saudi air superiority. More than 300,000 Yemeni civilians have been displaced.

Amr al-Bidh, special representative of the exiled Southern Transitional Council (STC) leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, a separatist anti-Houthi force that is opposed by Saudi Arabia, accused the Saudis of incompetence – and in effect warned Riyadh that unless it became more open to a southern state it would lack the cohesive forces required to prevent the Houthis becoming a permanent security threat.

He said: “When there is no strategy and no plan, it is inevitable the Houthis would take advantage. The STC will defend the south to the last man but we are fighting with one hand behind our backs since January after Saudi Arabia attacks on the STC.

“The STC forces retain a credible capability on the ground. But we need practical and political support from the region to counter the Houthis and create the basis for a negotiated settlement, one in which the pathway towards southern independence is fully recognised. We cannot continue like this or else the Houthis will keep expanding.”

The breadth of support for the STC, backed by the United Arab Emirates, however, remains disputed. The movement suffered a near fatal setback in January and since then some of the Giants Brigades have switched to backing Riyadh.

Saudi Arabia continues in effect to keep as many as 10 STC leaders hostage in Riyadh, and has refused to let al-Zubaidi to return from exile in Abu Dhabi. Al-Bidh argued the priority should be defensive, avoiding counteroffensives that backfire, improving command and control, and widening the coalition.

Al-Bidh said reconciliation would require Riyadh to acknowledge the political declaration al-Zubaidi made about a timetable for a southern state in January, and that al-Zubaidi’s return would boost morale and help unify chaotic southern military factions.

He said a recent Yemeni government cabinet reshuffle, including a new information minister, was designed primarily to try draw southerners into fighting the Houthis and not to change policy toward the south.

He also urged the UK to use its diplomacy to bring in other actors rather than simply backing Riyadh. A group of southern Yemenis have written to the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, seeking a review of UK policy. “We recognise that the longstanding advice from your office is to continue following the Saudi line while calling for unity among the anti-Houthi forces,” the letter said. “But you must surely recognise that every time Britain calls for ‘the unity and territorial integrity of Yemen’, it is asking the southern people and their armed forces to fight for a political outcome in which they do not believe”.

The former US special envoy to Yemen Tim Lenderking said the US administration was treating Yemen like a sideshow adding “world powers do not understand the gravity of what it is at stake here”. He warned “the problem is only going to get bigger through apathy and lack of attention”.

#97. The Death of ‘Keep 1.5 Alive’

Negotiators at COP31 are confronting a new reality as the world blows past a key warming target.

There was a reason, 11 years ago in Paris, that world leaders set themselves a target to keep the global rise in temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius compared with preindustrial levels. Beyond that, climate scientists say, warming will dangerously change our way of life.

We got a taste of it this year, as temperatures rose above the threshold for several months. Heat waves. Wildfires. Flash floods. And with a super El Niño year unfolding, next year might be worse. As one climate expert put it to me: This El Niño will effectively offer a time machine to the 2030s, showing what will happen if we don’t radically cut carbon emissions.

My colleague David Gelles, host of the Climate Forward newsletter, has been following the much diminished U.N. climate talks in Turkey. Today he writes about the death of 1.5 degrees and what that means for the planet.

It was the climate movement’s unifying slogan for the past decade: “Keep 1.5 Alive.”

The tagline referred to the central ambition of the 2015 Paris climate agreement, in which almost every country pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.

#96. Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

China thinks it's diplomatically isolating Taiwan. It isn't

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

What you need to know about China-Taiwan tensions

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

#95. Third US aircraft carrier brings thousands more troops to Middle East

The US president oscillates between strike threats on Iran and insisting the war ‘militarily is effectively over’

A third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, US Central Command said in a social media post on Monday, making a dramatic show of military might as Donald Trump keeps his options open for next steps in the Iran war.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt brings thousands of additional troops to the Middle East as Trump has oscillated between threatening additional large-scale strikes on Iran and insisting that the more than eight-month-old war “militarily is effectively over”.

The Roosevelt, along with its accompanying strike force, left San Diego in September. It joins the USS George HW Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller navy ships, which are in the region to maintain a naval blockade of Iranian shipping.

The George HW Bush arrived in the region in April, while the George Washington arrived in August. The navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April, for the first time since 2003.

In addition to the three aircraft carriers, the flotilla in the Arabian Sea now includes 13 destroyers, two cruisers and a littoral combat ship, according to the navy. Two more destroyers are in the Red Sea.

The Roosevelt had deployed along with the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships and around 2,000 marines. Those ships have yet to make it to the region.

The third carrier arrived nearly two weeks after midterm elections that saw voters deliver major losses to Trump’s Republican party, driven in part by the unpopularity of the Iran war and its economic effects. The results led JD Vance to publicly break with Trump over the conflict, posting on social media that “the reason we lost is the war”.

Trump has insisted it was the right thing to do and has not ruled out restarting the conflict, which has been locked in a stalemate for months.

Last week, Trump warned Iran that the US military is “locked and loaded” and that the US was keeping an eye on Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran’s nuclear program, for signs of activity.

“If something does not work out, I would not hesitate” to act, Trump told conservative broadcaster Hugh Hewitt on Thursday.

Yet, Trump also told reporters last week that he believed it was highly unlikely he would need to order new major strikes on Iran, declaring that the war “militarily is effectively over” after meeting with Qatar’s prime minister.

Trump also declared that the US no longer needs a deal with Tehran and told Vance – who was a chief negotiator in earlier ceasefire talks – instead to focus on the administration’s domestic anti-fraud campaign targeting Democratic-controlled cities and states.

Negotiations have stalled due to differences over Iran’s nuclear program, an issue that Trump insists be part of any deal meant to end the war. Iran wants the US first to agree to several core conditions, including lifting the naval blockade that is stopping its oil from getting to world markets.

In the meantime, a focal point of the simmering conflict remains the strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway where a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war.

Commercial ships are still coming under attack or facing other risks, while the US has carried out limited strikes on Iranian targets near the strait and is helping guide vessels through the contested waters.

Iranian state TV, quoting the naval arm of Iran’s revolutionary guard and the army, warned shipping companies Monday that a US-supported route through the waterway is dangerous because of mines.

Mines have damaged six oil tankers since Sunday, polluting the strait’s coastlines, according to the revolutionary guard’s navy.

Separately, a projectile struck a tanker trying to transit through the strait, starting an engine room fire, but no casualties were reported, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization said.

US Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, said it has redirected 150 merchant vessels and disabled five since June under the blockade.

Independent assessments from Lloyd’s List, a maritime tracking and analysis firm, show that traffic through the strait remains at less than a third of prewar levels.
